name: account-health
title: Account health
description: A customer success card where a health score gauge, a renewal countdown and five sourced signals with sparklines lead into an AI risk summary and one recommended next step, like scheduling a QBR before usage slips further.
whenToUse: A customer success or account page that needs a score, the signals behind it and a next step.
Renewal prep views where the countdown and risk drivers matter more than raw metrics.
Showing an AI written risk summary next to the evidence it was written from.
whenNotToUse: Portfolio views across many accounts; use a table with a score column instead.
Deep metric exploration with axes and ranges; use a full chart.
Single KPI tiles with no recommendation; use a stat card.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section; the gauge is one image with the score and band in its label.
Every status pairs an icon with a word (Good, Watch, At risk, Needs attention), never color alone.
Signal sources are named for screen readers; sparklines are decorative and hidden.
A polite live region reports the action result and says when it was simulated ("Simulated, no invite was sent").
The summary is aria-busy while it is written; the action row stays inert until it appears.
motion: On first view the gauge sweeps and the score counts up from one motion value (560ms ease-out), sparklines draw in with a 40ms stagger, and the term bar fills.
The summary thinks for about 0.9s with a shimmer on the label, then streams 3 to 6 words every 34ms, each chunk fading in over 140ms.
Switching the time range morphs each sparkline point to point and crossfades the trend line; no element changes size.
Reduced motion jumps to end states, shows the summary at once and keeps all feedback.

name: activity-feed
title: Activity feed
description: A team activity feed grouped by day on a quiet avatar timeline, with a type filter, a live new updates button, expandable details, and a mark all read sweep.
whenToUse: A workspace or project activity page for a team product.
A dashboard panel that shows what changed since someone last looked.
whenNotToUse: Use audit-log for compliance history that needs search, export, and exact timestamps.
Use notification-center for a personal inbox opened from a bell.
Use changelog-feed for public release notes.
accessibility: Each day is a labeled section with a heading; events are an ordered list.
Expandable events are buttons with aria-expanded and aria-controls.
Unread state is spoken as part of the event and shown with a dot and a stronger name, not color alone.
The type filter is a labeled group of toggle buttons with aria-pressed and arrow key navigation.
A polite status region announces new updates shown and how many were marked read.
motion: New events queue behind a button that opens its own row above the list, so no event is covered; showing them collapses that row and slides the new events in at the top.
Mark all read sends a hairline down the list; each row lets go of its dot exactly as the line passes it.
Changing the type filter crossfades the list, so rows never slide over each other.
Details open with a height spring; the one line preview gives way to the full detail.
Reduced motion removes the sweep delay and travel and keeps instant state changes.

name: activity-terrain
title: Activity terrain
description: A 3D terrain of hourly activity you can orbit, zoom, fly into and flatten into a heatmap.
whenToUse: Analytics or operations pages showing when a product is busiest across a week.
Showcase dashboards where a 3D view of a 7 by 24 grid adds impact, with a flat heatmap fallback.
whenNotToUse: Use activity-heatmap for a plain 2D grid that is easier to read.
Use bar-chart for totals by day or hour.
accessibility: The stage is a focusable group with a keyboard hint, and the canvas has a text summary as its label.
Peak hours are aria-pressed buttons that fly to or leave the hour.
A polite live region reads the highlighted hour's value.
motion: Columns rise in a wave on load and when the metric changes; camera moves use spring physics with momentum on drag.
Flattening to a heatmap springs the camera to a top view.
The engine watches prefers-reduced-motion and snaps the camera and heights with no wave.

name: agent-approvals
title: Agent approvals
description: One approval card for agents: the waiting tool call reads like a permission prompt with the tool's mark, the agent's reason and its arguments, and you approve, deny or allow it from now on.
whenToUse: Human in the loop control for agents that call tools with side effects: deploys, emails, database writes, payments and ticket changes.
An approvals card in an agent console or side panel where one person reviews, edits and decides tool calls quickly, from the keyboard if they like.
Products that let people turn repeated approvals into standing rules for one agent or a whole workspace.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run to follow one agent's steps and tool calls live, with an inline confirm inside the run.
Use mcp-servers to connect tools and set their permissions up front rather than per call.
Use agent-tasks or agent-orchestrator to plan and watch work across agents, not to gate individual tool calls.
Use code-review when the thing to approve is a diff with comments.
accessibility: The request in focus is a group named by its title, inside a region that takes focus after each decision, so the shortcuts keep working when the buttons that were pressed leave.
Shortcuts answer anywhere in the card, and after a click in it left focus on the page, but stay quiet in fields, the menu and the popover, so typing an edited value never approves anything.

Risk is a shield icon in its status color plus the word Low, Medium or High (with risk added for screen readers). Outcomes in the card and the log are an icon plus a word: Approved, Denied, Allowed by rule, Not sent.
Every decision, edit, new rule, removed rule and failure is announced in a polite status region, and the demo says that nothing reached a real agent.
Editable values are buttons named with their label, value and Edit; edited rows add a hidden "edited" to the label and a named Restore button.
Queue rows are buttons with the agent, the summary and the risk in their name. The Resolved toggle carries aria-expanded and aria-controls.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Bringing a queued request into focus is one crossfade of the request (the old one fades out in 100ms, the new one fades in over 200ms from 3px) while the card's height follows on a critically damped spring and the row closes its gap. Nothing bounces.
After a decision the next request slides up: it rises 14px into place on the same spring as its row collapses below.

Always allow sends a small rule chip from the menu up into the Rules button on an ease-in-out path, then the button's count rolls and a faint accent wash fades out of it. Covered rows swap their risk for Allowed by rule with one crossfade and collapse a moment later.
Sending shows a calm text shimmer that stops when the agent answers. The pending, rules and resolved counts roll with tabular numerals.
Reduced motion drops travel, the chip flight and the shimmer: requests, rows and labels change in place with every state, focus move and announcement kept.

name: agent-builder
title: Agent builder
description: A card for setting up an AI agent: an inline editable name, a model picker, instructions, tool toggles with real app marks, and knowledge files with upload progress. A Configure / Test switch opens a compact chat that answers with the tools you turned on, and Publish ships the setup with a saved or unsaved state.
whenToUse: Letting customers configure their own AI agent inside your product, like Intercom Fin, Zapier agents or an OpenAI GPT builder.
Internal admin screens where ops teams tune instructions, tools and knowledge for a support or billing agent.
A product tour or landing section that shows how an agent is set up and tested in one place.
whenNotToUse: Running or monitoring an agent in production: use agent-status or agent-routines.
Approving actions an agent wants to take: use agent-approvals.
A full chat product: use ai-chat. The Test view here is a compact preview, not a conversation app.
Only choosing a model: use model-picker.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section; the name field, instructions and every tool switch have labels, and the tool row text is part of the switch label so the whole row is clickable.
The model picker is a Radix menu with radio items, so the selected model is announced as checked.
Upload progress uses role="progressbar" with a value; failed uploads show an icon and the error message, never color alone.
Status changes (published, upload done or failed, reply ready) go to a polite live region, and simulated actions say so: "Simulated, nothing was deployed".
The inactive view is inert and aria-hidden, so screen readers and the Tab key only reach what is visible.
motion: Configure and Test crossfade in the same box (100ms out, 160ms in); Test overlays Configure, so the card never changes size.
Text swaps (model name, version, footer status, reply meta) are a single crossfade with a 2px rise. No blur or scramble.

Test replies: a short Thinking shimmer, tool chips that shimmer while running and reveal their result in place, then fast chunked streaming of three to six words every 34ms, each chunk only fading in.
Added and removed files animate their measured height with a bounce free spring; switches and the segmented control use the shared bounce free presets.
Reduced motion drops the rises, height animation and streaming (replies appear whole) but keeps every state and status change.

name: agent-gallery
title: Agent gallery
description: A marketplace card of AI agent templates where you filter by team, search by agent or app, preview a sample run and install an agent inline: choose a workspace, grant access app by app, and the card confirms with a check.
whenToUse: An agents or integrations page where people browse and install ready made AI agents.
Onboarding that suggests agent templates by team and installs one without leaving the page.
A marketplace teaser on a dashboard or settings page.
whenNotToUse: Configuring a single agent's prompt, tools or schedule: use a settings form or agent routines.
Showing a running agent's progress: use agent status or tool call.
Catalogs with hundreds of items that need pagination, sorting and facets: use a full page table or list.
accessibility: The root is a labelled section; chips are a radiogroup with a roving tab stop, and workspaces are a second radiogroup.

Each card is an article named after the agent. App marks are hidden from assistive tech and replaced by a sentence ("Connects to HubSpot, Slack and Gmail"); rating and installs are read as full words.
After every step change made by the person, focus moves to the new step's main control, so keyboard users never fall back to the page. A leaving step is inert.
A polite live region announces result counts, connect progress, errors and the installed result; without onInstall it adds "Simulated, nothing was connected".
Status is never color alone: connected apps show a check, errors show an icon with "Could not connect", installed cards show a check with "Installed".
motion: Filtering: removed cards fade out in 90ms and pop out of flow; remaining cards glide to their new cells on a critically damped spring (0.3s, no bounce), and the grid's height springs to the new row count.
The chip highlight slides between chips on a 0.24s spring with no bounce. Text never animates layout.
Card steps crossfade in place inside a fixed 176px card (out 100ms, in 160ms with 2px rise), so nothing changes size between states.
Granting access connects apps one by one (340ms apart): a spinner, then a check that scales in without overshoot. The install button keeps its width while loading.
Hover reveal of Preview and Install is a 160ms opacity and 2px rise. Touch screens show them permanently.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and feedback but drops travel, staggers and the layout glide.

name: agent-memory
title: Agent memory
description: One card for what an assistant remembers about you: filter and search memories, edit or forget one in place, and turn saved memories and chat history on or off.
whenToUse: Settings for an assistant that remembers people across chats, where people need to see, filter, search, correct and delete what it knows.
Showing the moment an assistant saves something from a chat, with a way to see where it was filed.
Any small personal knowledge store grouped by kind, where each entry is a sentence with a source and an undoable delete.
whenNotToUse: Use knowledge-base for documents and files an agent retrieves from, rather than short facts about the user.
Use context-window to show what fills a single conversation's token budget, rather than what persists across chats.
Use ai-chat for the conversation itself; this card only receives what the chat noted.
Use agent-routines for scheduled instructions the agent runs, not facts it recalls.
accessibility: The card has a level two heading; in the All view and in search results each group has a level three heading with its count, and every group is a labelled group of list items.
Switches are labelled by their visible titles and described by the line beneath; the meter is a meter role with a text value such as "62% full". Filter pills are toggle buttons with aria-pressed.

Status is never color alone: the pill reads Memory updated, then Saved to Preferences with a check; the meter's warning pairs color with an icon; the add field shows Added to People with a check or an error with an icon; a paused list carries a note with an icon.
Icon buttons name the memory they act on, such as "Forget memory: Prefers metric units and 24 hour times", and show a tooltip. Row actions stay visible on touch screens.

Focus follows each change: into the edit field, back to Edit after saving or cancelling, onto Undo after Forget, back to Forget after Undo, into the search field when it opens and back to the search button when it closes, and to the selected filter when an Undo button times out.

A polite status region announces captures, adds (including that the preview sorts with a keyword guess), saves, forgets with their undo window, restores, switch changes and the number of search matches.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring, and text fields show focus with their border.
motion: Capture and add: a copy of the new row lifts off the pill or the field and glides to the row's place in its group on the smooth spring (0.4s, no bounce), moving only by transform, while the row's slot opens beneath it. The row's own text takes over as it lands, under a soft tint that fades over about a second. If the memory's group is filtered out or a search is open, the filter switches or the search clears first, then the copy flies.

Filtering opens and closes groups and rows by height on a critically damped spring (0.32s, no bounce) with a quick fade, so the list closes its gap instead of jumping. The active pill's background glides to the new pill on a 0.26s spring without bounce.
The search button widens into a field over the pills with a 240ms ease-out width transition while the pills fade out.

A row swaps between reading, editing and the undo bar with one crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in) while its height follows on the smooth spring. A saved edit crossfades the old sentence into the new one. When the undo countdown ends, the bar folds away.

Labels that change (a switch's line, the pill, the add status) crossfade in place with at most 2px of rise; the pill keeps its width with an invisible sizer, so nothing shifts. No per-letter, blurred or morphing text.

The meter's percentage counts in tabular numerals inside a reserved width and the bar scales on the smooth spring. Sorting a typed memory shows a short shimmer on its status. The undo ring drains linearly.
Reduced motion skips the flight, places heights and rows immediately, stops the shimmer and the ring, and keeps every state, focus move and announcement.

name: agent-orchestrator
title: Agent orchestrator
description: A lead agent splits a goal into a plan, fans the subtasks out to parallel worker lanes and merges what comes back, with each lane's model, progress and result in view.
whenToUse: Showing a multi agent run where a lead model splits a task across subagents, such as research, audits, migrations or comparisons.
Debug or observability panels that need per worker progress, tool calls, errors, retries, tokens and cost in one view.
Explaining the cost and speed tradeoff of parallel agents, with a live concurrency control.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run for a single agent working through steps in one thread.
Use agent-plan when the job is to review and edit a plan before anything runs.
Use research-run for a single research answer with sources and citations.
Use agent-tasks to track many independent background tasks that do not merge into one result.
Use model-router when one request is routed to one model rather than split across several.
accessibility: The goal is the card heading, and the lead, the plan and the summary are labelled sections, so the flow reads top to bottom in the order the work happens.
Each lane is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls, named by its subtask, model and status. A closed transcript is inert, so it leaves the reading order.

Status never rests on color: every lane state pairs a glyph with a word (waiting, planned, queued with its place in line, starting, the running tool, failed with a retry countdown, returned, gave up, stopped).
A polite status region announces planning, dispatch, errors and retries, each returned lane, the start of the summary and the final totals, and says that the default run is a simulation.
Connectors and pulses are decorative and hidden from assistive technology; the plan's colored dots repeat information that the lane titles already give.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring, inset on lanes so it follows their corners.
motion: Plan items grow in one by one on a critically damped spring and their text streams in chunks of a few words that only fade in.

A dispatch sends a short colored packet down the connector to the lane; a returning result sends one from the lane to the summary. The simulation waits for the packet to land before the lane starts, so cause always comes before effect.
A lane's branch and port take its series color when work reaches it; queued branches stay dashed with a hollow port.

Tool, status and output swaps are one minimal crossfade: the old label fades out in 100ms while the new one fades in over 160ms from 2px below. Running labels carry a calm shimmer that stops when the lane settles.

One line of output streams on a steady requestAnimationFrame clock and glides left under a soft edge when it outgrows the lane, so the newest words stay in view; settled lines rest at the start with an ellipsis.
Tokens and cost count to each new value with tabular digits; elapsed times tick in tenths.
Transcripts and the totals row open with height and opacity on a spring without bounce.
Reduced motion removes pulses, spinners, shimmer, chunk fades and height travel, keeps every state, label and announcement, and never starts a run on its own.

name: agent-routines
title: Agent routines
description: Scheduled agents in one card: each routine reads as a sentence with its schedule, next run countdown, connectors and destination, and opens smoothly to edit or run it now.
whenToUse: Settings or automation screens where people schedule agents to run on their own and post results to Slack.
A card on a dashboard that shows at a glance which scheduled agents are healthy, which failed and when each runs next.
Products that let people create automations from a sentence and confirm the parsed schedule, sources and destination.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run to watch a single agent work through a task in real time with its tool calls.
Use agent-tasks for a queue of one-off jobs that run once rather than on a schedule.
Use agent-approvals when the agent's output needs a person to approve it before anything is posted.
Use agent-orchestrator to show several agents handing work to each other within one run.
accessibility: Each routine name is a real button with aria-expanded; the rest of the row also opens it on click, while Run now, the switch and the ticks stay separate controls.

Status is never color alone: the last run pairs an icon with its time, each tick has a full text label and a tooltip with an icon and a label, and the strip is a group named with its counts (for example 12 succeeded, 1 failed, 1 skipped).
Connector, destination and model marks are hidden from assistive technology and replaced by one sentence per row: what it reads, where it posts and which model runs it.
The run ticks are one tab stop with a roving index, so a list of routines does not add 14 stops per row.
Run starts, results, failures, stops, toggles, schedule changes and new routines are announced in a polite status region, including that the preview only simulates runs and Slack posts.
While a run is in progress the open row lists its steps as an ordered list with the current step marked aria-current="step"; a failure is announced as an alert with the step and the error.

The sentence parser's state and the simulation note sit in a polite live region. Chips are buttons named with their field and value, and their popovers use pressed buttons for sources and the destination.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: A row opens from height 0 to auto and back on a critically damped spring (about 340ms, no bounce). Opacity starts a beat after the height and ends a beat before it on close, the content rises 6px into place, and the chevron and the row's quiet tint change on the same timing. Opening one row closes the other at the same time, and the rows below glide with the height.
While a row is open its height keeps following its content on the same spring, so a streamed report or the step list never resizes the card in one frame.

Run now fills a 2px line under the row at the pace of the steps, in the routine's series color, then the line fades. A new tick slides in from one slot to the right while the others tween one slot left and the oldest fades out, on a 240ms ease-out tween. Ticks sit in fixed slots and never measure layout, so they do not drift while rows open or close.

Labels change with one minimal crossfade: the old one fades out in 100ms and the new one fades in over 160ms from 2px below. A schedule change slides the text after it as its width follows on a critically damped spring. The countdown uses tabular numerals in a reserved width.
The Running label and the active step carry a calm shimmer that stops when the run ends. Run now and Stop share one button and one width, so the swap never resizes it.
The latest report streams in chunks of 15 to 40 characters every 32ms on a requestAnimationFrame clock; each new chunk only fades in and settled text never re-renders.
Reduced motion opens, closes, shifts and swaps at once and keeps every state, label and announcement; the shimmer stops and streamed chunks appear without the fade.

name: agent-run
title: Agent run
description: A single card that follows one AI coding agent through a task: steps stream in with the live one shimmering, tool calls open in place, and the agent stops on a two-file diff for you to approve or send back before it writes. When the run ends, the steps fold into one line and a result shows the files changed, the checks that passed and a pull request button.
whenToUse: Coding agents and background jobs that read, search, edit and test, where people watch progress and approve the change before it is written.
Product surfaces that hand an agent a ticket and return a pull request, such as an issue tracker, a review tool or an IDE side panel.
Demos and onboarding that explain how an agent works step by step, with a real approval gate.
whenNotToUse: Use research-run for a research agent that reads sources and writes a cited report.
Use agent-approvals for an inbox of pending approvals across many agents and tools.
Use agent-orchestrator when several agents work in parallel on parts of one job.
Use code-review for reviewing a finished pull request line by line with comments.
accessibility: The card is a section named by the task. Steps are an ordered list named Steps; each expandable step is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls.

A polite live region announces each step as it starts, the wait for approval, the end of the run with the test count, and stopping. A second region reports the pull request, including that the preview only simulates it.
Status is never color alone: the status word sits beside an icon, finished steps change to past tense with a check, and a sent back step reads Sent back with the note.
Diff lines carry hidden Added and Removed prefixes; the + and − markers and the tints are decorative. The file tabs are a tablist with tabpanels, and the hidden panel is inert.
Approving or rejecting moves focus to that step's row, opening the note moves focus into it, and cancelling returns it to Reject.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: New steps open their height on a critically damped spring and fade in; nothing bounces.

The live verb shimmers with Text shimmer. When a step finishes, the verb crossfades to past tense (100ms out, 160ms in from 2px) while its slot follows the measured width, and the check draws its stroke once.
The header status word swaps with the same crossfade; the timer uses tabular numerals in a reserved width.
Every diff file shares one grid cell, so switching tabs only crossfades and the card never resizes. The reject note swaps in place while the footer height follows on the smooth spring.
At the end the steps fold to one line and the result opens below; the closing message streams in chunks of a few words every 34ms, laid out in advance so nothing reflows.
The pull request button keeps every label in one cell, so Open pull request, Opening and PR #482 opened crossfade without changing width.
Reduced motion drops travel, fades and the shimmer and keeps every state, label and announcement.

name: agent-tasks
title: Agent tasks
description: A home for background coding agents: start a task on a repository and branch, watch each card move from queued to running to ready for review, and open a pull request from the result.
whenToUse: A product surface where people hand coding tasks to background agents and come back later to review, open a pull request, retry or archive.
Dashboards for automated maintenance runs, such as dependency upgrades, flaky test fixes or codemods, where each run ends in a branch with a diff and checks.
Any queue of long running agent jobs where the current step, the elapsed time and a clear finished state matter more than a transcript.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run to follow one live agent run in detail, with its plan, tool calls and output.
Use code-review when people need to read the diff line by line and leave comments; this block only summarizes the change.
Use agent-approvals when the agent pauses for a person to approve a risky action before it continues.
Use agent-routines for scheduled, recurring agent jobs rather than one-off tasks.
Use ai-composer for a chat style prompt box without a task list.
accessibility: Each card's title row is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at its details; closed details are inert so their content leaves the tab order.
Status is never color alone: every state pairs an icon with a label, such as Ready for review, Failed or Checks passed, and the live step is read with its status.
The diff stat has a spoken label (lines added, removed and files changed); each file and step carries a hidden change or state word before it.
Elapsed time has a spoken label such as Running for 2 minutes 14 seconds, so the compact 2m 14s is never the only form.
Starting, finishing, cancelling, retrying, archiving and opening a pull request are announced in a polite status region, including that the preview simulates the run and the PR.
Focus follows the control that replaced the pressed one: Cancel to Retry, Retry to Cancel, a created PR back to its card, and an archived card to its neighbour.
Chips are Radix dropdown menus with radio items, so the chosen repository, branch and model are announced as checked. Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus uses Arc's shared ring.
motion: A started task grows in at the top on the critically damped smooth spring and its background flashes the accent tint once, so the eye lands on it.

The live step shimmers with a calm, linear sweep while the agent works. A new step crossfades in: the old line fades out in about 100ms and the new one fades in over 160ms from 3px below. The sweep stops the moment the run stops.
Status changes crossfade the state line once. Actions crossfade as a group and their slot follows the new width on the morph spring, which is how Create pull request becomes PR #482 open.
Filter counts roll up or down with tabular numerals on the snappy spring, and the tab highlight glides on the segmented control's morph spring.
Expanding a card animates height and opacity together on the smooth spring; new log lines grow in the same way. Archiving collapses the card so the list closes the gap.
Reduced motion keeps every state, label, announcement and focus move but drops the sweep, the spinner rotation, the travel and the springs; content crossfades quickly or appears at once.

name: ai-answer
title: AI answer
description: One AI answer set like a clean article: it thinks, shows its sources as small cards with colored marks, and streams a formatted answer where every citation lights the sentence it supports. Copy, regenerate with options, rate, share, page through versions and ask a related question in place.
whenToUse: An answer page where one question gets one well formatted, cited answer that people read, copy and share.
Docs and help center assistants that must show where each claim comes from.
Internal knowledge search where the answer mixes prose, steps, a comparison table and code.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-chat for a back and forth conversation with many turns kept on screen.
Use research-run for long multi step research that plans searches and reads many sources before writing.
Use ai-side-panel when the assistant sits next to a document or app the person is working in.
Use ai-inline-edit to rewrite a selection in place rather than answer a question.
accessibility: The block is a labelled region named by the question, with aria-busy while an answer streams. A polite status region announces Thinking, Writing the answer, Answer ready, Answer stopped or the error.
Action results (copied, link copied, feedback sent, version shown) go to a second polite live region; the share links say when the preview copies a sample link.
The reasoning and sources rows are buttons with aria-expanded and aria-controls; closed panels are inert, so their content leaves the tab order.
Citations are links named "Source n: title, site"; the source card opens on keyboard focus as well as hover, and a lit sentence is a visual aid only, never the only cue.
The comparison table keeps header cells with scope, and the table and code scroll inside focusable, labelled regions on narrow screens.
Status is never color alone: copied shows a drawn check, errors an icon and text, feedback a filled glyph with aria-pressed, and stopped or failed answers a note with a Try again button.
Asking a related question moves focus to the new question heading; New thread moves focus to the composer.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: "Thinking" uses the Arc text shimmer for about a second and settles to solid text as "Thought for 9s" when the first words arrive.

The answer streams in chunks on a requestAnimationFrame clock: about every 34ms, three to eight words commit at once and fade in over 160ms on a plain ease-out, with no blur, travel or stagger. A steady pace of about a hundred words a second plus catch-up drains bursts, so a full answer lands in two to four seconds. Settled text never re-renders or reflows.
Headings, list items, table rows and code lines appear as their text arrives; a line or row waits for its newline, so containers never pop in half built.
The reasoning and sources panels open on the smooth spring; source cards fade in 20ms apart, at most six steps. Hovering the sources row fans the mark chips apart on the CSS spring.
Regenerating or switching versions crossfades the answer while its height springs to the new length, and the version number rolls up or down.
Copy and Share morph their icon (a drawn check) and label in place without changing width; Send turns into Stop in the same spot.
Reduced motion keeps the chunked arrival but drops every fade, roll, fan and spring, and keeps all states and announcements.

name: ai-chat
title: AI chat
description: A full-screen AI chat where answers stream in as markdown with folding reasoning, tool chips and cited sources. People can switch chats and models, edit or retry a message into versions, rate replies and stop a reply mid-stream.
whenToUse: A multi turn assistant inside a product page, drawer or dashboard card, with streaming answers, reasoning, tools and citations.
Any place users need to retry, edit, rate or copy answers and switch models mid conversation.
Prototyping an LLM feature: with no props it plays a realistic scripted conversation and answers new messages with simulated replies.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-composer when you only need the prompt box with attachments, mentions and commands.
Use ai-answer for a single question and a long, article like answer with sources.
Use agent-run or research-run when the work is a multi step agent run with a plan and progress rather than a conversation.
Use model-picker for a standalone model selector with pricing and context details.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section. Each turn is an article; a reply that is still thinking or streaming sets aria-busy.

A polite status region announces when a reply starts, finishes, stops or fails, model and chat changes, copy results and feedback. In the preview every scripted reply and rating is announced as simulated.
The reasoning line and tool chips are buttons with aria-expanded and aria-controls. Citations are links named "Source 2: title, domain" and open a read only preview on hover or keyboard focus.
Icon buttons carry specific names (Copy, Retry, Good response, Bad response, Edit, Attach files, Send message or Stop reply), and the thumbs expose aria-pressed.
Status is never color alone: errors pair an icon with "Reply failed" and the message, a stopped reply says Stopped, and a failed tool shows an alert icon with its summary.
The version switcher is a labelled group ("Version 2 of 2") with Previous and Next buttons.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Answers stream in chunks of three or four whole words every 34ms on a requestAnimationFrame clock (about 90 to 120 words per second). Each chunk is its own span that fades in once over 150ms; nothing already on screen re-renders, moves or blurs, and list markers and code fences never appear before their first word.

Thinking and running tools use a calm text shimmer that stops when they finish. Labels such as Thinking to "Thought for 4s", tool states, the model chip and the title swap with one crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in from 2px) while the box follows the measured width on a critically damped spring.
Reasoning, tool details and attachments fold open by height on a spring with no bounce. Switching versions or opening the editor glides the turn to its new height and fades the new content in.
While stuck to the bottom the thread follows new lines on a soft lerp, so text glides up instead of jumping a line at a time. Scrolling up releases it and shows a jump to latest button.
Switching chats crossfades the thread (out in 100ms, in over 160ms from 4px), restores that chat's scroll position and never replays finished replies. Menus fade and scale from their trigger.
Reduced motion drops the chunk fade, travel and smooth scrolling and keeps every state, label and announcement.

name: ai-composer
title: AI composer
description: The prompt box at the bottom of an AI app: files upload in place, / opens commands, @ inserts mentions, a model and effort menu sits in the toolbar, and the send button turns into a stop control ringed by the reply's progress.
whenToUse: The prompt box of an assistant, a coding agent or an in-product AI feature where people attach files, mention docs and pick a model.
A new chat screen that should open on a greeting and suggestions, then show the first exchange.
Any place that needs a streaming send and stop control with honest progress and keyboard first commands.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-chat for a full conversation with history, message actions and a sidebar of chats.
Use ai-inline-edit to rewrite a selection inside a document instead of chatting about it.
Use voice-agent when speech is the main input and the reply is spoken.
Use model-picker when the job is comparing and choosing models rather than sending a prompt.
accessibility: The textarea is labeled Message and described by a hidden hint for Enter, Shift Enter, / and @. While a list is open it points at it with aria-controls and aria-activedescendant, and the list is a listbox of options grouped into Files and Docs.
Tokens are drawn by a mirror under a transparent textarea, so the field stays a real textarea for screen readers, spellcheck, undo and IME input.

The send button changes its accessible name with its state: Send message, Send after uploads finish, Send with the message over the limit, and Stop generating. It stays focusable while it cannot send and reports aria-disabled.
Web search, Extended thinking and the mic are toggle buttons with aria-pressed; on state also shows in the accent fill and a tooltip, never color alone.
Attachment chips name their remove control after the file, and a running upload's control reads Cancel upload. A failed file shows an icon and a short reason.

A polite status region reports what happened: uploads finished, a long paste added as an attachment, the model and effort chosen, sent with a simulated reply, reply finished or stopped, and that dictation and the Drive, GitHub and screenshot actions are simulated.
Menus come from Radix with focus moved in and returned on close; after picking an attach action focus returns to the textarea.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: The send arrow lifts out and a stop square scales in on the morph spring; a thin accent arc around the button fills with the reply, then fades as the button turns back into an arrow the moment the stream ends.

Replies stream in chunks of whole words every 34ms on an animation frame clock, about 80 words a second, with catch-up when a live stream runs ahead. Each new chunk only fades in over 160ms; settled text is static, and the reply grows line by line on a short ease-out.
A short Thinking shimmer covers the moment before the first token; with Extended thinking or Web search on, those steps shimmer instead and settle into Thought for 1s or Searched 6 sites.
The sent message lifts into its bubble on the snappy spring while the composer glides from the center to the bottom on the smooth spring.
Attachment chips scale in, their ring fills with the upload, and a check pops in before handing over to the remove control. The model chip springs to the width of its new label.
Reduced motion keeps every state and announcement but drops travel: chunks appear without a fade, the waveform holds still, the ring does not spin, and panels change at once.

name: ai-feature-launch
title: AI feature launch
description: An in-product launch card for an AI feature. A looping mini demo plays above a three-step tour (inline rewrite, thread summary, ask your workspace), with benefit rows, an admin-gated "Enable for my workspace" switch, and Try it now and Learn more actions.
whenToUse: Announcing a new AI feature inside the product, with a tour of what it does and a switch to turn it on for the workspace.
Admin-gated rollouts where an admin enables AI for everyone and members can still try it.
A what's new modal or popover that needs to look polished in a launch clip.
whenNotToUse: Multi-step configuration with real inputs (models, data sources): use ai-setup-wizard.
Ongoing activation tasks: use onboarding-checklist.
A long changelog or release notes page: render the entries as a page instead.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section whose name follows the current step title. Only the active step is exposed; hidden steps are aria-hidden and inert.
The preview stage is decorative (aria-hidden): the title, description and benefits carry the same message as text.
Dots are buttons named "Step 2 of 3: Catch up on any thread" with aria-current="step" and a roving tab stop.
The switch is labelled by its visible label and described by the admin note. Saving, cancelled, saved, error and simulated results are announced in a polite live region.
Status is never color alone: the saved note pairs a check with "On for all 48 members", the error note pairs an alert icon with text.
Autoplay stops on the first interaction and waits while the pointer is over the card, so nobody loses a step they are reading.
motion: One shared loop clock drives the mini demo, the dot fill and autoplay, so they never drift. It pauses off screen.
Step changes are a single crossfade: the old step fades out in 100ms, the new one fades in over 160ms and rises 2px. All steps share one grid cell, so the card never changes height.
Mini demos stream text in chunks of three words every 40ms, each chunk only fading in; thinking labels shimmer for under a second.
The active dot widens on a bounce-free spring (0.24s) and fills linearly with the loop.
Reduced motion: no autoplay or loops, each step shows a still frame at posterTime, and feedback (notes, spinner) stays.

name: ai-inline-edit
title: AI inline edit
description: A document you edit with AI in place: \u2318K on a selection, watch the rewrite stream in as a diff, accept each change, and Tab through ghost text.
whenToUse: Rewriting a selection: shorten, clarify, change tone or fix grammar in place.
Inline autocomplete while writing documents or messages.
Any AI suggestion that should be reviewed as a diff before it lands.
whenNotToUse: Rich formatting such as headings, lists or links; the block edits plain paragraphs.
Asking questions about a page; use ai-side-panel.
A single prompt box without a document; use ai-composer.
accessibility: The editor is a labelled region; each paragraph is a native contenteditable, so caret movement, selection and screen reader editing work as usual.
The prompt is a labelled dialog with a combobox input and a listbox of actions using aria-activedescendant.
Each change in review is a focusable group named with what it does, such as Change "very careful" to "carefully", with Enter and Backspace to decide.
Ghost text is aria-hidden and never part of the paragraph's text; the footer names the keys to accept or dismiss it.
Streaming, review and applied states are announced with role status; failures use role alert with Try again. Deletions and insertions pair color with strike through and highlight.
The block claims Cmd/Ctrl + K only while focus is inside it, so an app wide command menu still works elsewhere.
motion: One floating layer carries the whole edit: it opens under the selection, morphs its size on the smooth spring from prompt to a Stop status bar to the review bar to an Applied receipt, and follows the diff as it grows.

The rewrite is paced like any stream: buffered, drained on a frame loop that tracks the arrival rate, snapped to whole words. Inserted words develop in with opacity and a small blur that clears; deleted words have their strike drawn across as the stream passes them.
While streaming, a short word matched far ahead is not trusted yet, so the diff only grows at the stream edge and never flickers between alignments.
The active quick action is marked by a highlight that slides between rows on the snappy spring. Hunk toolbars fade up on hover or focus; a decided change settles with a brief tint.
Accepted ghost text glows for a moment using the CSS highlight API, without touching the text.
Reduced motion shows diffs, ghost text and the layer without fades, sweeps or morphs.

name: ai-insight-card
title: AI insight card
description: A KPI card that explains itself. Explain streams a short reason for the change and ranks three drivers with contribution bars. A numbered annotation lights up on the sparkline as each driver is read, and follow-up chips ask the next question in place.
whenToUse: A dashboard KPI where readers ask why it moved, such as net revenue, MRR, signups or churn.
Weekly business reviews and finance dashboards that want an explanation next to the number.
Products adding AI analysis to existing analytics without a separate chat.
whenNotToUse: Open ended questions across many tables: use ask-your-data.
A plain number with no explanation: use metric-card or stat-card.
Dense multi series charts: use a full chart component.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section; Explain carries aria-expanded and aria-controls for the answer panel.
A polite live region announces when the answer starts, the full answer when it is ready, Stop and errors. Without `explain` it says the answer is simulated from sample data.
Deltas carry a sign as well as color, and unread driver rows are hidden from assistive tech until the answer reaches them.
The chart is a focusable group with arrow key reading; values are announced through its own live region.
Follow-up chips use aria-pressed for the answer on screen and are disabled while a stream runs.
motion: The panel opens and closes on a critically damped 260ms spring; answers of a different length spring to their height. No bounce.
The answer streams 3 to 7 words every 34ms, each chunk only fading in over 140ms. Its full text is reserved underneath, so the card never grows while streaming.
Annotations fade and scale in over 200ms as their driver is read; the driver being read takes the accent on its badge, dot, guide, rank and underline.
Contribution bars grow to their share over 240ms ease-out; skeletons crossfade to labels in 160ms.
Reduced motion: the answer appears whole after the short thinking state, transitions cut, and the demo loop stays off.

name: ai-search-bar
title: AI search bar
description: A search card for an app or docs, where typing lists grouped results right away (Docs, Customers, Issues) and pressing Tab streams a short AI answer on top. The answer's numbered citations point to the results below it.
whenToUse: A product or docs search where people mix finding a page or record with asking a question.
Support and success tools that search docs, customers and tickets in one place.
A command bar or search dialog that should offer an AI answer without leaving the results.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-answer for a full answer page with long formatted answers, follow ups and feedback.
Use ai-chat for a back and forth conversation.
Use ai-command for an action palette that runs commands rather than searches content.
accessibility: The field is a combobox with aria-activedescendant, so focus stays in the field while the arrow keys move the active option. Results sit in a listbox with one labelled group per section; the Ask AI row is its own small listbox, and aria-controls names both.
Each option has a full label: title, description, meta or issue status, and "cited as source n" once the answer cites it. The number badges are aria-hidden because the label carries them.

The answer is a labelled region with aria-busy while it streams. A polite status region announces Asking AI, Answer ready with the source count, Answer closed, results opened and errors, and says Simulated when the demo stands in for a real model or link.
Citations are buttons named "Source n: title"; focus lights the matching result just like hover. Highlights in titles are a visual aid only.
Issue status is an icon plus a text label, never color alone. The error state shows an icon, the message and a Try again button.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Results update in the same frame as each keystroke with no animation, like a native search; the active row's background changes in 80ms.
Switching between the empty view and results crossfades (out 100ms, in 160ms). The body has a fixed height, so the card never resizes.
Asking AI crossfades the Ask AI row into the answer panel while the slot's height follows its content on a 240ms spring with no bounce.

The status shimmers "Thinking" for about half a second, then "Writing", then settles to "4 sources". The answer streams on a requestAnimationFrame clock: every 34ms three to eight words commit together and fade in over 140ms, with no blur, travel or stagger.
Number badges fade in on results as their citations arrive. Copy swaps its icon for a check in place.
Reduced motion keeps the chunked arrival and every state but drops the fades, shimmer, pulse and the auto play loop.

name: ai-setup-wizard
title: AI setup wizard
description: A three-step setup card for turning on an AI feature. You connect Notion, Google Drive, Confluence or Zendesk and watch each one sync. Then you pick the model, tone and guardrails, and ask a test question whose answer streams with numbered citations before you go live.
whenToUse: Turning on an AI answers feature for a support, sales or internal knowledge team, like Intercom Fin, Zendesk AI or Notion Q&A.
Onboarding admins to a copilot that needs data sources, a model choice and guardrails before it is enabled.
A landing page or product tour section that shows the full setup in one short, looping clip.
whenNotToUse: Configuring an agent's instructions, tools and files in depth: use agent-builder.
Only choosing a model: use model-picker.
A full conversation after setup: use ai-chat. The test step answers one question at a time.
Monitoring a running agent: use agent-status.
accessibility: The stepper is an ordered list of buttons; the current step has aria-current="step" and completed steps say so. Steps not reached yet are disabled.
Model cards are a radiogroup with roving focus; each radio is labelled with the full model name and note.
A polite status region announces step changes, finished syncs, answers and going live, and says when the sample is simulated.
Status is never color alone: synced rows show a check and "Synced", errors an alert icon and text, the header a Draft or Live label with its icon.
Focus stays on the footer button across steps because the same button changes its label; Back keeps its space when hidden so nothing shifts.
motion: Steps slide 32px horizontally with a bounce free spring (visualDuration .24) and an opacity crossfade, inside a fixed height viewport, so the card never changes size.
Stepper bars fill with scaleX and glyphs crossfade from number to check. Row meta, footer meta and status labels swap with one crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in, 2px rise).
Answers stream three to six words every 34ms and each chunk only fades in; citations fade in after the stream with a 40ms stagger.
The confirmation draws its circle and check with pathLength. Reduced motion drops travel, drawing and streaming (answers appear whole) and turns off the self playing demo.

name: ai-side-panel
title: AI side panel
description: An assistant docked beside a page that reads it and edits it: ask about the page or a selected passage, review each edit as a word diff, and apply it with a tint sweep on the page and one-click undo.
whenToUse: An assistant next to a document or record that can summarize it and propose edits.
Copilot style help where edits must be approved, applied visibly and undone.
Asking about a selected passage or table without leaving the page.
whenNotToUse: A standalone conversation; use ai-chat.
Rewriting a passage in place with no side panel; use ai-inline-edit.
A single prompt box; use ai-composer.
Showing an autonomous agent's steps; use agent-run.
accessibility: The panel is a labelled complementary region; the close and reopen buttons report aria-expanded and aria-controls.
A polite status region announces each step: reading the page, answer ready (and which part a change touches), applied with undo available, undone, discarded, stopped and errors.
After Apply focus moves to the Undo pill; after Undo it returns to the card's Apply button; after Discard it moves to the composer.
Diffs use real ins and del elements, so removed and added words are distinguishable without color.
Every status pairs an icon with a label (Applied to the page, Discarded, Undone, Stopped, did not respond).
In sheet mode the page behind is inert while the sheet is open.
motion: Closing the panel narrows the dock on a critically damped spring (no bounce) while the panel slides out; the page column widens and the document glides to center.
Answers stream in chunks of 3 to 8 words every 34ms on a requestAnimationFrame clock; each chunk fades in over 150ms and settled text never re-renders.
Apply sweeps an accent tint across the changed block once, while the old text fades out in 100ms and the new text fades in over 180ms; the block height follows on a spring with no overshoot.
Status swaps in the change card footer, chips and the Undo pill are single opacity crossfades in a fixed size slot, so nothing shifts.
Reduced motion keeps every state, drops the chunk fade, the slide and the sweep travel, and only fades the tint.

name: api-keys
title: API keys
description: API key management where Create key unfolds into its form and each secret is shown once.
whenToUse: The developer settings page of an API product.
Key management with scopes, environments, and a one-time secret reveal.
Revoking keys where a stray click must not fire.
whenNotToUse: Use webhooks for event endpoints and signing secrets.
Use integrations for OAuth connections to other apps.
Use roles-permissions for user access.
accessibility: Each key opens a labelled role="region" detail panel.
Revoke uses hold to confirm, so it cannot fire from a stray click.
Creation, copy, and revoke results are announced in a polite status region.
motion: The Create key button unfolds into its form, and new keys slide into the list.
Reduced motion replaces the unfold with an instant swap.

name: availability-picker
title: Availability picker
description: Find a meeting time across people and see the choice come together.
whenToUse: Picking a meeting time that works for several attendees.
Booking flows that show a few days and open slots with a confirmation step.
whenNotToUse: Use calendar or date-picker to pick a single date.
Use time-picker for a free time input.
Use event-invite to show and respond to an invite.
accessibility: Days and times are labeled groups of buttons with aria-pressed.
The selected day and the final selection are aria-live regions.
motion: Time slots slide in from the direction of the day change.
The selected slot highlight moves with a shared layoutId on a responsive spring.
Reduced motion removes the horizontal offset and uses zero durations.

name: billing-overview
title: Billing overview
description: A billing page where the plan card morphs into a picker and usage, invoices, and card follow.
whenToUse: The billing settings page of a SaaS app.
Pages that show plan, usage, payment method, and invoices together.
Plan changes that should happen in place without leaving billing.
whenNotToUse: Use plan-comparison or usage-pricing on a public pricing page.
Use cancel-flow for the cancellation journey.
Use usage-meter to show a single quota elsewhere.
accessibility: The plan picker is a role="radiogroup" of role="radio" buttons; unavailable plans are disabled.
The price quote updates in a polite live region, and actions are announced in a status region.
motion: The plan card morphs into the picker and back inside a region whose height springs; the selected plan highlight glides with a shared layoutId.
Changing copy rises into place while the old line lifts away; totals roll with AnimatedCounter and card digits turn one column at a time.
Usage bars fill when they scroll into view.
Reduced motion makes the morph and fills instant.

name: blog-grid
title: Blog grid
description: A blog index with a featured post, category filter, post cards, pagination and an in-place reader.
whenToUse: A marketing site blog or journal index.
Resource hubs with a few categories and a featured story.
whenNotToUse: Use changelog-page for release notes with versions.
Use a data table for large archives that need sorting and search.
accessibility: Filters are buttons with aria-pressed; pagination is a nav with aria-current on the active page.
Each card is one link with the title, excerpt and byline as its content, so screen readers announce it once.
The reader moves focus to its back button, and closing returns focus to the card you opened.
Images carry real alt text; author avatars are decorative.
motion: The filter and page highlights glide on the morph spring.
Filtering crossfades the grid with a short rise; paging slides it in the direction of travel.
Opening a post morphs the card image into the reader hero, and back on close.
Card images zoom 3% on hover (fine pointers only).
Reduced motion swaps travel and morphs for plain fades.

name: budget-variance
title: Budget variance
description: Budget against actual operating spend by department as aligned bullet charts, with favorable and unfavorable variance, a month, quarter and year to date switch that springs every bar, in-place drill-down into budget lines, and a total row.
whenToUse: Monthly close and budget review screens that compare planned and actual operating spend by department or cost center.
Finance dashboards where a controller needs to see at a glance which teams are over, which are under, and by how much.
Any plan against actual comparison with a meaningful tolerance band, such as headcount cost or cloud spend by team.
whenNotToUse: Use mrr-waterfall to explain how a single total moved from one value to another.
Use usage-forecast to project spend against a cap over time.
Use a line or bar chart to show a trend across many periods; this block compares one window at a time.
Use a sortable data table when there are dozens of cost centers and sorting matters more than the visual comparison.
accessibility: Each department is a heading with a disclosure button (aria-expanded, aria-controls) whose name is a full sentence: spent, budget, variance and whether it is favorable.
The total and every budget line carry the same sentence in visually hidden text; the charts and the counting numbers are hidden from assistive technology so nothing is read twice or mid-count.
Changing the window announces the new window and the total through a polite live region.
Variance never relies on color: amounts carry a sign and every share ends in over, under or on plan.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. The focused department shows a filled row.
motion: Switching the window springs every bar to its new length on one critically damped spring and counts every amount and share to the new value, all written to the DOM from motion values.
The overspend is the same bar clipped to the space past budget, so the danger color appears exactly as the bar crosses the tick, with no second animation to keep in sync.
Opening a department grows its lines in height and opacity together without overshoot; closing is faster. The chevron turns on the shared spring curve.
Every animation is interruptible: a new window or toggle starts from wherever the bars and numbers are.
Reduced motion jumps bars and numbers to their final values and opens lines at full height.

name: call-insights
title: Call insights
description: A sales call insights card where talk time, flagged pricing, competitor and objection moments, an AI summary and owned next steps sit in one view. Selecting a moment plays its quote, and checking off next steps lowers the deal risk.
whenToUse: A deal page that shows the latest sales call with talk ratio, flagged moments, summary and next steps.
A call review queue for sales managers who coach on talk time and objection handling.
A research or support tool that recaps a recorded customer call with jump-to-quote clips.
whenNotToUse: Full transcript reading or editing: use transcript-studio.
An internal meeting recap without a prospect or deal: use meeting-summary.
A pipeline overview across many deals: use a table such as crm-contacts.
accessibility: The card is a section named after the company. Markers are a radio group named Key moments; each radio names the type, timestamp and speaker, so type never relies on the icon alone.
The waveform is a slider with the clip position as value text (0:03 of 0:07).
Deal risk is an icon plus the words High, Medium or Low risk. Talk time is an image whose name lists every speaker and share.
Playback, pauses, load failures and next step changes (with any change in risk) are announced in a polite status region, which also says clips are simulated with no audio.
The summary is aria-busy while it streams and only exposed once complete; the thinking label is hidden from assistive tech.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Selecting a moment fills the rail up to it on one 240ms ease-out transform and crossfades the quote (old out in 100ms, new in over 160ms from 2px). All quotes share one grid cell, so the well never changes height.
The waveform reshapes per clip with a 240ms height ease, and the played part is clipped in from a CSS variable each frame, so playback never re-renders React per frame.

The summary waits 0.7s on a calm shimmer, then streams 3 to 8 words every 35ms with each chunk fading in over 140ms. Talk time reveals left to right once. The risk chip crossfades its icon and label inside the width of its longest label.
The tour pauses while the card is off screen and stops at the first interaction. Nothing bounces.
Reduced motion skips the tour, streaming and reveals and drops travel; selection, playback and every state and announcement stay.

name: cancel-flow
title: Cancel flow
description: A cancellation flow that answers each reason with a tailored offer and a calm hold-to-cancel.
whenToUse: Subscription cancellation in billing settings with a reason step and a retention offer.
Flows that offer a discount, pause, or downgrade before confirming the cancel.
whenNotToUse: Use dialog with hold-to-confirm for a one step destructive action without offers.
Use plan-comparison when people are choosing a plan rather than leaving.
Use billing-overview for the billing page itself.
accessibility: Reasons form a role="radiogroup" with aria-checked cards.
The pause length is a role="spinbutton" whose aria-valuetext includes the resume date.
A polite role="status" region announces offer changes and the outcome.
motion: Steps slide between reason, offer and confirm, the selection highlight glides with a layoutId, and prices roll with Animated counter.
Reduced motion swaps slides for fades and figures change without rolling.

name: cart-drawer
title: Cart drawer
description: Products fly into the cart, counts roll, and a drawer handles quantities, shipping progress, and checkout.
whenToUse: Product listings where people add several items and review them in a side cart.
Stores that show a free shipping threshold and promo codes before checkout.
Demos of an add to cart interaction with clear feedback on where the item went.
whenNotToUse: Use checkout-flow for a full multi-step checkout with address and payment.
Use checkout-summary when you only need the order summary and totals.
Use drawer for a generic side panel that is not a cart.
accessibility: The cart button has aria-haspopup="dialog", aria-expanded, and a label with the item count. The drawer is role="dialog" with aria-modal and moves focus to its close button.
The shop behind an open drawer is inert, and the drawer body is inert while an order is placing.
Quantity steppers are labelled groups; the minus button becomes "Remove" at quantity one. Swipe to remove has button equivalents.
The shipping bar is a role="progressbar"; an invalid promo sets aria-invalid and swaps the note under the field.
Adds, removals, promo changes, and the placed order are announced in a polite live region.
motion: The product photo flies along a quadratic arc into the cart over 780ms, shrinking and tilting; the badge count only changes when it lands, then the cart bumps and rings.
The drawer slides in on a critically damped spring. Rows collapse in height when removed and the totals roll with AnimatedCounter.
Swipe a row left past 110px, or flick it, to remove; short drags snap back with the release velocity.
The checkout button shares a layoutId with the confirmation disc, then a checkmark draws in.
Reduced motion skips the flight and the bump, disables row dragging, fades the drawer instead of sliding it, and zeroes the remaining springs.

name: catch-up
title: Catch up
description: A catch me up digest for when you return, where one button reads Slack, Linear, GitHub and Gmail for the range you pick and streams back a short ranked summary: Needs you, Decisions made, Shipped and FYI. Each item is one sentence with its source mark, people and a jump link, and marking items as read clears them with a smooth collapse.
whenToUse: A home or inbox screen that summarizes what happened across connected tools while the user was away.
An AI assistant feature that turns hundreds of notifications into a short ranked list with jump links.
A weekly or daily digest preview inside a product's notification settings.
whenNotToUse: A live notification feed where every event matters; use a plain activity list instead.
A long-form report or meeting summary with paragraphs; use a document view or ai-chat.
Approving agent actions; use agent-approvals.
accessibility: A polite live region announces each phase: reading, digest ready with the item count, marked as read with the count left, and all caught up. The sample adds that it is simulated and nothing was read.
Sections are labelled regions with a heading that includes the count, and each sentence starts with its source name for screen readers.
Rows that have not streamed in yet are hidden from assistive tech and their buttons are out of the tab order.
After marking an item as read, focus moves to the next item's mark as read button, or to the footer action when the list is clear.
Status is never color alone: sections pair an icon with a label, and the reading state uses a spinner then a check per source.
motion: The digest streams four words every 34ms; each chunk only fades in. Rows reserve their full height up front behind quiet skeleton bars, so nothing shifts while text streams.
Switching between sources, digest and outcome is one crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in) while the card height springs to the new size with no bounce.
Mark as read collapses the row's height and opacity in 200ms; an emptied section collapses the same way. The card follows the collapse frame by frame instead of chasing it with a second spring.
Labels, counts and the summary line swap with a single crossfade and a 2px rise. The button keeps a fixed minimum width across labels.
Reduced motion shows the finished digest at once, keeps crossfades as plain fades, and stops the spinner.

name: login-centered
title: Centered login
description: A passkey-first login card on a quiet ring backdrop that morphs through email and code.
whenToUse: A full screen sign in or sign up page where passkeys are the main method.
Auth flows that fall back to a six digit email code.
Products that want one card for both sign in and sign up.
whenNotToUse: Use login-split for password sign in beside a brand photo.
Use login-immersive for magic link auth over a full-bleed photo.
Use sign-in for a simpler embedded sign in form.
accessibility: The email field uses autoComplete="email" and the code step uses the OTP input group.
Busy buttons use aria-busy and aria-disabled so focus stays put during simulated requests.
A polite role="status" region announces step changes and errors.
motion: Steps slide and blur between passkey, email, code and done while the card height follows; the resend label rolls.
Reduced motion swaps slides for fades and shows the passkey check without drawing its stroke.

examples.title: Route sign ups to onboarding
examples.code:
<LoginCentered
  fullScreen
  onSignIn={(email, method, mode) =>
    router.push(mode === "sign-up" ? "/welcome" : "/app")
  }
/>

name: changelog-feed
title: Changelog feed
description: Release notes you can filter, open in place, and scroll through month by month.
whenToUse: A product changelog or release notes page grouped by month.
Release notes with type filters such as features, fixes, and improvements.
Changelogs that should offer an email subscribe action in the header.
whenNotToUse: Use timeline for a short vertical list of events without filters.
Use accordion for plain expandable content that is not dated.
accessibility: Each entry row is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at its detail panel.
Filter chips are toggle buttons with aria-pressed, and the visible count is announced in a polite status region.
The month nav marks the current month with aria-current, and the scroll area is focusable with an aria-label.
motion: Entries open in place on a spring while the chevron rotates; the month label slides in the scroll direction.
The subscribe control morphs from button to form to a drawn check with a short blur crossfade.
Reduced motion makes these changes instant.

name: checkout-summary
title: Checkout summary
description: An order summary with a promo code that becomes a chip, discount and tax lines, and pay button states.
whenToUse: The last step before a hosted checkout such as a Stripe session redirect.
A single product purchase with launch discounts or promo codes.
A pricing page side panel that confirms the final total.
whenNotToUse: Use checkout-flow when you collect shipping and card details in the page.
Use cart-drawer for a cart with several items and quantities.
Use billing-overview for an existing subscription's invoices and plan.
accessibility: The block is a section labelled by title with an h3 heading.
The promo field has a visually hidden label. Errors set aria-invalid, aria-describedby, and a role="alert" message.
The applied code chip has a remove button labelled Remove code followed by the code.
The pay button is aria-live="polite", so Processing, Paid, and Try again are announced. A payment error adds a role="alert" line.
The total has visually hidden formatted text, while the rolling digits are aria-hidden.
motion: Adjustment and coupon lines open with a height spring and fade.
The promo form swaps to the applied chip with a small scale and blur. An invalid code shakes the field horizontally for 360ms.
The total rolls through AnimatedCounter. The pay button's label and icon swap with a rise and blur on each state change, and a spinner turns while processing.
Reduced motion skips the shake, makes lines appear instantly, reduces swaps to fades, and slows the spinner to 1.6s per turn.

name: choropleth-explorer
title: Choropleth explorer
description: A filled-region map that shades every state or region by revenue, growth or penetration on a stepped scale, with a country switch (United States, Canada, Brazil, United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Australia), a hoverable legend, a synced ranked list and a camera zoom into local detail.
whenToUse: Sales, revenue or usage dashboards that break a metric down by state, country or territory.
Market coverage and penetration reviews where a region's own subareas explain its number.
Any analytics view where readers compare neighbouring areas and need the ranked numbers beside the map.
whenNotToUse: Use offices-map to place pins at specific locations such as offices or stores.
Use revenue-globe for flows and totals on a spinning globe when geography is ambience rather than the comparison.
Use a bar chart or sortable table when the regions are few, or when area size would mislead (a large, sparse region draws more attention than a small, dense one).
accessibility: The map is an image with a label naming the area and the metric; the ranked list next to it is the accessible path to every value and every zoom.
The list is one tab stop with roving focus. Each row names its rank, region, value and whether it opens counties.
Zooming, zooming out, switching the metric and pinning a county are announced through one polite live region, including the highest region for the new metric.
Legend steps are toggle buttons with aria-pressed and a label that counts their regions and states their range. Values carry a sign and a true minus, so direction never depends on color alone.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. Keyboard position shows as a filled row and an outline on the map.
motion: Switching the metric fades each region to its new fill with a delay set by its position, so the change sweeps across the map from west to east in under 800ms.

Selecting a state moves one camera on a critically damped spring: translate and scale travel together, so the state glides to the center in a straight line and can be reversed mid-flight. Counties fade in while the camera is still arriving; other states recede to context.
The headline total counts to each new value on a motion value, list rows glide to their new rank with a layout spring, and rank bars resize on a transform.
The tooltip follows the pointer on motion values without React renders; the hovered row scrolls into view inside the list, never the page.
Reduced motion makes every fill, zoom, count and reorder instant.

name: cohort-retention
title: Cohort retention
description: A cohort retention triangle that morphs into retention curves and rewashes by segment.
whenToUse: Growth or customer success dashboards comparing how signup cohorts retain month over month.
Views that need both the cohort triangle and retention curves from the same data.
whenNotToUse: Use journey-flow for paths between funnel steps.
Use activity-heatmap for activity by day rather than by cohort.
Use revenue-explorer for revenue over time.
accessibility: The chart is a focusable role="group" with aria-describedby, and a polite live region reads the focused cohort, month and rate.
Decorative cells and curves are aria-hidden; the legend is a labelled role="img".
motion: Cells morph into curves on the view switch and rewash their colour when the segment changes; headline figures roll with Animated counter.
Reduced motion jumps values instantly and follows the pointer without springs.

name: command-palette
title: Command palette
description: A complete keyboard driven action surface with search, grouped results, and shortcuts.
whenToUse: App-wide command search opened with Cmd or Ctrl plus K.
Jumping to pages, creating items, and running actions from one input.
Inline search panels that group results with shortcuts.
whenNotToUse: Use combobox to pick a value inside a form.
Use dropdown-menu for a short list of actions.
Use expanding-search or search-field to search page content.
accessibility: The input is a combobox with aria-controls and aria-activedescendant pointing at the listbox option, so focus never leaves the input.
Results are role=option buttons with aria-selected, grouped in labelled role=group containers.
A polite live region announces the result count, or No results, as the query changes.
It renders inline, not in a modal. Put it in a dialog yourself if it should trap focus and close on outside click.
motion: The panel rises in on a spring; the results frame springs to the list height as the query filters.
Remaining rows glide into place when the shift is small and snap when it is a long jump; the highlight follows the active row on the snappy spring for pointer and arrow keys.
Reduced motion removes the entrance, glides, and highlight travel.

examples.title: Inside a dialog
examples.code:
<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>
  <DialogContent title="Command palette">
    <CommandPalette
      items={items}
      onSelect={item => { run(item.id); setOpen(false); }}
      onClose={() => setOpen(false)}
    />
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>

name: comparison-table
title: Comparison table
description: An us versus them table with a sticky header, a highlighted column, and a stacked phone view.
whenToUse: Showing how your product stacks up against named alternatives.
Feature matrices with three to five columns and grouped rows.
whenNotToUse: Use plan-comparison to compare your own pricing tiers.
Use a sortable data table for large datasets.
accessibility: Built with table, row, columnheader, rowheader and cell roles, so screen readers navigate it as a table.
Marks have text alternatives: Included, Partial (with its note), Not included.
The switch is a real checkbox with role switch; a polite live region says when rows are filtered.
Meaning never relies on color: checks, half circles and dashes differ in shape, with a legend.
motion: Checks in your column draw in once, staggered down the table, when they scroll into view.
Differences only collapses matching rows on the smooth spring and closes the gap.
Picking a competitor on phones swaps its header and marks with a small pop.
The call to action morphs its label to the done state.
Reduced motion shows every mark at once and swaps collapses for instant changes.

name: connected-scatter
title: Connected scatter
description: A connected scatterplot of monthly CAC against LTV where the path draws itself in, a scrubber moves a head along the curve, and a channel switch morphs the path against a shaded 3x target line.
whenToUse: A growth or finance screen that shows whether unit economics are moving toward or away from a target ratio.
Comparing how a few segments or channels travelled through the same two metrics over the same months.
A report where specific months (a pricing change, a campaign) explain a turn and deserve a label on the path.
whenNotToUse: Use line-chart or metric-explorer when time itself is the axis and one metric is enough.
Use efficient-frontier for risk against return of a portfolio you can change.
Use a plain scatter or beeswarm when points have no time order to connect.
accessibility: The scrubber is role="slider" over the months, with a value text that reads the date, both values, the ratio and whether it is above or below the target.
A polite live region announces the month when the head settles and the new values when the channel changes. Playback announces only where it stops.
The readout is a description list, so the selected month, both values and the ratio are always available as text.
The chart drawing is hidden from assistive technology; a visually hidden table lists every month with both values and the ratio for the current channel.
Above or below target is written out beside a status dot, never shown by color alone.
