Choosing a suggestion types through execCommand insertText, so native undo keeps working.
motion: The field height springs to its content between minRows and maxRows.
Suggestions pop in from the caret with a small scale and a snappy spring; the highlight glides between rows and the panel height springs as results change.
Reduced motion jumps the height and highlight and fades the panel without scale or offset.

name: money-input
title: Money input
description: A currency field with live grouping, stable width, rolling digits, and minor-unit output.
whenToUse: Payment, tip, transfer, or budget amounts entered by hand.
Invoice and expense forms where the currency may change.
Amount fields that benefit from quick add chips such as +$10.
whenNotToUse: Use number-field for quantities and non currency numbers.
Use slider or price-ladder when people pick from a range rather than type.
Use scrub-input for design tool style drag adjustments.
accessibility: The input has role="spinbutton" with aria-valuenow in major units, aria-valuetext as the full currency string, and min and max when set.
The animated digits are aria-hidden; the real input carries the value, so screen readers and autofill see plain text.
The range, hint, and error are linked with aria-describedby; limits, chip adds, and currency changes are announced politely.
The currency menu is a listbox with aria-activedescendant and typeahead.
motion: Chips and arrow keys roll each digit column in the direction of change while new columns open their width; typing cuts straight to the result so the caret never lags.
A refused change kicks the amount sideways on a bouncy spring and flashes the range.
The currency symbol swaps with a short roll while its slot springs to the new width; long amounts scale down to fit on a spring.
Reduced motion removes the rolls, kick, and width springs; digits fade and sizes jump.

name: morph-select
title: Morph select
description: A select whose trigger grows into the list, with a gliding highlight and type-ahead.
whenToUse: Form fields and property panels where one value is picked from a known list.
Grouped lists like time zones, assignees, or projects, with optional icons and meta.
Compact toolbars where the picker should look like a pill until opened.
whenNotToUse: Use combobox when users type free text or the list is very long and remote.
Use multi-select when more than one value can be chosen.
Use dropdown-menu for actions rather than a stored value.
accessibility: The trigger is a role="combobox" with aria-haspopup="listbox", aria-expanded, and aria-activedescendant pointing at the active option.
With search on, the input takes over as the combobox with aria-autocomplete="list", and the trigger turns inert.
Options are role="option" with aria-selected and aria-disabled; groups are role="group" labelled by their heading.
A polite status announces the number of search results or No matches.
motion: The trigger surface grows into the list on a physical spring with slight bounce and folds back without overshoot; the corner radius morphs with it.
One highlight glides between options; the chosen label lifts out of the list and flies into the trigger while the trigger width springs.
Values in the trigger roll up or down depending on whether the new option is later or earlier in the list.
Reduced motion jumps the size, removes the fly and roll, and uses short fades.

name: multi-select
title: Multi-select
description: Select several values while keeping the field readable.
whenToUse: Picking several values from a fixed list in a compact field, such as labels or assignees.
Filters where the chosen values should show in the field with a +N overflow.
whenNotToUse: Use chip-group when every option should stay visible.
Use tag-input for free-form values.
Use select for a single value.
accessibility: Trigger has aria-haspopup="listbox", aria-expanded, and aria-labelledby combining the label and a hidden list of selected labels.
The menu is role="listbox" with aria-multiselectable; options carry aria-selected and aria-disabled.
Clear button is labelled "Clear selections"; chips are aria-hidden in favor of the spoken summary.
motion: Chips open their slot width on a smooth spring and grow in from 0.9 with a blur; the +N count rolls up or down.
Checks draw in the menu; the menu springs in from slightly above.
Reduced motion turns every change into a short crossfade with no scale or width travel.

name: number-field
title: Number field
description: Enter a bounded number with clear increment controls.
whenToUse: Bounded quantities like seats, items, or prices where the exact number matters.
Values people nudge with steppers, arrow keys, or by dragging the label with scrub.
Numbers with units, using a prefix or a pluralizing suffix function.
whenNotToUse: Use slider when the approximate position matters more than the exact number.
Use input for numeric strings like phone numbers or codes.
accessibility: The input has role="spinbutton" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, and aria-valuetext including prefix and suffix.
Stepper buttons are labelled "Increase <label>" and "Decrease <label>" and marked aria-disabled at a limit.
Changes are announced through a polite aria-live region, and a clamp says which limit it met ("10 seats, maximum"); rolling digits are aria-hidden.
A typed value past a limit sets aria-invalid and adds the limit note to aria-describedby until it commits. The warning also uses copy, never color alone.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. Focus darkens the shell border, and a focused stepper button takes its hover fill.
motion: Digits roll on wheels in the direction of change (up rolls up, down rolls down) with tabular numerals, and affixes reword in place.
Holding a stepper repeats after 400ms and ramps from 150ms to 40ms per step.

At a limit the value strains a few pixels toward the press and springs home; pushes in a row strain a little further, capped like overscroll. The refused button shakes once and the limit note rises in beside the label.
A typed value past a limit tints the shell with the warning role; on Enter or blur it springs back to the limit with a digit roll.
Reduced motion changes the value at once and answers a press at a limit with a brief warning tint on the number instead of the strain and shake.

name: password-field
title: Password field
description: Capture sensitive text with a visible reveal control.
whenToUse: Sign in forms and password confirmation fields.
Any secret the person may want to check by revealing it.
whenNotToUse: Use password-strength when creating or changing a password.
Use input for non-secret values.
accessibility: Toggle is a native button with aria-pressed and a label that switches between "Show password" and "Hide password" (messages.showPassword and messages.hidePassword).
Description is linked through aria-describedby.
Set autoComplete to current-password or new-password so password managers work.
motion: A slash draws across the eye and masks the outline beneath it instead of swapping icons.
After the first toggle, the value resolves through a short CSS reveal on each change; reduced motion draws the slash instantly.

examples.title: Translated
examples.code: <PasswordField label="Passwort" messages={{ showPassword: "Passwort anzeigen", hidePassword: "Passwort verbergen" }} />

name: password-strength
title: Password strength
description: Show how strong a new password is while it is typed.
whenToUse: Sign up and change password forms.
Password rules that should check off live as the person types.
whenNotToUse: Use password-field for sign in.
Use progress for measurable progress unrelated to passwords.
accessibility: The meter is role="meter" with aria-valuenow 0 to 4 and aria-valuetext set to the strength word.
The rules list is linked to the input through aria-describedby along with any error; errors set aria-invalid.
A role="status" region summarizes strength and rules met; the reveal button uses aria-pressed and aria-controls.
motion: Segments fill and change tone in a staggered wave, rules check off with drawn ticks, remaining counts roll, and the word morphs up or down with strength.
Reduced motion, applied after hydration, drops the shake, wave, and roll in favor of instant changes.

examples.title: Gate submit on strength
examples.code:
const [level, setLevel] = useState(0);

<PasswordStrength
  label="New password"
  name="password"
  autoComplete="new-password"
  onValueChange={(_, strength) => setLevel(strength.level)}
/>
<Button type="submit" disabled={level < 3}>Create account</Button>

examples.title: Translated, with your own length policy

name: phone-input
title: Phone input
description: A phone field with a country picker, formatting as you type, and E.164 output.
whenToUse: Sign up, checkout, and contact forms that need a phone number in E.164.
International audiences where the country and calling code must be clear.
Two factor setup before sending an SMS code.
whenNotToUse: Use input with type="tel" when you only store free text and never dial or text the number.
Use otp-input for the verification code itself.
Use a full metadata library if you need carrier or number type validation beyond length.
accessibility: The search is a combobox with aria-activedescendant over a listbox of options grouped into Suggested and All countries.
The country button reads "Country, <name> +<code>"; picks, pasted country changes, and result counts are announced politely.
The number input is type="tel" with autocomplete="tel"; errors are linked with aria-describedby and shown with role="alert" after blur.
A valid number is announced as "Valid <country> number" while a check appears.
motion: One surface springs its width, height, and corner radius from the country button into the list, and back when closing.
The flag and code roll in the direction of the list when the country changes; the highlight glides between rows.
Messages open on a height spring with a small rise and blur; the valid check pops in.
Reduced motion jumps the surface to size and replaces rolls, blurs, and glides with short fades.

name: radio-cards
title: Radio cards
description: Selectable option cards with a sliding selection ring, price and description slots, and radio keyboard behavior.
whenToUse: Choices where each option needs a description, price, or estimate to decide.
Plan, shipping, region, or size pickers inside checkout and setup flows.
Options that may be unavailable and need a visible reason.
whenNotToUse: Use radio-group for short text-only options.
Use segmented-control for two to four view modes that switch content instantly.
Use select or combobox for long lists.
accessibility: role="radiogroup" with role="radio" cards, aria-checked, and aria-disabled; give the group an aria-label or aria-labelledby.
Each card is labelled by its label and described by its description, or by disabledReason when disabled.
Selection is shown by a ring and a filled indicator dot, not color alone.
motion: One ring springs to the selected card's box and its size; resizes snap it without replaying the glide.
The indicator dot scales in on the snappy spring.
Reduced motion jumps the ring and dot to their final state.

name: radio-group
title: Radio group
description: Choose one option from a visible set.
whenToUse: Two to six mutually exclusive options that need descriptions, such as plans.
Form choices that should submit natively through name.
whenNotToUse: Use segmented-control for short inline view options.
Use select for longer lists.
Use checkbox when several options can be on at once.
accessibility: Uses a fieldset and legend with native radio inputs wrapped in labels.
The highlight and dot are aria-hidden decoration.
motion: One highlight glides to the chosen row on the morph spring while the new dot springs in and the old one shrinks away.
Reduced motion places the highlight and dot instantly; resizes never animate.

options.label: Monthly
options.description: Billed on the 1st of each month

name: range-histogram-slider
title: Range histogram slider
description: A price range over a live histogram of the data, lighting the bars inside the range and settling on bar edges.
whenToUse: Marketplace and search filters for price, size, or distance where the distribution guides the choice.
Analytics filters that trim outliers from a numeric column.
Any min and max choice where people benefit from seeing how many results fall inside.
whenNotToUse: Use slider for a plain range without data behind it.
Use elastic-slider or slider for a single value.
Use number-field pairs when people type exact bounds more often than they drag.
accessibility: Each thumb is role="slider" with its own name, aria-valuetext, and aria-valuemin/max that reflect the other thumb, so the pair never reads as crossing.
The histogram and the readout are aria-hidden; the thumbs carry the values.
Pass thumbLabels in the product's language when the defaults do not fit.
motion: Lit bars and the track fill are clipped by one path, so both cut exactly at each thumb on the same frame.
Thumbs follow the pointer 1:1, rubber-band a few pixels past their limit, and settle with the release velocity; momentum can carry them at most one bar.
Pressing the histogram or track springs the nearest thumb to that spot.
Reduced motion removes the stretch and springs; thumbs jump to their values.

name: rating
title: Rating
description: A simple, accessible way to capture a numeric opinion.
whenToUse: Collecting a 1 to N score in reviews or feedback forms.
Displaying average scores, with readOnly and allowHalf.
Forms that submit natively, via name.
whenNotToUse: Use slider for continuous values.
Use reactions for emoji feedback on content.
Use radio-group when options are labelled choices rather than a scale.
accessibility: Interactive ratings are role="radiogroup" with one role="radio" per step and a roving tab stop on the checked value.
Each radio is labelled like "Great, 4 of 5 stars"; commits are announced in a polite live region.
readOnly renders role="img" with an aria-label such as "Quality: 4 out of 5".
motion: The fill sweeps star by star with a small stagger in the direction the value moved; a commit pops the stars in a wave.
Pressed stars dip to 0.86 scale and the value word rolls in the direction of change.
Reduced motion sets fills instantly and drops the pop, press scale, and word roll.

name: rich-text-editor
title: Rich text editor
description: A lightweight editor with markdown shortcuts, a floating toolbar, a slash menu, and HTML and markdown output.
whenToUse: Comments, notes, and posts where people expect markdown shortcuts and a selection toolbar.
Forms that need Markdown or clean HTML out without pulling in a full editor framework.
Short to medium documents with headings, lists, quotes, and code blocks.
whenNotToUse: Use textarea for plain text, or mention-input when the only rich part is tagging people.
Use inline-edit for a single line edited in place.
Use code-block to display code, not to write prose.
accessibility: The editing surface has role textbox with aria-multiline and aria-label, and aria-readonly when read-only.
The slash menu is a listbox wired to the textbox with aria-controls and aria-activedescendant.
The floating toolbar has role toolbar with toggle buttons using aria-pressed; titles show shortcuts.
A polite live region announces Formatted, Link added, Undone, and similar results.
Toolbar buttons prevent mousedown so the text selection survives clicks.
motion: The toolbar glides with the selection and its surface springs between the formatting face and the link face, which slide and blur across each other.
The slash menu pops from the slash, its highlight glides between rows, and its height springs as results filter.
Reduced motion jumps the toolbar position and size, crossfades the faces, and fades menus without scale or offset.

examples.title: Controlled HTML with custom undo buttons

name: ruler-slider
title: Ruler slider
description: A tape of ticks that slides under a fixed needle, with momentum, snapping, and a rolling readout.
whenToUse: Onboarding and profile flows that ask for body measurements or goals.
Mobile-first inputs where dragging a scale is easier than typing.
Wide ranges with fine steps that a short slider track cannot resolve.
whenNotToUse: Use number-field when people know the exact number and prefer to type it.
Use slider or elastic-slider when the value is relative, like volume.
Use range-histogram-slider to pick a range.
accessibility: The tape viewport is role="slider" with aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, aria-valuenow, and aria-valuetext that includes the unit.
It is labelled by the visible label through aria-labelledby.
The rolling readout and needle are aria-hidden; the slider announces the value.
Horizontal trackpad scrolling moves the tape; vertical scrolling is left to the page.
motion: Dragging moves the tape 1:1; a flick coasts with scroll-like deceleration and lands on a tick.
Pulling past either end rubber-bands, and releasing pulls the tape home with the throw's speed.
Taps and keys glide on a spring that keeps any speed already in the tape; grabbing a coasting tape catches it in place.
Each digit of the readout rolls on its own column as ticks pass the needle.
Reduced motion removes coasting, rubber-banding, and glides; the tape jumps to the nearest tick.

name: scrub-input
title: Scrub input
description: A Figma-style number field: drag the label to scrub, or type values, units, and arithmetic.
whenToUse: Position, size, rotation, and opacity fields in an inspector panel.
Dense settings where typing exact values and dragging both matter.
Values with units such as px, %, or deg that people type mixed.
whenNotToUse: Use number-field for a normal form with stepper buttons and a visible label.
Use slider when the range and position matter more than the exact number.
Use money-input for currency amounts.
accessibility: The input is role="spinbutton" with aria-valuenow, finite aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax, and aria-valuetext that spells out percent and degrees.
The label is a real label for the input; clicking it focuses and selects the value.
Invalid typed text sets aria-invalid for 900ms and keeps the previous value.
The unit cycle button is labelled Unit: <unit>. Change unit.
motion: Past min or max the field strains with rubber-band resistance, up to 12px, and springs back on release; the number leans with it.
The track fill follows a drag one to one and glides to typed or stepped values.
Invalid input and steps against a limit kick the field with a short shake; unit changes rise from a small blur.
Reduced motion removes the strain, shake, and glide, and swaps the unit with a fade.

examples.title: Rotation that wraps
examples.code: <ScrubInput label="R" min={0} max={360} wrap unit="°" units={["°"]} fineStep={0.1} onValueCommit={value => setRotation(value)} />

name: search-field
title: Search field
description: A recognizable search entry point with clear affordances.
whenToUse: Filtering a visible list or table in place.
Toolbar search where the query should be clearable with one click.
whenNotToUse: Use expanding-search for compact header search with results.
Use combobox when the search sets a form value.
Use filter-toolbar when search sits with other filters and sort.
accessibility: Native input type="search" with a real label.
Clear button is labelled "Clear search" and returns focus to the input.
The search icon is aria-hidden.
motion: The clear button scales in from 0.8 with a slight blur on a snappy spring and presses to 0.96.
Reduced motion fades it in and out without scale or blur; the reserved slot keeps the field width fixed either way.

name: segmented-control
title: Segmented control
description: Switch between a small set of related views.
whenToUse: Two to five short view options like Day, Week, and Month.
Toolbar toggles between layouts or modes that apply immediately.
whenNotToUse: Use tabs when each option swaps a panel of content.
Use radio-group in forms or when options need descriptions.
Use switch for a single on and off setting.
accessibility: Renders role="group" labelled by label, with native buttons using aria-pressed for the selected segment. Only the selected segment is a tab stop.
The sliding pill is aria-hidden.
motion: A shared layoutId pill slides to the selected segment on the morph spring, scoped per instance by a LayoutGroup.
Reduced motion moves the pill instantly and disables button transitions.

name: select
title: Select
description: A compact choice field with a keyboard friendly menu.
whenToUse: A short fixed list where typing is not needed, such as region or sort order.
Form fields that should submit natively through Radix's hidden select via name.
whenNotToUse: Use combobox for long or searchable lists.
Use multi-select when several values can be chosen.
Use segmented-control for two to four choices that should stay visible.
accessibility: Built on Radix Select, so the trigger, listbox, and options get the right roles and focus handling.
The real value renders in a visually hidden Radix Value; the animated copy is aria-hidden.
Label is linked with htmlFor, and description through aria-describedby.
motion: A later option rises in from below and an earlier one drops from above, with a soft blur.
Reduced motion swaps the value with an instant crossfade.

name: shortcut-recorder
title: Shortcut recorder
description: Record key combinations into key caps, with conflict warnings, Kbd, and a searchable cheatsheet.
whenToUse: Settings pages where people remap keyboard shortcuts.
A keyboard shortcut cheatsheet or help dialog, with ShortcutList.
Inline key hints in menus, tooltips, and docs, with ShortcutKbd or ShortcutKeys.
whenNotToUse: Use ShortcutKbd alone when shortcuts are fixed and only need to be shown.
Use command-palette to let people run actions by name rather than bind keys.
Avoid it on touch-only products where no hardware keyboard is expected.
accessibility: The recorder is a button with aria-pressed while recording, named by the label plus the spoken shortcut, such as "Command Shift K".
Recording, results, conflicts, and clears are announced through a polite live region; the message row is linked with aria-describedby.
Key caps are aria-hidden inside the recorder; ShortcutKeys uses role="img" with a spoken aria-label.
Conflicts offer Use anyway and Cancel as real buttons, and focus returns to the recorder after either.
motion: Caps pop in with a small scale and blur, staggered when a finished shortcut settles, and slide on a snappy layout spring as the chord changes.
A recording dot pulses; the message row opens on a height spring.
In ShortcutList, groups and rows collapse on a height spring as search filters them.
Reduced motion removes the scale, stagger, layout slide, and height springs; caps and messages fade.

name: signature-pad
title: Signature pad
description: Smooth ink that thins with speed, with undo, replay, and PNG or SVG export.
whenToUse: Contracts, delivery confirmations, and consent forms that need a drawn signature.
Initials or quick sketches where pen pressure and natural stroke width matter.
Flows that need a clean, cropped PNG or SVG of the signature.
whenNotToUse: Use input for a typed name when a legal drawn signature is not required.
Use file-upload when the user already has a scanned signature image.
Use hold-to-confirm for a simple deliberate confirmation without a signature artifact.
accessibility: The pad is focusable with role="img", aria-roledescription="signature pad", and a label that states the stroke count.
Keyboard shortcuts are described through aria-describedby on a visually hidden paragraph.
Ink color and width are radio groups with roving tabindex; toolbar icon buttons carry aria-label and title.
A polite status region announces strokes added, undo, redo, clear, replay, and export results.
motion: Clear sweeps a squeegee edge across the pad while a clip-path wipe removes the ink over 0.56s.
Replay redraws each stroke in its original rhythm with a nib dot, capping gaps between strokes and fitting the whole replay into about 3.2s.
The hint fades up from a soft blur; the selected color and width highlight glides with a shared layout spring.
Reduced motion skips the wipe and blur and uses short opacity fades.

name: slider
title: Slider
description: Pick a value or a range on a track that follows your finger.
whenToUse: Approximate values like volume, opacity, or a price range.
Ranges with two thumbs, labelled marks, and a formatted readout.
whenNotToUse: Use number-field when the exact number matters.
Use progress to show a value people cannot change.
accessibility: Each thumb is role="slider" with aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, aria-valuenow, aria-valuetext from format, and aria-orientation.
Thumbs are named by label, or by thumbLabels for ranges.
The readout, bubble, and marks are aria-hidden because the thumbs carry the value.
motion: Released drags carry a little momentum before snapping; the bubble springs up over an active thumb and digits roll in the readout. At a limit the thumb strains toward the key press and springs back.
Reduced motion removes momentum, the strain, and digit rolling, and turns off CSS transitions.

name: switch
title: Switch
description: A tactile toggle for settings that take effect immediately.
whenToUse: Settings that take effect as soon as they are flipped, like notifications.
Settings lists where each row is one on and off preference.
whenNotToUse: Use checkbox when the choice waits for a submit button.
Use segmented-control for a choice between named options.
Use theme-switch for a light and dark toggle.
accessibility: Radix renders a button with role="switch" and aria-checked.
The label prop becomes aria-label unless one is passed; icon-only usage needs an aria-label.
motion: Pressing stretches the thumb toward the other side like a held finger; releasing sends it across on a snappy spring.
Reduced motion removes the stretch and moves the thumb instantly; CSS transitions are also disabled.

name: tag-input
title: Tag input
description: Turn short text values into removable tags.
whenToUse: Free-form lists of short values like tags, keywords, or emails.
Fields where people add values by pressing Enter or comma.
whenNotToUse: Use multi-select or chip-group when values come from a fixed list.
Use input for a single value.
accessibility: Each tag has a remove button labelled "Remove <tag>".
Adds, removals, picks, and duplicates are announced in a polite aria-live region.
Blurring the input commits any typed draft as a tag.
motion: New tags blur and scale in where the text was typed; removed tags leave and the rest glide on the morph spring. The shell follows wrapped rows on a smooth spring.
A ring glides between picked tags. Reduced motion removes layout travel, scale, and blur, keeping fades.

name: textarea
title: Textarea
description: A multiline field for notes, descriptions, and longer text.
whenToUse: Free-form multi-line text like bios, comments, or feedback.
Fields with a live character count, which rolls its digits in the helper row.
whenNotToUse: Use input for single-line values.
Use inline-edit with multiline for a description edited in place on a page.
Use tag-input when the text is really a list of short values.
accessibility: Native textarea with a real label.
Description and error ids are merged into aria-describedby; errors set aria-invalid and use role="alert".
Animated copy is aria-hidden and mirrored in a visually hidden plain-text span.
motion: Message rows open their height on a smooth spring; changed words rise in with a soft blur and counts roll only the digits that changed.
Reduced motion drops the roll, blur, and height spring for instant changes.

name: time-picker
title: Time picker
description: Choose a time with sensible keyboard behavior.
whenToUse: Picking a time of day at a fixed interval, such as meetings or reminders.
Fields that show 12-hour times but store 24-hour HH:mm values.
whenNotToUse: Use date-picker for dates, pairing the two for a timestamp.
Use time-dial for a more tactile, showcase time selection.
Use select when only a few named times are allowed.
accessibility: Trigger has aria-haspopup="listbox", aria-expanded, aria-controls, and aria-labelledby combining the label and a hidden value.
The menu is role="listbox" with role="option" items carrying aria-selected.
The list opens centered on the selected time and scrolls only itself, never the page.
motion: A later time rises in from below and an earlier one drops from above with a soft blur; the menu springs in from slightly above.
Reduced motion crossfades the value and opens the menu with opacity only.

name: toggle-group
title: Toggle group
description: A row of icon or text toggles, single or multiple: one pressed fill glides between options, or each fades in on its own and neighbours join, as in a formatting toolbar.
whenToUse: Formatting toolbars: bold, italic and underline as multiple, alignment as single.
Compact view options on a canvas, map or editor, such as grid or list, or which layers to show.
Any short row of icon toggles that apply immediately.
whenNotToUse: Use segmented-control for switching between views, ranges or tabs of content.
Use checkbox or switch for settings in a form that are saved together.
Use chip-group for filters with long text labels or many options that wrap.
accessibility: Single mode renders role="radiogroup" with role="radio" items and aria-checked; multiple mode renders role="group" with aria-pressed buttons. Both are labelled by label.
Roving tabindex: only one item is a tab stop, so a toolbar with several groups stays quick to cross with Tab.
Icon only items take their accessible name and tooltip from label. Pressed state is shown by fill and text contrast, and exposed through aria-checked or aria-pressed.
The fills are aria-hidden decoration.
motion: Single: one fill with a shared layoutId moves to the chosen item on the morph spring, scoped per group by a LayoutGroup; its radius is scale corrected so it keeps its shape between items of different widths.

Multiple: every item owns a fill that fades in over 180ms while it settles from 86% scale on the spring curve. When two neighbours are on, the fills close the gap and square off their inner corners, so a run of pressed items reads as one shape.
Pressing an item gives its icon and label a small 92% press and spring back; the item box never scales, so neighbours never shift.
Reduced motion moves the single fill instantly and replaces fades and presses with instant color changes.

name: window-range
title: Window range
description: A time window over a live area chart: drag its edges to resize, drag or flick it to pan with momentum, and the dates roll to their new values.
whenToUse: Choosing the date range of an analytics report while seeing the shape of the data behind it.
Scrubbing a window over usage, revenue or latency to compare periods.
A compact overview with a movable window above a detailed chart or table.
whenNotToUse: Use date-range-picker when people pick exact dates from a calendar or the range spans years.
Use brush-chart when the window should zoom a large detailed chart and show events in place.
Use slider or gooey-range for numeric ranges that have no series to show.
accessibility: The component is a group named by label with three focusable role="slider" elements: the start edge, the window and the end edge.

Each edge speaks its formatted date, with aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax that respect minSpan and maxSpan. The window speaks both ends, such as Aug 31 to Sep 29, and its range is the start positions it can take.
The chart, the frame and the rolling readouts are decorative and hidden from assistive technology; the sliders carry every value.
Pressing into a limit with a key nudges the frame against it instead of failing silently.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. A pressed part takes focus so keys continue where the pointer left off.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop steps the frame's springs at 240 Hz and writes transforms straight to the DOM through a cache; it stops at rest, offscreen and in background tabs.
Dragging an edge or the window follows the finger one to one with coalesced pointer events. Past either end of the domain, or past the span limits, the frame rubber bands.

Releasing a pan keeps the measured speed: the landing point is projected from the flick, snapped to a step and reached on a critically damped spring that starts at the flick's speed, so the window decelerates like a scroll view and bumps softly into either end. Grabbing it mid coast stops it where it is.
A press outside the window glides it to center on the finger on a softer spring; dragging on moves it from there. Keys, presets and new values from props glide the same way.
The full color chart shows through a clip that is scaled to the window while its content is scaled back, so moving the window never relayouts or repaints the chart; outside it the muted copy shows.
The readouts roll each changed digit, and month names as a whole word, in the direction of change. During a drag or a coast they update in place so they never trail the frame.
New data morphs the line and area from the old shape on a smooth spring. The live dot pulses with a compositor animation.
With reduced motion the frame jumps to each value, there is no coast, rubber band, roll, chart morph or pulse, and every value, key and readout still works.

name: action-morph
title: Action morph
description: A floating button that morphs into a quick-action menu, then an inline form, then back with a check.
whenToUse: Quick capture of tasks, notes, or comments without leaving the page.
Apps with a few frequent create actions that deserve a persistent button.
Mobile layouts where a corner button should expand into a small form.
whenNotToUse: Use dialog or drawer for longer forms with several fields.
Use dropdown-menu when actions run immediately and need no input.
Use action-button for one async save on a button in place.
accessibility: The button has aria-haspopup="menu"; after success its label adds the success message.
The menu is role="menu" labelled by its title, with role="menuitem" buttons and aria-keyshortcuts for letter shortcuts.
Composer fields set aria-invalid and aria-describedby on an empty or failed submit; the form sets aria-busy while sending.
A polite status region announces the success label, and focus moves into each new face and back to the button on close.
motion: One surface animates width, height, and corner radius on physical springs: growing carries a little bounce, folding settles without overshoot.
Going deeper slides the new face in from the right and pushes the old one left; menu rows stagger in; a highlight glides between actions.
Submitting folds the composer into the button, which tints to success while a check draws itself, then the plus rotates back in.
Reduced motion jumps the size, swaps faces with fades, drops the press scale and shake, and slows the spinner.

name: activity-rings
title: Activity rings
description: Daily goals as tick rings that sweep, count up, and trace a second lap past 100%.
whenToUse: Daily goals that fill up and can be exceeded, like move, exercise, and stand.
Fitness or habit dashboards with a week picker to compare days.
whenNotToUse: Use progress or gauge for a single value.
Use usage-meter for quotas and limits.
Use activity-heatmap for streaks across many weeks.
accessibility: The rings are an img whose label lists each goal's percent for the day.
Legend rows are toggle buttons with aria-pressed and a spoken summary such as "Move, 420 of 500 kcal, 84 percent".
The week picker is a radiogroup with a roving tabindex, named by each day's full label.
motion: Every change sweeps from what is on screen to the new values, so a quick second change redirects mid flight; past 100% a second lap traces the inside edge.
Hovering or selecting a goal dims the others, and numbers count to their new amounts.
MotionConfig follows the user's reduced motion setting, and values jump without the sweep.

name: agent-cursor
title: Agent cursor
description: A live document where Claude edits like a collaborator. Its labeled cursor comes out of its avatar, selects a paragraph and streams in a rewrite, adds a heading and fixes a typo, while a teammate's cursor reads along. Changes stay tinted until someone accepts or undoes them from a floating review bar.
whenToUse: Showing an AI writing assistant that edits a doc alongside people, with accept and undo.
Landing or onboarding sections that demo a collaborative AI editor in motion.
A product surface that streams structured edits from an agent and needs a human review step.
whenNotToUse: Free form chat or Q&A: use a chat transcript component.
A real rich text editor: wire your editor's own collaboration cursors; this card renders read-only blocks.
Long documents with many sections: the card is built for a short excerpt of five to ten blocks.
accessibility: A polite live region announces each step (reading, the current edit, edits ready, accepted, undone, errors), and adds "Simulated, nothing was saved" for simulated runs.
Cursors, selections and the visual status line are decorative and hidden from assistive tech; the document stays real headings and paragraphs, marked aria-busy while the agent edits.
Status never relies on color: every terminal state pairs an icon with a label, and pending changes are tinted and listed in the review bar with a count.
Focus inside the card or a hovering pointer holds the looping demo in review, so nobody loses the bar mid reach.
motion: Cursors glide on a gentle quadratic arc with an ease-in-out curve, 280 to 600ms by distance, driven by motion values so nothing re-renders per frame.
Selections fill line by line in step with the drag. Rewrites fade the old text out in 110ms, then stream 3 to 6 words every 34ms, each chunk fading in over 140ms with no blur or slide.
Block heights follow measured content with a bounce-free spring (0.24s); inserted blocks grow from zero, then their text fades in.
Status labels crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in). The review bar rises 8px and fades in 200ms.
Reduced motion: cursors jump to each target, text appears whole, the loop and idle drift stop, and every end state stays.
Playback pauses while the card is off screen.

name: agent-handoff
title: Agent handoff
description: A support conversation where an AI assistant hands off to a person. When it transfers, a card shows the summary it passes to the team and the typical wait. The person then joins and takes over, and a thin timeline on the left marks each step.
whenToUse: A support widget where the AI answers first and escalates to a human agent.
Showing customers what the assistant shared with the team, so they do not repeat themselves.
Marketing or docs pages that explain an AI to human handoff flow.
whenNotToUse: A general chat with one assistant and no handoff: use chat-thread.
Showing an agent's internal steps or tool calls: use agent-timeline or tool-call.
A full help desk inbox for agents: build it from list and detail layouts instead.
accessibility: The thread is a focusable log so keyboard users can scroll it; it does not announce every streamed chunk.
Stage changes and action results are announced once through a polite status region, including that the demo is simulated.
Every status pairs an icon with a label: Transferring, With Jordan, Resolved, No one available. Color is never the only signal.
The summary toggle uses aria-expanded and aria-controls. Typing dots carry a label such as Jordan is typing.
Marks and avatars on the timeline are decorative next to their visible labels.
motion: Assistant replies stream in chunks of 3 to 8 words every ~34ms; each chunk only fades in over 140ms.
The thread animates to its measured height with a bounce-free spring (0.24s), so new rows and streamed lines push it up without a snap.
While transferring, a small accent dot travels down the timeline beside the handoff card.
Status labels crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in, 2px rise). Loops pause off screen.
Reduced motion: replies appear whole, no travel dot, typing dots and spinner hold still, no height animation, the demo plays once.

name: agent-loop
title: Agent loop
description: An illustration of the agent loop: gather context, take action, verify, repeat, with a bright head circling three stations around the model.
whenToUse: Docs, explainers and landing pages that teach how an AI agent works: it gathers context, calls tools, checks the result and repeats until the task is done.
Showing why agents take several passes, with a failed check or a failed tool call that sends the loop round again.
A visual summary of a finished agent run with the tools it used and the context it built up.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run or research-run to show a real agent's live steps and streamed output.
Use tool-call for a single tool call card inside a chat or a log.
Use reasoning-tree to explain search over thoughts rather than tool use.
Use mcp-flow to explain how a host talks to MCP servers over a transport.
Use context-window to show what fills a model's context and how close it is to the limit.
accessibility: The card is a labelled group. Station names, tool calls, results, checks and context blocks are real text, and the ring drawing itself (track, pins, head) is hidden from assistive technology.
A polite status region speaks each beat when you step or pause (for example "GitHub returned: EU cards, since Oct 18"), and the summary at the end, but stays quiet while the loop plays on its own.

Status never relies on color: ready, running, paused, done and stopped each pair an icon with a label; a tool result shows a check or a cross, a failed call says failed to screen readers, and a check shows a check icon with "Check passed" or a rotate icon with "Retry".
The context list is an ordered list, read in the order blocks were gathered.
When stepping reaches the end, Next step turns off and focus moves to Restart instead of falling back to the page.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus uses Arc's shared focus outline on every control.
motion: The head eases from station to station round the ring and drags a soft gradient trail that stretches with its speed and shrinks to nothing when it lands, so it never sits still with a tail. Small chevrons on the track show the direction.
The active station's node fills, a thin ring settles around it and its label carries a calm shimmer that stops with a clear solid state.

A tool call drops out of the ring: the pin under Take action draws down in about 180ms, then the chip lands at its end with a 6px drop and a slight scale on a critically damped spring (no bounce), growing from the pin. Its spinner crossfades to a check or a cross as the result fades in. A second call crossfades into the same lane after the old one fades out in 80ms, so nothing reflows. Checks drop from Verify the same way.
A new context block fades in at the end of the stack with a short drop while the token count rolls up in tabular numerals; the space for every block is reserved, so the card never grows.
The loop counter rolls its digit up inside a fixed width. Labels such as the status and the caption swap with one short crossfade.
At the end the ring draws in clockwise in about 760ms and the head fades out. A stopped run leaves the ring neutral.
Reduced motion opens on the done state. Playing and stepping still work, with no travel and no trail: the head jumps between stations and each change applies in place.

name: agent-plan
title: Agent plan
description: The plan an agent writes before it acts: edit, reorder or add steps while it is a draft, then watch it work through them as a live checklist.
whenToUse: An agent should show and get approval for its plan before it edits code, runs commands or touches production.
A person needs to adjust the agent's plan (rename, reorder, remove or add steps) and then watch the same plan execute.
A side panel or chat message that tracks a multi-step task with a live current step, failures that need a decision, and a final summary.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run for a streaming transcript of everything the agent did, with tool calls and output, rather than a checklist of steps.
Use agent-approvals when the person approves individual risky actions one at a time instead of a whole plan up front.
Use agent-tasks for a queue of independent tasks across agents rather than one ordered plan.
Use research-run for search and reading progress that ends in a cited answer.
accessibility: The plan is a section named after the model and the goal; the steps are an ordered list, so a screen reader announces the count and each position.

Every step announces its state in words (Pending, In progress, Done, Failed, Skipped) before its title. Each state also has its own shape, a ring, a spinning arc, two bars, a disc with a check, a disc with an exclamation mark or a dashed ring, so it never rests on color.
A failed step shows the word Failed with its reason and two labelled buttons. Skipped steps say Skipped beside the title.
Titles are labelled text areas described by a hidden hint that explains Alt plus the arrow keys and Escape. Grips and remove buttons are named after their step and position.
Edits, approval, each finished step, an inserted step, a failure, pause and the final summary are announced through one polite status region, including that the preview is a simulation.
Focus follows the action: a moved step keeps focus, a removed step hands it to its neighbour, Approve plan hands it to Pause, and Retry or Skip hand it back to Pause.
The progress line is a progressbar with a text value ("2 of 6 steps finished"), hidden while the plan is a draft.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring, inset on controls inside clipped rows.
motion: Reorders, inserts, removals and activity lines move on a critically damped spring (about 260ms, no bounce), so rows slide and grow without overshoot.
Completing a step draws its check as a stroke over about 220ms while the disc fades up beneath it, and the title color settles from primary to secondary.
The current step's title shimmers with Arc's text shimmer beside a spinning arc; pausing stops both and swaps the arc for a pause glyph.
A suggested step streams its title in chunks of a few words every 34ms, each chunk only fading in. A step the agent inserts arrives with a faint accent wash that fades out over about 1.8s.
Counts roll with tabular digits in a reserved width. The header label, footer actions and status icons swap with one short crossfade, and the footer's height follows on the same spring.
Reduced motion keeps every state, label, focus move and announcement but drops travel, the spinner, the stroke draw, the wash and the chunk fades.

name: agent-status
title: Agent status
description: A compact live status pill for a running AI agent: the agent's mark in a live ring, the current activity and an elapsed timer, opening into the steps so far.
whenToUse: An app header, title bar or composer that needs to show at a glance that an agent is running, what it is doing and for how long.
Coding, research or browser agents that pause for approval, so the person can approve or deny without opening a full run view.
Background runs that people check on occasionally: the pill stays small, and the panel shows recent steps and controls on demand.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run or research-run when the run itself is the page and every step, tool call and output needs room.
Use agent-approvals to review a queue of pending approvals across several agents.
Use agent-orchestrator or agent-tasks to compare many agents or runs at once.
Use text-shimmer alone for a single inline working label without a timer, steps or controls.
accessibility: The pill is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at the panel, and an accessible name that reads the agent, the activity, the count and the elapsed time.

A polite status region announces each new activity and the outcome ("Claude Sonnet 5.5: done in 14 seconds, 6 files changed"), not every tick of a count or the timer. Pass notice to add the result of an action.

Status never relies on color: every state pairs the ring and glyph with words (Ready, Paused, Needs your approval, Done in, Failed, Stopped after), and steps use present tense while running and past tense once finished.
The step progress bar is a progressbar with a value text such as "4 of 6 steps finished".

Pause and Resume, and Approve and the Pause that follows it, share one button, so keyboard focus stays in place. If a focused control disappears with a state change, focus moves to the pill instead of the page.

In narrow containers the inline Approve, Deny and Retry and the Open run button become icon buttons with accessible names. A truncated activity stays readable in full through the pill's name and the panel's step list.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring, inset on the pill.
motion: A new activity rolls in vertically in about 180ms while the old one leaves upward; the pill's width follows on the morph spring, and the label fades at its right edge only while it is wider than its room, so nothing snaps or wraps.

Opening the panel springs width and height together on the smooth spring from the pill's own footprint; the header row stays where it is and the panel content fades in after a beat. Closing reverses it with a faster fade.

The live ring spins a short arc while working, freezes in place when paused, gives way to an accent dot with one soft ping when input is needed, and closes around the glyph as the mark morphs into a drawn check (done) or cross (failed).
The working label carries a calm shimmer that stops in every other state. Counts and the timer change in place with tabular numerals.
New steps fade in at the bottom of the panel while older ones slide up; segments of the progress bar fill from the left.
Reduced motion swaps every spring for an instant change, drops the roll, the spin, the ping and the shimmer, and keeps all states, text, focus and announcements.

name: agent-timeline
title: Agent timeline
description: A compact timeline of one orchestrated agent run: the orchestrator and its subagents share a time axis, handoffs draw in between rows, and a playhead replays thinking, tool calls and waiting while the header counts time, tokens and cost. Hover a span for what it did, or click it to trace its handoff path.
whenToUse: Showing how an orchestrator split work across subagents and how long each part took, in a run history, a trace viewer or a debugging panel.
Replaying a finished agent run in a product demo or changelog, with real numbers for time, tokens and cost.
Following a multi-agent run live as events stream in from your backend.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-orchestrator for a full screen of agent lanes with streaming text and messages; this timeline is the compact, reusable view of timing.
Use observability-trace for distributed request tracing across services rather than agents.
Use agent-run or research-run when people need the agent's steps, sources and answer, not the timing.
Use tool-call for the detail of a single tool invocation, and agent-status for one agent's current state.
accessibility: The root is a labelled section. Each row of spans is a group named by its agent label, and every span is a button whose name reads the agent, the kind, the tool, failure, what it did, its time range and tokens; aria-pressed marks the pinned span.
Spans use a roving tab index, so the chart is one tab stop and arrow keys move between spans by row and by time.
The scrubber is a slider with a value text such as "12.4s of 26.4s" and full keyboard support; dragging anywhere on the axis moves it.

Status is never color alone: a failed call shows a cross icon and the word Failed in its card and the legend, a retry shows a retry icon and its note, and the finished state shows a check with the summary.
A polite live region announces replay, pause and the finished summary. The counting status line is not live, so it never floods a screen reader.
The span card repeats what the span's accessible name already says, so it is hidden from assistive technology.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring on spans, the scrubber thumb and the controls.
motion: Bars and the playhead read one CSS variable for the current time, updated every animation frame, so spans grow smoothly without React rendering per frame; React updates counters and states about twenty times a second.

An active span has a square, solid leading edge and a short shine that stops when it ends; its corner rounds off as it completes. A failed call changes to its failed look with a quick color fade when it returns.
Connectors draw in with a clip reveal from the side the handoff leaves, about 360ms, and the port dot pops in at the start of a dispatch or after a result lands.
The span card glides between spans on the morph spring, crossfades its content and springs to its new height; the status line and play button swap with one minimal crossfade.
When the run ends the playhead fades out and the status settles into the summary.
Reduced motion starts on the finished run and drops the shine, the connector draw, the card glide and the status crossfades. Playback still works when the person asks for it.

name: ai-command
title: AI command
description: A Cmd+K command palette with an AI mode. Search pages and actions, or press Tab to ask a question: the answer streams inside the palette with numbered sources, and the next steps it suggests, like filing a Linear issue or opening a Notion doc, run straight from the list.
whenToUse: A global Cmd+K in a SaaS app where people both jump to pages and ask questions about their workspace.
Search that should fall back to an AI answer when nothing matches.
Answers that lead straight to an action in another tool, like filing a Linear issue or posting to Slack.
whenNotToUse: A long, multi-turn conversation: use a chat thread.
Plain navigation with no AI: use command-palette.
Inline field suggestions while typing in a form: use an autocomplete input.
accessibility: The input is a combobox that owns a listbox; the active row is announced through aria-activedescendant, so focus never leaves the input.
A polite live region announces questions, finished answers, action results and simulated runs ("Simulated, nothing was sent").
Status is never color alone: running, done and failed actions change both the icon and the label.
Citations and source chips are buttons with full descriptions as their accessible names; hovering or focusing one highlights its partner.
The mode toggle uses aria-pressed buttons and keeps input focus.
motion: The palette never changes size: the results area has a fixed height and views crossfade in place (100ms out, 160ms in, 2px rise).
One highlight glides between rows in 130ms and jumps without travel when the list itself changes, so typing never animates.
Answers stream 3 to 7 words every 34ms, each chunk fading in over 140ms; the view follows the text down unless you scroll up.
Labels, status icons and footer hints swap with a single crossfade. The done check draws once.
Reduced motion: no walkthrough, no chunk fades or travel; the answer reveals in large steps and every state stays.
The walkthrough pauses off screen through IntersectionObserver and restarts from a clean state.

name: ai-mascot
title: AI mascot
description: A small assistant character, a soft pebble with pill eyes and a companion dot, that shows what the AI is doing. It breathes and glances when idle, leans in to listen, looks up while the dot orbits its head, reads along the line it writes, squints with a sparkle when done and shakes once with worried brows on an error.
whenToUse: Give an assistant a face that shows what it is doing: in a reply header, beside a composer, on an image canvas while it generates, or in an empty state.
Products that want generation to feel alive and friendly without a spinner, with states that read at 24px.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-status when people need the steps, tools and elapsed time of a run, not just a mood.
Use text-shimmer alone for a plain "Thinking" line in dense interfaces where a character would distract.
Do not use it as a progress indicator with a known percentage; use a progress bar.
accessibility: The SVG has role img and a label built from name and status, for example "Atlas, thinking", which updates with every state.
With announce, status changes are read in a polite live region outside the image. Use it on one mascot per view so screen readers do not hear duplicates.
Status is never carried by motion alone: each state changes the face (wide eyes, eyes up, eyes down, happy squint, worried brows) and the label. Show a text status next to it where the state matters.
Pointer following ignores touch and is off under reduced motion.
motion: Every state is a continuous function of time (sums of slow sines, an orbit angle, a writing cycle whose start and end meet at zero length), so loops never restart and have no seam.

A status change blends the old pose into the new one over 420ms with an ease in and out; a change during a blend starts from the frame on screen. The first paint (and the server render) is the still pose, and the loop eases out of it over the same 420ms, so nothing jumps on mount. Eyes ride a critically damped spring: quick saccades when idle, a soft follow while thinking, tight tracking while writing. Nothing bounces.
Done passes the eyes through a closed line into the happy squint while the dot shrinks and the sparkle grows in its place. Error shakes once, decaying to rest in about .7s.

The dot is drawn twice, behind and in front of the body, and switches layers only at the ends of its orbit where it is clear of the body. While it crosses the crown in front it fades into the eye color, so it stays visible on the body.
Blinks come every 2.4 to 5.2s, sometimes twice, and take 160ms.

Reduced motion shows a still, representative pose for each state (eyes up with the dot over the head, half a written line, the squint and sparkle, the brows), switches in place and drops every loop, glance, blink and shake.

name: ai-spark
title: AI spark
description: A brand-quality animated spark mark. Four tapered rays and four lighter diagonals breathe at rest, ripple while thinking, pulse like a heartbeat while writing, then gather and settle when done. Every status change blends from the pose the mark is already in.
whenToUse: Showing that an assistant is thinking or writing, inline above a streaming reply.
A send or generate button that turns into a working indicator inside a composer.
An image or canvas tool that needs a calm, branded working mark over the canvas while a render runs.
Empty states and onboarding where a 64 to 96px hero mark gives the AI feature an identity.
whenNotToUse: Determinate progress with a known percentage; use a progress bar or the generation stats component instead.
Multi step agent runs where each step needs its own state and detail; use agent-status or agent-run.
Plain text loading lines with no mark; use text-shimmer.
accessibility: The root is a polite live region (role="status"): a status change is announced once, as "AI is thinking" for the mark or as the label text for the pill.
aria-busy is set while thinking or generating.
Status is never color alone: each state has its own shape and motion, error shortens the rays and dims the diagonals, and the pill adds a text label.
Set announce={false} on decorative copies (lists, size ladders) so screen readers hear one voice. They then render as role="img" with an accessible name.
The SVG is aria-hidden; the name comes from the label or a visually hidden phrase.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop per spark writes eight small ray paths, a core radius and two group transforms. React never re-renders per frame and nothing triggers layout.
Every status is a periodic function of time and of position around the ring, so idle, thinking and generating loop with no seam.

Idle: a 6.4s breath of the whole mark while one diagonal at a time softly reaches out. Thinking: one crest ripples around the ring every 1.9s, with small per-ray phase offsets, while the mark turns at 26 degrees per second. Generating: a lub dub heartbeat every 1.04s, axes firing in sequence and diagonals answering, 46 degrees per second, with two particles orbiting just outside the rays (40px and up).
Done: the rays gather toward the center in 170ms and ease back to rest over 510ms with no overshoot, while the spin glides into the home angle on an ease-out whose speed only falls.
Error: one small decaying shake over 460ms, shorter rays, dimmer diagonals and a muted danger tone over 320ms.

Status changes blend over 420 to 560ms from wherever the mark is; an interrupted blend becomes the new starting point, and the gather and shake gestures always finish smoothly even if the status changes again. Pill labels crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in, 2px rise) while the pill eases to its new width.
Reduced motion: no spin, loops, gather, shake or particles. Each status shows a still pose with a 200ms blend between poses and the color change.
The loop pauses when the spark is off screen or the tab is hidden, and stops entirely once a resting state has settled.

examples.title: Assistant avatar
examples.code: <AiSpark variant="avatar" size={32} status={phase} announce={false} />

examples.title: Inline in a sentence
examples.code: Drafting a reply to Maya Chen

examples.title: Custom progress label
examples.code: <AiSpark variant="pill" status="thinking" label="Searching 4 sources" />

examples.title: Hero mark in an empty state
examples.code: <AiSpark size={96} status="idle" />

name: ai-translate
title: AI translate
description: A message card where picking a language streams the AI translation in place, sentence by sentence over the dimmed original, with a detected-language chip, a Show original toggle and a status line credited to the model's mark.
whenToUse: Messages, comments, reviews or support tickets written in another language, translated on demand inside the product.
Release notes or announcements that readers in several regions open in their own language.
Any place you want an AI translation to feel inline and reversible, with the original one click away.
whenNotToUse: Translating a whole page or app interface; use your i18n framework.
Long documents with headings and lists; this renders one plain paragraph.
Live captions or speech; use a realtime stream component.
accessibility: The card is a section named after the author. The paragraph carries the lang attribute of the language on screen, and dimmed old sentences keep their own lang, so screen readers pronounce both correctly.
Start, completion, the original and failures are announced in a polite status region; the paragraph is aria-busy while it streams. The simulation says that nothing was sent.
The language menu is a radio group with a checkmark on the current language. The Show original toggle is a pressed button whose label switches to Show translation.
Status is never color alone: the model mark plus a label (Translating to German, Translated from French, Showing original), or a warning icon plus Couldn't translate.
Every control is at least 32px tall, and labels reserve the width of their longest version, so nothing moves under the pointer.
motion: Streaming: chunks of 3 to 6 words (about 10 characters in Japanese) land every 34ms and only fade in over 140ms. No blur, slide or per word spring.

The text on screen dims to 45% over 200ms as translating starts, and each sentence that starts in the new language removes one dimmed sentence, so the translation replaces the paragraph sentence by sentence.
Cached translations and the original swap with one crossfade: the old text leaves in 100ms, the new one fades in over 160ms with a 2px rise.
The paragraph's height follows its text with a critically damped spring (visualDuration 0.24, no bounce); window resizes cut straight to the new height.
Status labels crossfade in one shared cell; the picker and toggle labels crossfade inside their reserved width. The menu fades and scales from 98% in 150ms.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and announcement but drops chunk fades, crossfades and the height spring, and autoplay runs once.

name: ai-workflow
title: AI workflow
description: A Linear-style AI workflow card where a Gmail trigger, a Claude step, a branch and Slack and Linear actions sit on one hairline rail, and a test run glides down it, opening each step's output inline. Steps are added from a compact command menu with real app marks.
whenToUse: An automation or integrations page where people assemble a short trigger, AI step and action flow and want to test it in place.
Onboarding or marketing surfaces that show how an AI step slots between real apps, with a working test run.
Reviewing what an existing workflow does and seeing a sample run's outputs step by step.
whenNotToUse: Large free-form graphs with many branches, loops or merges: use a canvas editor instead.
Showing a single tool call or a live agent's steps: use tool-call or agent-run.
Scheduling recurring agent jobs: use agent-routines.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section with aria-busy while a run is in progress or steps are loading; steps are an ordered list, and each branch path is its own labelled list.
Every step title carries its app and status for screen readers ("Create Linear issue, Linear, Done in 700ms"). Status is shown as an icon plus a short label, never color alone.
A polite live region announces run start, each step's result, failures with their message, and the outcome, including "Simulated, nothing was sent" when no onRunStep is wired.
The add step menu is a combobox: the search field owns focus and points at the highlighted option with aria-activedescendant; options are a listbox. Branch paths are a radio group with roving focus.
Remove buttons are named per step ("Remove Create Linear issue") and are hidden only visually on hover devices until the row is hovered or the button is focused.
Brand marks are decorative next to the visible step title; marks whose brand color is near black draw in currentColor so they keep contrast in dark mode.
motion: A test run moves one thing at a time: a 5px accent dot glides down the next connector in 240ms while the line behind it fills, then the step crossfades to Running (icon and label) and its detail line crossfades to a shimmering activity line.

Everything is bounce-free and 100 to 240ms. Output previews and added or removed steps open and close on measured height with a critically damped spring (visualDuration 0.22, bounce 0); switching paths crossfades the lists (100ms out, 160ms in) while the container height follows, and the tab highlight slides on the same spring.
Status labels crossfade in a fixed 72px slot, so titles never shift. Reasons and drafts stream five words every 34ms, each chunk only fading in, with the final layout reserved from the first frame.
The add step menu fades and settles in 150 to 180ms with no spring overshoot; filtering animates the list to its new measured height.
Autoplay pauses while the card is off screen and stops for good after the first press or key inside the card.
Reduced motion drops the traveling dot, line growth and height animation; states, outputs and the live region stay the same.

name: ask-your-data
title: Ask your data
description: A natural language to chart card: you ask a question, PostgreSQL streams into a collapsible, syntax highlighted panel, the query runs with a rolling row count, and the answer builds as stacked bars, lines or a table, with a one line insight streamed in underneath.
whenToUse: Letting people ask product or business questions in plain words and see a chart, with the SQL one click away to verify or copy.
Embedding an analytics answer in a dashboard card, an admin page or an AI assistant's result view.
Teaching or auditing text to SQL, where showing the generated query builds trust.
whenNotToUse: Use bar-chart or line-chart when the query is fixed and there is no question to ask.
Use tool-call to show a database query as one step inside a longer agent transcript.
Use sql-editor when people write and tune queries by hand.
accessibility: A polite live region narrates the run: writing SQL, running the query, then the chart title, row count and insight. Without generateSql and runQuery it adds "Simulated with sample data, nothing was queried."
Status is never color alone: a spinner, a drawn check, an alert or a stop glyph sits beside a text label in the SQL row and the stage header.

The SQL row is a real button with aria-expanded and aria-controls, labelled with its title and meta, such as "Generated SQL, PostgreSQL · 48 rows · 214ms". Text not yet streamed is hidden from assistive technology.

The chart is a focusable group: arrow keys move a readout that is announced, such as "Aug 10: Free 61, Pro 26, Team 10, Enterprise 2, total 99". The table view keeps real table semantics with column and row headers.
The stage sets aria-busy while working. Text fields get no focus ring by design; the field border shifts to the accent on focus, and every other control uses Arc's shared keyboard ring.
motion: SQL streams four tokens every 34ms, each chunk only fading in over 140ms. The full query is laid out invisibly first, so the panel holds its final size and nothing below moves.
The SQL panel opens and folds on a 300ms bounce free spring; it folds once the query starts, before the chart builds, so only one region moves at a time.
Bars rise from the baseline in 320ms with at most 180ms of stagger; lines draw in 460ms. Switching views crossfades (100ms out, 160ms in) in a fixed area.
Header text and the SQL meta crossfade as single lines with a 2px settle. The row count rolls in tabular numerals in reserved width.

The insight streams four words a tick with its two lines reserved. Reduced motion shows SQL and insight whole, drops the bar rise, line draw, spinner and breathing skeleton, and keeps every state and announcement. Loops pause off screen.

name: black-hole
title: Black hole
description: A delete transition that pulls the chosen items into a tiny singularity while the rest of the list bends around it; undo spins them back out.
whenToUse: Deleting or archiving a handful of selected rows, cards, or files, with an Undo right after.
Emptying a trash, clearing notifications, or dismissing a batch where the removal should feel final.
whenNotToUse: High frequency deletes such as clearing a single chip or tag. Use a quick height collapse instead.
Irreversible actions without undo. The spectacle should not stand in for a confirmation.
Very long lists that scroll; the effect paints the visible wrapper, so wrap only the scrolling viewport.
accessibility: The canvas is aria-hidden and only covers the content while the effect runs; the real DOM is back in place the moment it ends.
Announce the result yourself (for example "2 conversations deleted" with an Undo button in a live region). The effect is visual only.
Pointer events are not blocked on the rest of the page; disable the trigger while a transition runs to avoid double deletes.
motion: Items fall along a logarithmic spiral. Points nearer the hole start earlier, so the inner edge falls faster than the outer one and rows stretch into arms.
The rest of the content is lensed with the Einstein ring relation, so text near the hole bends and briefly mirrors around it.
The hole opens with a slight overshoot, grows a little as it eats, then collapses and sends out one soft shockwave ring. Undo plays the same path backwards.
With reduced motion, or without WebGL2, the items fade out in 200ms and fade back in on release.

name: booking-pill
title: Booking pill
description: One pill that reshapes through party size, date, time, and a ticket.
whenToUse: Venue or service pages where booking a table or slot is the one action people came for.
Mobile-first flows that walk through party size, date, time, and confirm in one surface.
whenNotToUse: Use date-picker and time-picker inside a regular form for multi-field checkouts.
Use stepper or multi-step-form for longer flows with many fields.
Use calendar when people need to see a whole month.
accessibility: The date strip is a role="slider" with a spoken aria-valuetext; times are a role="radiogroup" with unavailable times marked aria-disabled.
Every round icon button has an aria-label (Back, Fewer guests, Next, choose a date).
Step changes are announced in a polite live region, and booking errors use role="alert".
motion: The pill's shape springs to fit each step while content slides in a beat later in the direction of travel.
The date strip follows drags 1:1, rubber-bands at the ends, and flicks glide to a day; party count digits roll.
Reduced motion jumps the strip, drops slides and blurs, and swaps faces with fades.

name: branch-graph
title: Branch graph
description: A git commit graph where branches draw in as colored lanes, merge commits join lines, a rebase lifts commits and replays them onto main, a squash folds them into one, and hovering a commit shows its message, author and diff stats.
whenToUse: A merge strategy picker in a code review or pull request screen, showing exactly what main will look like afterwards.
A commit history panel in a developer tool, with hover details and keyboard browsing.
Docs and landing pages for version control or CI products that explain merge, rebase, and squash.
whenNotToUse: Use git-branches for a looping, non-interactive illustration of a branch, pull request, and release.
Use a timeline or changelog for releases people need to read rather than a commit graph.
Use a virtualized table for long real histories; this graph is built for a focused slice of about five to fifteen commits.
accessibility: The root is a labelled section. The strategy control is a radiogroup of real radio buttons with a roving tab stop; arrow keys, Home, and End pick a strategy.

Commits form a listbox in visual order, newest first. Up and Down, Home, and End move through commits with aria-activedescendant; Escape closes the commit card. Each option is named with its message, hash, author, date, diff stats, and the branches that point to it.
A polite live region announces the result of every strategy picked by the user, such as how many commits were replayed and that they got new hashes. Autoplay changes are not announced.

The graph and the commit card are aria-hidden because the listbox carries the same information. Branch color is always paired with a named tag, merge commits carry an icon and a hollow dot, and additions and deletions carry + and − signs, so nothing relies on color alone.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. The keyboard commit takes the hover fill and shows its card.
motion: One rAF loop writes SVG path data, transforms, and opacity straight to the DOM and skips every value that did not change. React renders only when the strategy or the inspected commit changes.

Edges are computed each frame from the live positions of their two commits, so lines stretch and bend with them. A branch bends near its parent and a merge bends near its child, like a real git client.
The entrance draws each line up from the oldest commit at a constant pace, and every commit lands as its line reaches it.

A rebase lifts the branch's rows into floating cards, carries them one after another along an eased arc into the base lane, and sets them down with a soft ring while their hashes rewrite in place. The old branch point retracts first and the new link to the base tip draws in after the commits land.

A merge makes room at the top, then the merge commit lands and both lines draw into it. A squash flies the commits into one point where the squashed commit appears; undoing it replays them back out. Every transition starts from wherever things are, so picking a new strategy mid-flight never jumps.

The loop runs only while something moves or autoplay is waiting, and stops off screen and in hidden tabs. With reduced motion the graph shows each state immediately with no entrance, flights, or autoplay.

name: card-to-article
title: Card to article
description: Story cards that open into full articles with one seamless morph and shrink back into their exact slot when dragged down.
whenToUse: Blogs, journals, and changelogs where each entry has a strong image.
Case study and portfolio grids.
Editorial landing sections that preview stories without leaving the page.
whenNotToUse: Use a normal link to a page when articles are long or need their own URL and SEO.
Use expandable-card for small inline details.
Text only lists with no imagery.
accessibility: Cards are buttons with aria-haspopup="dialog" and aria-expanded.
The open article is a modal dialog labelled by its title, with focus moved to the close button and trapped inside.
Closing returns focus to the card it came from.
Page scroll is locked while the article is open, keeping the scrollbar's space so nothing shifts.
motion: The card itself becomes the article: its box and corners spring to the sheet while the hero scales as one piece, so image and title never distort.
The body rises in after the morph; the close button pops in last.
Drag down on touch, drag the hero with a mouse, or pull past the top with a trackpad: the sheet shrinks and drops with the gesture and closes past a threshold or on a flick.
Closing re-measures the card's slot and lands flush in it, no bounce. A reading progress bar tracks the scroll.
Reduced motion opens and closes without travel.

name: charge-session
title: Charge session
description: An EV or device charging card. Energy packets flow from a charger along the cable into the battery pack, which fills toward a draggable charge limit. The charge curve tapers near full, and power, energy, time to limit and cost update live. Stop charging drains the flow.
whenToUse: An EV or fleet app that shows a live charging session with a charge limit.
A charge point operator console where staff watch power, energy and cost for one bay.
A product page that demonstrates how your charging network reports time to full and cost.
whenNotToUse: Use usage-meter or progress for a static quota or a simple percentage.
Use gauge for a single live reading without a session, curve or cost.
Use a table or a chart block to compare many sessions at once.
accessibility: The card is a labelled group with a real heading. Power, energy added, time to limit and cost are a description list, so each value is read with its name.

The limit marker is a focusable role="slider" named Charge limit, with aria-valuetext such as Charge limit 80%, about 23 minutes to go. Arrows move it by 1%, Shift with an arrow or Page Up and Page Down by 10%, Home and End jump to the minimum and to 100%. The drag hint is linked with aria-describedby.
Stopping, resuming, reaching the limit, starting a new session and a settled limit change are announced in a polite live region with the charge, energy and cost at that moment.
The action button keeps one accessible label at a time (Stop charging, Resume charging, Start new session) and its width never changes.
The scene and the curve plot are hidden from assistive technology; every value they show is also in the stats, the header or the slider.
