State never relies on color: the header pairs an icon with Charging, Stopped or Charged to limit, and time to limit reads Paused or Done.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop advances the session and writes SVG attributes, CSS variables and text directly; React renders only when the session state changes.

Packets move along an arc length table of the cable curve, so they travel at an even pace, ease out of the charger, glide through the nub and slow as they meet the fill front, where each landing briefly brightens the front.

Power follows the charge curve times an availability level that ramps up on start and drains exponentially on stop, so the numbers, the LED, the cable core, the packet pace and the live point on the curve all fall away together.
Dragging the limit is one to one with the pointer; the pill lifts slightly while held. Raising the limit after the pack is full resumes charging, lowering it below the charge completes the session.
The loop stops offscreen, in background tabs, when paused, and once the flow has fully drained.
With reduced motion the session holds still: packets sit at even spacing along the path to show direction, values are current, and stop, resume and the limit all update at once.

name: code-suggestion
title: Code suggestion
description: An AI code edit suggestion where the model's proposed changes stream into a small editor panel as inline diff hunks, and you accept or reject each one, or all at once with Cmd+Enter. Accepted hunks fold into the file with a smooth height change.
whenToUse: Showing an AI's proposed edit to a file as an inline diff the person accepts or rejects hunk by hunk.
Approving an agent's file change before it is written, with a clear record of what was kept.
Landing pages and docs that demonstrate an AI coding feature with a realistic, self playing edit.
whenNotToUse: Use a dedicated diff tool for large multi file diffs or side by side comparisons; this card is for one file and a handful of hunks.
Use code-magic-move to animate code from one version to another without a review step.
Use code-block to show code without changes.
Use tool-call for an agent step that is not a file edit.
Use agent-approvals when the person approves actions in general (emails, payments, deploys) rather than code.
accessibility: The card is a labelled group ("Code suggestion: Add retry with backoff") and the code is a focusable region named after the file.

Each pending removed or added line starts with a visually hidden "Removed:" or "Added:", so the diff never relies on the red and green tints; the visible minus and plus signs carry it for sighted readers too.
Accept and Reject name their hunk ("Accept Retry 429 and 5xx with backoff"). Accept all and Reject all expose their shortcuts with aria-keyshortcuts.

A polite status region speaks the state ("3 changes to review"), each decision ("Accepted: Add retry limits. 2 changes to review") and the result. The simulated suggestion adds "Simulated, nothing was written to disk" when it finishes. Streaming is announced once, not per line.
Status always pairs an icon with a label: a spinner for reading and writing, a dot for review, a check for applied, a cross for rejected and an alert for errors.
Focus never falls back to the page when the pressed control leaves with its hunk or state. Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus uses Arc's shared focus outline.
motion: Thinking lasts about 0.8s with a calm shimmer on "Reading fetch-invoice.ts". Then each hunk opens: its removed lines tint red in 240ms and its new lines stream in one every 38ms, each opening to its 20px row in 120ms while it fades in. The whole sample streams in about 1.6s.
Review bars open under every hunk at once on a critically damped spring (0.24s, no bounce).

Accept folds the removed lines and the bar to zero height on the same spring (0.26s), so the code below glides up, while the green tint and the plus signs fade out. Reject does the same for the new lines and lets the red fade. Rows have fixed heights, so nothing is measured mid animation and nothing jitters.

The footer status icon, label and actions each swap with one short crossfade in place (old out in 100ms, new in 160ms, the label with a 2px rise). The icon only swaps when its kind changes, so the spinner keeps turning from Reading to Writing and a count change swaps only the text. Zero counts in the tab turn muted.

Reduced motion opens on the finished suggestion with no streaming, no autoplay and instant folds; decisions still apply and the status still updates. Autoplay waits until the card is in view and its replay waits until the card is back in view.

name: connector-setup
title: Connector setup
description: A "Connect your tools" card for an AI assistant. Each app connects inline: it redirects, authorizes and runs a first sync with a progress hairline, then lists the scopes it was granted and offers Disconnect with an inline confirm.
whenToUse: An assistant's settings or onboarding step where people connect workspace apps.
A first-run checklist that needs to show the OAuth handshake and first sync inline, without leaving the page.
Reviewing which scopes an assistant holds per app and revoking them.
whenNotToUse: Browsing dozens of integrations by category: use the integrations-grid block.
Approving a single action the agent wants to take: use agent-approvals.
Showing a tool the agent is calling right now: use tool-call.
accessibility: The card is a labelled group with a real heading; the list is a ul with one li per app.

A polite live region announces each step: connecting, connected with the sync count, failed with the reason, cancelled and disconnected. With the built-in simulation it adds "Simulated, nothing was sent."
Status is never color alone: errors pair an alert icon with the message, connected apps show a check with the word Connected.
The Connected button carries aria-expanded and aria-controls for the details region; Disconnect asks for confirmation and focuses the destructive button only after a deliberate press.
Content that is fading out leaves the accessibility tree and stops taking clicks immediately.
motion: Status lines and actions swap with one crossfade (out 100ms, in 160ms with a 2px rise) in a shared grid cell, so the row never reflows.
Progress is a 2px hairline that eases between steps and tracks the sync count linearly; the count rolls in tabular numerals inside a width reserved for its final value.
Details open with a bounce-free spring on measured height (visualDuration 0.24).
The scripted run starts only once the card is on screen and stops at the first interaction. Reduced motion keeps every state and announcement but cuts the crossfades and height springs.

name: context-window
title: Context window
description: An AI context window as a grid of 200 cells: the system prompt, tools, files, summary and messages fill it in order, a threshold row marks where compaction starts, and sending a message, attaching a file or compacting shows exactly how much still fits.
whenToUse: Showing developers or power users what fills a model's context and when it will compact.
Agent and coding tools that compact long sessions and want the effect to be understandable.
Docs and onboarding that explain context windows, compaction and output reserves.
whenNotToUse: A simple quota or plan usage bar; use usage-meter.
Choosing a model; use model-picker.
Billing or spend over time; use usage-billing.
accessibility: The grid is one image with a full text description: model, tokens used, every category with its tokens, and the threshold.
The legend is a list with tokens and percent for each part, so nothing depends on color.
Every send, attachment, model switch and compaction is announced through a polite status line with an icon and text.
The model menu is a Radix dropdown with radio items; the trigger names the model and its window.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared ring.
motion: New tokens fill cells in a short wave from where the change happened, about 4 to 9ms per cell and never more than 360ms in total.
Compaction dims the messages in one sweep from oldest to newest, then the summary lands right after the files and the freed cells turn back to free space in the same wave.
Switching models re-scales every cell in one quick pass from the first cell.
Token counts and percentages roll to their new values; status lines crossfade in place.
Pointing at a legend row lights its cells and quiets the rest.
Reduced motion changes cells and numbers at once and keeps every status line.

name: control-center
title: Control center
description: Workspace quick settings: tiles that morph into detail, a duration dial, and rubber-banded meters.
whenToUse: A quick settings panel with a handful of toggles and levels for a web workspace.
Focus session controls with a duration dial and allowed people.
Notification channel toggles grouped behind one tile.
whenNotToUse: Use switch, slider, and radio-group directly in a regular settings form.
Use time-dial to pick a time across time zones.
Use dropdown-menu for a short list of commands.
accessibility: Tiles are toggle buttons with aria-pressed; chevrons open a modal dialog with a focus trap and aria-haspopup.
Meters and the session dial are sliders with formatted aria-valuetext; channel toggles use role="switch".
Focus modes are a radiogroup, and the grid behind an open detail is inert. Clicking the scrim closes the detail.
motion: A tile grows into its detail with a shared element morph, and meters follow the pointer 1:1 from where they were grabbed, with rubber-banded edges. A tap without a drag jumps the meter to that spot, and the track swells slightly while held.
The session dial counts minutes as the knob travels, keeps counting across twelve o'clock, resists past 5 and 120 minutes, and snaps to 5 minute steps on release.
Icons and status text swap with a short blur; the dial knob springs to snapped values.
Reduced motion is applied through MotionConfig, removing travel and keeping fades.

name: cover-flow
title: Cover flow
description: A depth rail of images you can throw, with soft grounded shadows and a quiet reflection.
whenToUse: Six to twelve visual items where looking at one at a time is the point, such as albums, places, or collections.
Showcase rails that should respond to drag, throw, and sideways trackpad scroll.
whenNotToUse: Use carousel for general slides or content cards.
Use photo-grid or lightbox-gallery for a large library.
Use depth-cards for about three rich choices that open into detail.
accessibility: The root is labelled with aria-roledescription="carousel"; each card is a group with aria-roledescription="slide" and a label like "2 of 8: Ridge Loop".

Cards away from the front are aria-hidden, and position ticks are labelled "Show <title>" with aria-current on the front one. Ticks are out of the tab order; the rail itself takes focus and handles the keys.
The front card is announced in a polite live region.
motion: Drag or throw the rail and it lands on the card its momentum reaches, on a spring tuned to the release speed; a quick flick always moves at least one card. The ends rubber-band.
Sideways trackpad scrolls move the rail directly, then settle on a card with the swipe's momentum. Clicking a card beside the front one brings it forward.
Cards scale, dim, turn toward the center, and recede with distance while each image drifts inside its frame; the caption rises in from the direction of travel.
Reduced motion jumps between cards, turns off the drift and the turn, and keeps short fades. A drag past 40px or one trackpad swipe steps one card.

name: cube-mascot
title: Cube mascot
description: An isometric cube mascot where three shaded faces and a painted-on face show what the assistant is doing. It turns a quarter turn in eased steps while thinking, prints lines onto the floor while writing, settles with a sparkle when done, and shakes once on error.
whenToUse: Give an assistant a recognisable, product-like character that shows it is generating: in a reply header, in a composer, on an image canvas or in an empty state.
Brands with a geometric, technical feel where a soft blob would feel off.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-mascot for a softer, rounder character, or when you need a listening state.
Use agent-status when people need the steps, tools and elapsed time of a run.
Do not use it as a progress indicator with a known percentage; use a progress bar.
accessibility: The SVG has role img and a label built from name and status, for example "Atlas, writing", which updates with every state.
With announce, status changes are read in a polite live region outside the image. Use it on one mascot per view.
Status is never motion alone: each state changes the face (eyes up, eyes down, happy squint, worried brows and frown) and the label. Show a text status next to it where the state matters.
Under reduced motion every state is a still pose that switches in place.
motion: The cube is real 3D: eight corners are rotated (yaw, roll, pitch, then a fixed 32 degree camera) and projected each frame. The silhouette is their convex hull with rounded corners, used as a clip, so the outline stays soft while edges between faces stay exact.
Each face is shaded by its normal against a light from the upper left, interpolating between three anchors (top, front, side), so a face turning away darkens continuously.

Thinking holds for .5s, then turns a quarter turn over .8s with a cubic ease in and out, rising slightly and leaning into the turn. A cube looks identical after 90 degrees, so the end of each step is the start of the next and the loop has no seam. The face on the leaving side fades as it turns edge on; the face on the arriving side fades in and its eyes open as it reaches the front.

Writing prints a line every 360ms: each line slides out from under the face along the ground for 1.44s and only fades in and out, and its length changes while it is invisible. Eyes sweep slowly and the cube nods once per four lines.
Idle is a sum of slow sines with incommensurate periods (tilt, sway, float, glance), so it never repeats or restarts. Blinks come every 2.6 to 4.9s, sometimes twice, and take 170ms.

Done dips once and settles while the eyes pass through a closed line into the squint and the sparkle grows and turns in, then twinkles slowly. Error shakes 3.5 times in .56s under a squared envelope that reaches rest with zero velocity.

A status change blends every pose value from the frame on screen to the new state over 420ms (240ms into error) with an ease in and out. A change caught mid turn keeps turning forward instead of unwinding. Nothing bounces.

name: cursor-trail-draw
title: Cursor trail draw
description: A whiteboard where ink is smoothed and shaped by pressure, a laser pointer leaves a fading trail, and rough circles, boxes, triangles and lines snap to clean shapes on a small spring when the pen lifts.
whenToUse: A design review, planning or teaching tool where people sketch boxes, flows and circles quickly and want them tidy.
A live walkthrough or demo where a presenter points with a laser that cleans up after itself.
A landing page that lets visitors try a sketching feature directly.
whenNotToUse: Use signature-pad to capture a signature to sign a document.
Use annotation-board to pin comments on a screenshot or design.
Use a full canvas editor when people need selection, text, layers or infinite zoom.
accessibility: The root is a labelled section. The drawing surface is a focusable application region with a whiteboard role description, linked to its key help and to a written summary of what is on the board.

Full keyboard drawing: arrow keys move the cursor (diagonals by holding two, Shift for slow), Space or Enter puts the pen down and lifts it, Escape cancels a stroke. P and L pick the pen and the laser, S toggles snapping, and Control or Command Z undoes.
The toolbar is a labelled toolbar; arrow keys, Home and End move between its buttons. Tools, colors and snapping are toggle buttons with aria-pressed and specific names.
Snaps, kept strokes, undo, clear, tool changes and pen down or up are announced in a polite live region. The snap confirmation has a real Keep as drawn button.
The drawing itself is hidden from assistive technology; the summary lists every item by shape.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop eases the pen tip toward the pointer in substeps and writes each stroke outline straight to its path; React renders only when a stroke lands, is undone or the tool changes.
Width follows real pen pressure, or speed for a mouse and finger, and every stroke tapers in and lifts off with a taper.

On release, the stroke is resampled and each point travels to the matching point of the clean shape on a lightly underdamped spring, so it lands with a small physical settle, then swaps to an exact vector path. Keep as drawn runs the same spring back.
The laser trail thins from head to tail and fades out on its own; lifting leaves it to shrink away.
The loop runs only while something moves, and stops offscreen and in background tabs.
With reduced motion or paused, the finished sketch is shown at once, snaps land immediately and the laser shows only its dot.

name: data-flow
title: Data flow
description: Data flow illustration. Sources (app, database, events) are on the left, a processing core with a live count sits in the middle, and destinations (warehouse, dashboard, alerts) are on the right. Records leave as hollow dots and travel curved paths. In the core they turn into solid accent squares, then fan out to each destination; alerts receives about every third record.
whenToUse: A hero or feature section explaining how data moves through a product.
Docs pages introducing an ingestion, transform, or routing concept.
Integration pages that show which sources feed which destinations.
whenNotToUse: Use sankey-flow to show real volumes between stages.
Use pipeline-status for the live state of a CI or data job.
Use a table or list when people need to act on individual records.
accessibility: The diagram is one element with role="img" and an aria-label that describes the whole flow, built from the labels unless label is passed.
Nodes are not controls, so nothing enters the tab order; hover tags repeat detail that is optional.
Raw and processed records differ in shape (hollow dot, solid square), not only color.
Pass caption for a visible explanation under the diagram.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One rAF loop writes SVG transforms, opacity, and dash offsets straight to the DOM, and only when a value changed; React does not render per frame.
Records travel along real cubic paths at an even pace from an arc length table, eased in and out on each leg, with a short trail that stops at the core outline.

In the core each record swells slightly as it morphs from a hollow dot into an accent square, the core outline widens and fades, and the dashed ring quickens for a moment. On the way out one copy carries the record while the others fade in as they split off, so the fan out never clumps.
Six records per 6.6 second cycle are a pure function of time, so the loop repeats seamlessly; ports and node borders light up as records leave and land.
Speed changes, pausing, and hover (which slows the flow a little) ease on a critically damped spring.
The loop stops off screen, in hidden tabs, and when paused. Reduced motion shows a still frame: a raw record on each in path and a processed record on each out path.

name: date-reel
title: Date reel
description: A 3D wheel date and time picker (like iOS reels) with momentum scrolling, snapping, curved perspective, and full keyboard support.
whenToUse: Scheduling a send, reminder or post where a phone-style wheel is familiar and faster than a calendar grid.
Touch-first flows and mobile web, where flicking a reel beats typing a date.
Birthdays and other dates far from today, using date mode with its month, day and year reels.
whenNotToUse: Use date-picker or date-range-picker when people need to see a whole month or pick a range.
Use time-picker for a compact field inside a dense form.
Use time-dial to compare times across cities.
accessibility: The picker is a named group; each reel is a role="spinbutton" with its own name (Day, Hour, Minute, AM or PM) and aria-valuetext that reads the entry, such as "Fri, Sep 25".
A polite live region announces the full moment once the reels come to rest after a change, and again when the confirm button succeeds or fails.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. The focused reel shows its entry in the accent color inside the lens, and quick picks use aria-pressed.
Dates that do not exist, such as February 30, are dimmed on the reel and the day reel turns back to the last real day by itself.
Drawn entries and the visual summary are hidden from assistive technology so a moving reel never floods the reader.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop runs only while a reel moves and writes transforms, opacity and text straight to recycled DOM nodes; React re-renders only when a value is committed.

Each reel is projected onto a cylinder: entries rise on a sine curve, compress with the cosine of their angle and fade toward the edges, and a second copy clipped to the lens shows the crisp selected text.

A flick keeps its measured velocity on an exponential glide that is solved to land exactly on an entry, then hands the last half row to a critically damped spring; drags past the ends stretch like rubber and bounce back.
Keyboard steps, taps, wheel scrolling and quick picks all spin on the same spring, so pressing again mid-spin adds to the motion instead of restarting it.
The loop stops when the picker leaves the viewport or the tab is hidden and resumes where it left off. With reduced motion every change lands at once and there is no intro.

name: dictation-button
title: Dictation button
description: A chat composer with voice input, where the mic springs into a recording pill with a smooth live waveform, a timer, and cancel and insert buttons. Words stream into the field as you speak, muted until the recognizer settles them.
whenToUse: Chat and agent composers where people would rather talk than type: mobile, long prompts, accessibility.
Notes, comments and support replies where dictation saves time and the person still edits before sending.
Any field that already has a send action and needs a voice entry point with clear listening state.
whenNotToUse: Full duplex voice conversations with spoken replies; use a voice agent pattern with call controls instead.
Recording audio files to keep (voice memos); this inserts text and discards audio.
Command palettes where a single spoken command should run immediately; confirm hands-free from onSpeechEnd only if you are sure.
accessibility: A polite live region announces listening (and that the default recognizer is simulated, nothing is recorded), transcribing, the inserted word count, cancel, send and every error with how to fix it. Streaming words are not announced, to keep screen readers quiet.
Status is never color alone: denied shows a mic-off icon and "Microphone blocked in site settings"; errors show an alert icon and a short reason; Try again keeps the same icon.

Only the visible face of the pill is focusable (the other faces are inert), and focus follows the action: mic to Insert, Insert back to the field at the end of the text, cancel back to the mic, a failed start to Try again.
The elapsed time is a role="timer" with tabular numerals in a reserved width; the waveform is decorative and hidden from assistive tech.
Mic, cancel and Insert are icon buttons with accessible names and tooltips (Dictate, Cancel, Insert, Transcribing).
Interim words use a muted tone between --text-muted and --text-secondary and settle to --foreground, so the difference reads in both themes without relying on hue.
motion: The mic springs leftward into the recording pill (up to 216px, measured from the toolbar) with a critically damped spring (0.24s visual duration, no bounce); Try again springs to its measured label width. The mic's spot becomes Insert, so the next action sits where the pointer already is.
Faces crossfade (out 100ms, in 160ms). The toolbar label swaps with a single 2px crossfade. Insert crossfades its check into a spinner while transcribing.
Words only fade in (140ms). A corrected interim guess refades just the words that changed. The field springs to each new line.

The waveform fits as many 3px rounded bars as the track holds with an even 2px gap, so no bar is ever clipped. A level sample enters on the right every 60ms and each bar eases toward it every frame, so heights glide without steps or jitter, written straight to the DOM with no React renders. When listening stops, the bars settle in place to a row of dots.
Reduced motion: no size springs, no word fades, the waveform stops travelling and pulses in place with the voice. Loops pause off screen and in background tabs.

examples.title: Only the control, in your own composer
Your own speech service

name: dns-resolution
title: DNS resolution
description: A browser asks for a domain and the query hops from the resolver to a root server, the TLD server and the authoritative nameserver, each pointing to the next, until an IP address comes back and the page connects. The resolver keeps the answer with a TTL ring that drains, and a second lookup is answered straight from that cache in one short hop.
whenToUse: A docs or marketing section that explains how a domain name turns into an address and why the second visit is faster.
Custom domain setup, DNS hosting, resolver or CDN pages that need the chain of servers and the role of TTL to click.
Teaching material where viewers should be able to step back and forth through each hop.
whenNotToUse: Use webhook-fanout to show one event delivered to many endpoints with retries.
Use data-flow for a general pipeline between services.
Use a real status or table component to report actual DNS records or propagation.
accessibility: The drawing is role="img" with an aria-label that tells the whole story: the chain of servers, the address, the connection time and that the next lookup comes from the cache. Pass label to write your own.

The labels, moving record chips and hover tags inside the drawing are part of that image, and the narrated caption is hidden from assistive technology, so screen readers hear one stable description instead of a changing loop.

The scrubber is a group of real buttons named Step 1 of 6 and so on; the current step carries aria-current="step", arrow keys, Home and End move between steps, and the pause button reports its state with aria-pressed.
Status is never color alone: every status chip pairs its dot with words such as Resolving, Try .dev, Cache hit or Connected in 84 ms.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop writes SVG attributes, transforms, opacity and text directly, and only when a value changed; React never re-renders per frame.

Packets travel along real quadratic arcs at an even pace (arc length lookup) with a sine ease, a short lit trail and a shadow that slides along the floor and shrinks as the packet rises, which gives the 2.5D depth.

Every frame is a pure function of one clock, so the counters, statuses, TTL ring and scrubber stay in sync, jumps land exactly, and the loop joins seamlessly when the cached record expires and the scene fades back to its start.
Pausing, speed changes and the gentle hover slowdown ease on a critically damped spring. The loop stops offscreen and in a hidden tab and resumes where it left off.
With reduced motion there is no travel or loop: the stage shows a settled frame of the cached state, and the scrubber switches between settled frames of each stage.

name: dock
title: Dock
description: A floating tool dock with a gliding label, a springy selection, and trays that grow out of it.
whenToUse: A floating tool or mode switcher, such as the tools of a canvas or whiteboard editor.
Toolbars where related tools share one slot and open a tray, like shape variants.
Tool sets people may reorder by drag or Alt with the arrow keys.
whenNotToUse: Use segmented-control for two to four inline options.
Use action-button for one-off actions that do not stay selected.
Use liquid-tab-bar for switching between app sections rather than tools.
accessibility: Items sit in a horizontal toolbar with a roving tabindex; plain items use aria-pressed for selection.
Groups use aria-haspopup, aria-expanded, and aria-controls pointing at the tray, which is a labelled group that stays inert while closed.
Accessible names include the shortcut hint and badge count, such as "Pen, P". A group reads as its label and shown member, such as "Shapes: Ellipse, O", plus "selected" when it holds the value.
The floating label is aria-hidden. It shows on mouse hover and on keyboard focus, not on touch.
A pointer down outside the dock closes an open tray.
motion: The label glides between items after a short first hover delay and stays warm so the next one follows at once; the accent tint springs between items with a shared layoutId whose corner radius is corrected, so it never distorts.
A group's glyph crossfades with a short blur when its member changes; a press dips the item on a quick spring and releases with a little overshoot.
Opening a group grows a tab of the same material out of the dock with members staggering in; dragged items lift and neighbours reflow on a layout spring.
Reduced motion makes the label, tray, and selection jump and keeps short fades.

name: dot-grid
title: Dot grid
description: A dot field that bulges around the cursor like a lens and ripples from every click.
whenToUse: A landing page hero that should feel alive without video.
A background for an empty state, a sign in panel, or a launch countdown.
A playful section divider people can poke at.
whenNotToUse: Behind dense text or data; the moving dots compete with reading.
Use a static CSS dot pattern when no interaction is wanted.
Avoid stacking several on one screen; one reactive background is enough.
accessibility: The canvas is aria-hidden and not focusable; the field is decoration and adds nothing to the reading order.
Children render as normal DOM above the canvas, so links and buttons keep their semantics and pointer events.
With reduced motion dots never move; the lens only tints dots near the pointer and clicks do not ripple.
motion: Each dot rides its own damped spring toward the lens and ripple offsets, so the field wobbles and settles instead of snapping.
The lens peaks a third of the way out and fades to nothing at its rim, and it trails the pointer slightly and fades in and out.
Ripples travel at about 620px per second, fade over 1.5s, and up to six can overlap.
Dots under the lens and in a ripple grow and take the active color.

name: enrich-column
title: Enrich column
description: An AI enrichment column for a data table, where one prompt runs down every row and each cell shimmers while it works, then settles into a value with its source or a failure you can retry.
whenToUse: Enriching a list of companies or leads with facts an agent can look up (headcount, funding, tech stack).
Classifying or summarizing rows with one prompt, with a visible source per answer.
Showing per-row AI progress with stop, re-run and retry in a CRM, sales tool or internal admin.
whenNotToUse: Large spreadsheets with many columns and editing; use Data grid and add an AI column there.
A single question over a dataset; use Ask your data.
A log of one agent's tool calls; use Tool call.
accessibility: A real table: the company is a row header and the AI column's name and prompt are its column header.
Every cell state pairs an icon with text (Queued, a shimmering activity, the value, Failed with a reason), never color alone.
A polite live region announces runs, stops and the final count, and says when values are simulated and nothing was sent.
Icon buttons carry labels that name the row (Run Linear, Retry Retool); source links say they open a new tab.
motion: Cell swaps are one crossfade in a shared grid cell: old content out in 100ms, new in 160ms with a 2px rise. Nothing changes size.
Status icons crossfade with a bounce-free scale; the done tick draws in 240ms; the running label uses a calm text shimmer.
The editor opens with a critically damped height spring (240ms, no bounce).
Reduced motion keeps every state and cuts travel and the tick draw; the spinner slows down.

name: generation-stats
title: Generation stats
description: A live stats strip for a streaming LLM response where time to first token, speed with a sparkline, output tokens and cost count up in tabular numerals beside the model's real mark, then settle and open into a latency and token cost breakdown.
whenToUse: Under assistant messages in a chat product that shows people what a response cost or how fast it was.
Playgrounds, eval runners and internal dev panels comparing models on latency, throughput and cost.
Admin or debugging views that inspect a single request's token usage and cache hit rate.
whenNotToUse: Use context-window to show how much of a model's context a conversation has used.
Use a chart or table for spend across many requests or days; this strip describes one response.
Use agent-status for a long running agent with steps; this measures one model call.
accessibility: The strip is a group named after the model ("Claude Sonnet 5.5 stats"). The four stats are a description list, so each value is read with its label: "First token, 412ms".
Details is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls; at narrow widths it becomes an icon button that keeps the name Show details or Hide details.

A polite status region announces settled outcomes ("Claude Sonnet 5.5 done in 4.18s, 284 output tokens at 88 tokens per second, $0.0077"), failures and stops, never the live counts. The self-playing preview says once that it is simulated and stays quiet until someone interacts with it.
Status never relies on color: a spinner, drawn check, alert or square always sits next to a word. The latency bar is decorative; its values are listed beside it in text.
The breakdown is a real table with column and row headers and a caption, so screen readers can navigate tokens, rates and cost by cell.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Numbers glide toward each new value in about 100ms per step with tabular numerals in reserved cells, so chunks of tokens read as one smooth count and nothing beside them moves. A drop, like a new request, cuts straight to the new value instead of counting down.

While streaming, speed is measured when each chunk lands, so it holds still between chunks instead of sagging and jumping. The sparkline adds a smoothed reading every 160ms and compresses to keep the whole run's shape.
Status labels swap with a single crossfade (out in 100ms, in over 160ms with a 2px rise); the done check draws itself once.
The breakdown and the error row open on a 260ms critically damped spring for height with a 160ms fade. Nothing bounces.
The preview loop pauses off screen and holds on a settled run while someone has the breakdown open.
Reduced motion shows final values at once, drops the spinner, the check drawing and the height springs, and stops the preview on a settled run.

name: ghost-mascot
title: Ghost mascot
description: A floating ghost mascot whose soft sheet ripples at the hem while it hovers. It blinks when idle, turns toward you to listen, fades a little translucent while thinking, draws a tiny pen line while writing, smiles with a sparkle when done and wobbles once on an error.
whenToUse: Give an assistant a light, friendly face that shows what it is doing: in a reply header, in a composer, over an image canvas while it generates, or in an empty state.
Products that want generation to feel alive without a spinner, with states that still read at 24px.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-status when people need the steps, tools and elapsed time of a run, not just a mood.
Use text-shimmer alone for a plain "Thinking" line in dense interfaces where a character would distract.
Do not use it as a progress indicator with a known percentage; use a progress bar.
accessibility: The SVG has role img and a label built from name and status, for example "Atlas, thinking", which updates with every state.
With announce, status changes are read in a polite live region outside the image. Use it on one ghost per view so screen readers do not hear duplicates.

Status is never carried by color or motion alone: each state changes the face and marks (wide eyes, eyes up with a swirl, a pen and line, happy eyes with a sparkle, droopy eyes) and the label. Show a text status next to it where the state matters.
motion: Every loop is a function of a phase that only grows: the float, the two hem waves, the swirl and the writing cycle. Rates blend by integrating into those phases, so speed changes never jump and nothing restarts.

The hem is two traveling sine waves drawn as exact Hermite curves through rounded corners, rebuilt every frame. It trails the float: the sheet stretches on the way up, and the hem lifts and flares on the way down.

A status change blends every pose value from the frame on screen to the new pose over 400ms with an ease in and out. Eyes ride a critically damped spring: quick saccades when idle, a slow drift up while thinking, tight tracking of the pen tip while writing. Nothing bounces.

The swirl draws in from its outer end and erases behind itself; the writing line draws word by word, the pen lifting between words, then erases while the pen glides back. Both are empty at the moment their cycle wraps, so there is no seam.
Done grows the sparkle in 320ms with an ease out and a quarter turn, then a slow twinkle. Error wobbles once, decaying to rest in about 1.2s, softened at the start so it never kicks.
Reduced motion shows a still, representative pose for each state (a half drawn swirl, half a written line, the sparkle, the droop), switches in place and drops every loop, glance, blink and wobble.

name: ghost-text
title: Ghost text
description: An inline AI autocomplete where muted ghost text continues your sentence exactly at the caret and Tab turns it solid in place. Cmd+Right takes it one word at a time, Escape fades it away, and a calm chip shows the model behind it.
whenToUse: Long-form fields people write in product: pull request descriptions, emails, support replies, issue bodies, release notes, CRM notes.
Short single-line fields where a likely completion saves typing, such as an email subject or a commit message.
Anywhere you want AI help that stays out of the way until the person pauses, and never changes their text without an explicit key press.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-composer for a chat-style prompt box that sends a message to an assistant.
Use code-suggestion for code diffs with accept and reject per hunk.
Use a combobox or command menu when the person picks from a list of known options rather than free text.
Avoid it in fields with sensitive content (passwords, card numbers, health data) unless your model provider and data policy allow it.
accessibility: The field is a native textarea (or input), labelled by aria-label or the label row, and described by a hidden sentence that explains Tab, Cmd or Ctrl+Right and Escape.

The ghost text lives in an aria-hidden mirror behind the field, so it is never read as content. A polite status region reads the finished suggestion ("Suggestion: date the plan changed. Press Tab to accept."), then Suggestion accepted, Suggestion dismissed or Couldn't get a suggestion.

The chip is a button with a clear name in each state (Accept suggestion, Retry suggestion). It is reachable with Tab only in the error state, where Retry is the action; in the ready state Tab itself accepts. Pressing the chip never steals focus from the field.
State is never shown by color alone: Thinking, the Tab key cap with "to accept", Accepted with a check and No suggestion with an alert icon all carry words.
Keyboard focus draws Arc's focus ring around the whole field; pointer focus does not.
On touch screens, where there is no Tab key, the chip reads Tap to accept.
motion: Ghost text only fades in, chunk by chunk as it streams (140ms each, opacity only, no blur or slide), so a suggestion settles without any movement. Escape and leaving the field fade it out in 110ms; typing a different character clears it at once so nothing lingers over new text.

Accepting turns the ghost solid in place: for 200ms an aria-hidden mirror with the field's exact metrics draws the text while the native glyphs go transparent (the caret stays), and the accepted range eases from muted to text color. Cmd+Right does the same per word, and the rest of the ghost never re-fades.
The field's height follows the text, ghost included, on a 180ms tween and never bounces. The box is clipped while it grows, so the browser cannot scroll it under the caret mid-tween.

Chip states crossfade in place (old out in 100ms, new in 160ms) while the chip's width follows on a 200ms tween, anchored to its right edge. Key caps press for 160ms when their key or the matching handle method fires. Thinking carries a calm shimmer.

Reduced motion removes the fades, the ink merge, the shimmer and the height tween and keeps every state, text and announcement. The preview plays once and stops instead of looping, and it pauses while off screen.

name: glass-card
title: Glass card
description: A glass info panel over a photo whose rim catches a pointer-following highlight while the card tilts; tap to morph it into a detail sheet.
whenToUse: Profile, host, or creator cards on a landing page or in a discovery grid.
A featured product or stay where the photo sells and the details can wait for a tap.
whenNotToUse: Dense grids of many cards; tilt and glass on every tile gets busy. Use card.
Cards that should open a full page; use card-to-article.
accessibility: The glass header is a real button with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at the detail region.
Clicking anywhere on the photo is a pointer shortcut for the same toggle; keyboard users use the header.
Detail content is removed from the DOM when collapsed, so hidden buttons are never focusable.
Under prefers-reduced-transparency the glass turns solid.
motion: Tilt and highlight follow the pointer through springs, so the card eases into position and settles back when the pointer leaves. Touch input skips the tilt.
Expanding is one shared-layout spring on the panel; the header keeps its position and the details fade up with a short blur.
The photo scales up slightly and the floor shade deepens while open.
Reduced motion removes tilt and the morph; the panel switches size and the details fade.

name: glass-menu
title: Glass menu
description: A glass action menu whose trigger morphs into the panel, with a highlight pill that glides between rows, one in-place submenu, and full keyboard support.
whenToUse: Actions for a photo, file, or card shown over an image or a colorful canvas.
A title menu in an editor or viewer, where the title itself opens the actions.
whenNotToUse: Plain settings pages with no imagery behind the menu. Use dropdown-menu on a neutral surface.
Navigation between pages. Use morph-nav or tabs.
Deep hierarchies. Use a command palette or a dedicated screen.
accessibility: The trigger has `aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded`, and `aria-controls` pointing at the open menu.
Rows are `menuitem`, or `menuitemcheckbox` with `aria-checked` when `checked` is set; rows with a submenu carry `aria-haspopup`.
Focus moves to the highlighted row, so screen readers announce it; with no row highlighted the menu itself holds focus.
Pressing outside closes the menu without stealing focus from what was pressed.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. The highlight pill marks the active row for keyboard and pointer alike.
motion: The trigger's glass and the panel's glass share a layout id, so opening is one spring morph from the trigger's box to the panel's, and closing morphs back.
Rows fade and sharpen in a beat after the glass starts to grow, so text never shows outside the glass.
The highlight pill glides between rows on the shared morph spring.
The submenu slides in the direction of travel while the panel height follows on a critically damped spring.
With reduced motion the panel and submenu appear in place and the pill jumps.

name: glass-segmented
title: Glass segmented
description: A glass segmented control whose liquid indicator stretches between segments and can be dragged and flung.
whenToUse: Switching the view of a photo, map, or media surface.
A compact filter over imagery, such as day, week, month on a hero chart.
whenNotToUse: Plain forms on neutral surfaces. Use segmented-control.
More than five options or long labels. Use tabs or a select.
accessibility: The control is a `radiogroup` with a roving tab stop; each segment is a `radio` with `aria-checked`.
The indicator is decorative SVG and hidden from assistive tech.
Selection is also shown by label color, not only by the indicator.
motion: Each edge of the indicator has its own spring: the edge facing the travel is quick, the other lags, so the drop stretches and then settles.
The drop thins as it stretches, like liquid keeping its volume.
Drag the selected segment and the drop follows with the same liquid lag; on release, velocity is projected to pick where it lands.
With reduced motion the indicator jumps and dragging tracks directly.

name: glass-tabbar
title: Glass tab bar
description: A floating Liquid Glass tab bar that refracts what scrolls beneath it, with a glass lens that glides, magnifies and can be dragged between tabs, and an optional search bubble; it compacts on scroll down.
whenToUse: Mobile web apps and PWAs with three to five top level sections and one global action such as search.
Content feeds where the bar should step aside while reading and come back on scroll up.
whenNotToUse: Desktop layouts with many sections; use a sidebar or morph-nav.
Switching views inside a card; use segmented-control or tabs.
accessibility: Renders a nav landmark around a tablist; every tab, including the action, has role="tab" and aria-selected, with a roving tabindex.
Labels stay in the accessibility tree when the bar is compact, so each tab keeps its name.
Badges carry hidden text such as "3 new" for screen readers.
Selection is carried by the lens, the accent tint, and aria-selected, never by color alone.
Reduced transparency swaps the glass for a solid raised surface; increased contrast strengthens the tint, border, and ink.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: The lens glides on the smooth spring, which never overshoots. Its speed lifts it off the bar: it grows, stretches along the direction of travel, and turns into a clear lens that magnifies the icons under it, then settles back into a soft fill.
Each tab's tint and icon scale follow the lens position, so the accent glides with it instead of switching.
Press the selected tab and the lens lifts; drag past a few pixels and it follows the pointer across the bar; release snaps it to the nearest tab and selects it.
One spring drives the compact morph: slot width, bar height, icon lift, and label fade all read from it, so the lens stays on its tab mid morph.
Reduced motion moves the lens and the size instantly, with no lift, stretch, or magnification.

name: gravity-well
title: Gravity well
description: A grid of tiles that bends toward the cursor like spacetime, with a click that sends a shockwave through it.
whenToUse: A team, customer, or moodboard wall where playfulness is the point.
Landing page sections that show breadth: many logos, avatars, or photos at once.
whenNotToUse: Grids people must scan or click precisely, like file pickers; use a plain grid.
Large collections; use infinite-moodboard or photo-grid.
accessibility: The root is a named group with aria-roledescription="gravity well". Tile content keeps its own semantics and alt text.
Motion is decorative: tiles keep their grid slot and only move with transform, so reading order never changes.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. The well itself shows where keyboard focus is.
motion: The well follows the pointer on a critically damped spring, and each tile follows the field on an underdamped spring, so fast moves leave a jelly wake.
Tiles deeper in the well shrink, dim, and slide under their neighbours.
A click drops a shockwave that travels at 900 px/s and rings each tile once as it passes.
Reduced motion leaves the grid static.

name: holo-card
title: Holo card
description: A member card that tilts toward you with a holographic foil and flips to its back.
whenToUse: A membership or subscription card on an account or welcome page.
A shareable profile, badge, or achievement that people will screenshot.
A collectible or reward reveal.
whenNotToUse: Use card for ordinary content; the effect is too loud for lists.
Use depth-cards when several items need a subtle parallax.
Avoid it for text people need to read carefully; the sheen moves over the content.
accessibility: With a back, the card is role="button" with aria-roledescription="flip card" and aria-pressed for the flipped state.
The hidden face is aria-hidden, so assistive tech reads only the side that is showing.
Foil, glitter, and glare layers are decorative and aria-hidden.
prefers-reduced-transparency removes the foil and glitter.
motion: Tilt follows the pointer on a lightly underdamped spring, and the light position trails on a softer one, so the sheen lags the lean just enough to feel physical.
The foil slides and shifts hue with the angle; glitter drifts against the tilt and only sparkles near the glare.
Each flip adds half a turn toward the side that was pressed on a spring with a little bounce, and the foil sweeps across the card mid spin.
A floating shadow moves opposite the lean.
Reduced motion removes tilt, spin, and glitter; the faces cross fade.

name: image-generation
title: Image generation
description: An image studio where each image forms on a dot matrix: a soft halftone wave breathes across the grid, the dots take the colours of the coming photo and grow into a coloured halftone, then blur away into the sharp photo. One large canvas with a mono size label, a filmstrip of four variations, a prompt bar with model and ratio, and upscale with a sweeping dot band, vary or download, with real provider marks and a built-in simulation.
whenToUse: A text to image feature inside a product: marketing asset tools, listing photo helpers, slide or doc illustration.
Any flow where people compare a few candidates and continue with one (upscale, vary, download).
Prototyping an image model integration before the backend exists, using the built in simulation.
whenNotToUse: A full canvas editor with layers, masks and inpainting; build on a canvas library instead.
Drawing a sketch to turn into an image; use sketch-to-image.
Showing a single image with a loading state and no generation controls; use blur-image.
accessibility: Model and aspect chips and the filmstrip are radio groups with a roving tab stop; collapsed model chips keep their name as the accessible label and in a tooltip.
The canvas is labelled with the image description once done, or with the variation's state while it generates, fails or stops; each thumbnail names its number and state.
A polite live region reports starts, finishes, failures, picks, upscales and downloads, and says when results are simulated.

Status is never color alone: failures pair a danger icon with "Failed" and the error, stops a square icon with "Stopped", the chosen thumbnail an accent ring with aria-checked, progress a spinner with a percentage.
Icon only actions at narrow widths keep Upscale, Vary and Download as their accessible names.
motion: Each image loads on a canvas of small neutral dots, drawn at device pixel ratio. A soft radial halftone wave breathes and wanders across the grid: dots under it grow and darken, and a blurred twin of them glows like a lens.

From 20% the dots take the colour of the coming photo at their cell (the preview downscaled to the grid, cover fitted), showing first under the wave, and grow by the photo's darkness, so by 78% the image reads as a coloured halftone.

Over the last fifth the dots blur and fade while the photo sharpens out of them from 12px blur and 4% zoom. The final frame is the photo, and the real lands on it without a cut; an image that differs from the preview resolves from soft to sharp in 480ms.
The filmstrip thumbnails run their own small dot fields, so all four variations show their progress at once. Picking another variation crossfades the canvas in 200ms.

Upscale sweeps a vertical band of halftone dots in the photo's colours left to right: soft ahead of it, sharp behind it, the dots and their blurred twin in it, all from one motion value. The size label crossfades to the new size.
The status pill carries a 3×3 dot spinner whose dots light in turn around the ring, with a mono percentage; pills crossfade by key so a label never resizes in a frame.

The canvas springs to a new aspect ratio; a container resize cuts straight to the new size. Labels that change inside buttons (Generate and Stop, Upscale, Upscaling, Upscaled, Download and Saved) are stacked in one cell and crossfade, so no button changes width.
Reduced motion draws a still dot grid with the halftone glow at rest, crossfades the photo in by progress, keeps the spinner still and drops the upscale sweep.

name: image-reveal
title: Image reveal
description: An image generation canvas where a soft, blurred preview made from the image's own colors sharpens top to bottom behind a soft-edged band. It works the way ChatGPT, Midjourney and Gemini show images forming, with fine film grain, a translucent progress pill and calm queued and error states.
whenToUse: Showing an image model's progress on a canvas or in a chat reply.
A batch of image variations sampling side by side.
A queued image job that should feel alive before it starts.
whenNotToUse: Plain image loading from a CDN; use a blur-up placeholder or a skeleton.
Text generation or tool calls; use text-shimmer or tool-call.
Determinate file uploads; use progress.
accessibility: The canvas has role img; its label names the state while generating and becomes the alt text once done.
A polite live region announces Queued, Generating image, Image ready and the error message, not every step. Auto mode appends simulated.
While generating, the pill is a progressbar with aria-valuenow and an aria-valuetext of Step n of total.
Status is never color alone: the pill pairs a ring or check with a short label, and the error state pairs an alert icon with its message.
motion: Queued is the calm surface tone with one broad, soft shimmer that starts and ends fully off canvas, so its 2.6s loop has no seam.
Generating starts from pure latent noise: per-cell gaussian color at about 1/8 of the output resolution, drawn as crisp blocks, with a new seeded frame every step crossfaded in 35ms.

Under the noise is the model's current prediction, built from the image itself (6 to 96 px wide copies, smoothly upscaled). It moves along that chain per step, so color blobs come first, then composition, then shapes.
Noise strength follows a schedule that drops fast early, so the composition reads by about a third of the steps and the last steps only refine. Steps run at a constant rate, like a real sampler.
After the last step a tiled decode lands the sharp image tile by tile in raster order, each tile crossfading in, and the pill switches to Decoding.
One soft-light sheen sweeps across once at completion (1.1s), the pill shows the elapsed time, then fades out.
Starting over or swapping the photo fades the decoded image straight back to the surface before anything resets underneath, and a photo swap crossfades from a snapshot, so there is never a hard cut.
Pill labels crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in after a 60ms gap) and the pill width springs with no bounce.
Reduced motion keeps one static noise frame, decodes as a single crossfade and drops the shimmer travel, spinner and sheen.
The frame loop stops off screen (IntersectionObserver) and in background tabs, and draws nothing once the image is resolved.

examples.title: Estimated duration, no progress events
examples.code: <ImageReveal src={url} status={url ? "done" : "generating"} duration={8000} />

examples.title: Batch of four with a Generate again button

name: image-trail
title: Image trail
description: Moving the pointer leaves a curated trail of photos that pop in, lean, and fade away.
whenToUse: A portfolio or agency hero that should feel alive on first move.
Travel, food, or product stories told through a sequence of photos.
Launch pages that want an instantly playful surface.
whenNotToUse: Use photo-grid or lightbox-gallery when people need to look at each photo.
Use hover-image-list to preview one image per row in a list.
Avoid it behind long text that people need to read.
accessibility: Trail photos are decorative and aria-hidden; put anything people need in children.
Children stay in normal reading order and remain interactive.
The effect is pointer only and adds nothing a keyboard or screen reader user misses.
motion: A new photo appears only after the pointer has travelled spacing px, and never faster than every 40ms, so the trail stays curated.
Each photo enters on the shared spring curve from 60% scale, leans with horizontal speed plus a small fixed variation, then drifts along the pointer's path as it shrinks and fades.
Photos are pooled DOM nodes animated with the Web Animations API on transform and opacity only.
Reduced motion keeps the trail as a calm crossfade in place, with no scale, tilt, or drift, and wider spacing.

name: ink-fluid
title: Ink fluid
description: A real time fluid simulation behind your hero: the cursor stirs soft ink that swirls, settles and fades; calm when left alone.
whenToUse: A landing hero or sign in screen that should feel alive without a video.
Empty states and waiting screens where a gentle, interactive background rewards curiosity.
whenNotToUse: Dense product surfaces such as tables and forms. Movement behind data distracts.
More than one per page; each instance runs its own simulation.
accessibility: The canvas is aria-hidden and ignores pointer hits; content inside stays fully interactive and readable.
Ink is capped at a low opacity so text over it keeps its contrast in both themes.
With reduced motion it renders one composed still frame and stops.
motion: Semi Lagrangian advection, vorticity confinement and a 20 step pressure solve on a small grid, drawn with linear upscaling and a soft light term from the ink gradient so wisps read silky.
Pointer velocity drives the force; the amount of ink scales with speed so slow moves leave faint trails and quick flicks bloom.
Ink fades over a couple of seconds; accent tinted ink turns neutral as it spreads, so fresh strokes carry colour and old ones go grey.
It pauses when scrolled out of view or when the tab is hidden, and resumes where it left off.

name: install-snippet
title: Install snippet
description: A "get started in 30 seconds" card where framework tabs, three numbered steps and highlighted snippets take a developer from install to first event. Generate key wipes a fresh API key into the placeholder in place.
whenToUse: A quickstart that has to work for several frameworks without three pages of docs.
Onboarding where creating an API key is part of getting started.
Marketing pages for developer tools that want to show how little setup it takes.
whenNotToUse: A single code sample with no steps: use code-block.
Trying requests against a live API: use api-playground.
Long setup guides with many branches: write docs pages and link to them.
accessibility: Framework and package manager tabs are real tablists with roving tabindex; the steps list is the framework tab panel.
Steps are an ordered list with h4 titles; a finished step announces ", done" and swaps its number for a check, so progress is never color alone.
A polite live region announces framework changes, key generation, and that the default key is simulated. Copy buttons announce Copied on their own.
Errors show an alert icon plus text, and the button changes to Try again.
Marks are decorative (aria-hidden); every tab has a text label, and package manager tabs keep an aria-label when the narrow layout hides their names.
motion: Tab highlights slide to the measured tab on a bounce-free spring (visualDuration .24).

Snippets, file names and step descriptions crossfade: the old one fades out in 100ms, the new one fades in over 160ms with a 2px rise. Old and new share one grid cell and every code block reserves the height of its longest snippet, so nothing moves.
A new key eases the slot from the placeholder width to the key width (exact, in ch) while the key wipes in from the left over 340ms, then its tint fades out.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and drops the wipe, rise and slide.

name: keycap-keyboard
title: Keycap keyboard
description: Mechanical keycaps that sink and light up as you type, with the text above the board.
whenToUse: Landing pages for keyboard-first products and developer tools.
Onboarding that teaches shortcuts by lighting the keys they use.
Playful empty states and easter eggs.
whenNotToUse: Form input; use a real text field.
On-screen keyboards for accessibility needs; use the platform's.
accessibility: Every cap is a real button named by its character or function (Space, Delete, Return, Shift).
The typed text is a read-only, multiline textbox named Typed text; focusing it lets physical keys type in focus mode.
Shortcuts with Command, Control, or Alt pass through untouched, and window mode never captures keys typed into other fields.
motion: A cap drops 92% of its travel in 35ms on key down and returns in 200ms with a small lift past rest, so each press feels crisp.
A faint light blooms on the board under the cap and fades over 700ms; fast typing leaves a soft trail.
The caret holds still while you type and starts blinking again after 600ms idle. New characters fade in over 140ms.
Reduced motion removes cap travel, character fades, and the blink; the light and legend color still respond.

name: lightbox-gallery
title: Lightbox gallery
description: A masonry grid where photos zoom from their slot into a viewer you can swipe, pinch, and drag away.
whenToUse: Photo collections people browse and inspect up close, such as trips, portfolios, or listings.
Mixed portrait and landscape sets that should keep their aspect ratios in a masonry grid.
whenNotToUse: Use photo-grid for a square grid with pinch zoom between densities.
Use carousel for a single inline row without a viewer.
Use dialog to show one arbitrary piece of content.
accessibility: The grid is a labelled region of buttons named like "Open Harbor, photo 1 of 3"; the viewer is a portalled role="dialog" with aria-modal and a focus trap, and focus starts on Close.
Only the current slide is exposed to assistive tech, and a polite live counter reads "2 of 12" as photos change.
Zoom is an aria-pressed toggle, previous and next are disabled at the ends, and the thumbnail strip marks the current photo with aria-current.
motion: Opening flies the photo from its grid slot to fit the stage on a spring with a constant corner radius; closing flies it back to the current photo's slot while the backdrop fades.
Drag down to dismiss with resistance, swipe between photos with momentum, and pinch, Ctrl+scroll, or double click to zoom around the pointer.
Reduced motion skips the flight and swiping springs, fades the viewer in and out, and jumps zoom and slides into place.

name: link-unfurl
title: Link unfurl
description: A composer where pasting a URL shows a loading shimmer on the link, then unfurls it into a rich preview card with title, image and favicon in one morph, which can be collapsed back to the inline link or removed.
whenToUse: A message or comment composer where pasted links should show what they point to before sending.
Product marketing that shows how a chat or notes app handles links.
whenNotToUse: Use hover-card to preview a link someone reads, not writes.
Use mention-input when the tokens are people or records rather than web links, and rich-text-editor for long formatted documents.
accessibility: The message is a contenteditable element with role="textbox", aria-multiline, a label, and a description of its keys. Pasting inserts plain text, and a pasted or typed address (followed by a space) becomes an atomic link that deletes as one unit.

Keyboard: Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, and Alt+Enter shows or collapses the preview of the link before the caret. Every card has a named collapse button and a named remove button, and its title is a real link.
A folded card is inert and hidden from assistive technology, so only open previews are in the tab order.
A polite live region announces a link being added and loading, the preview opening with its site and title, collapsing, removal, a failed preview, and the sent message. Send errors use role="alert".
Loading is shown by the sweep and by muted text and a globe instead of a favicon, and announced, never by color alone.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. Focused controls take a muted fill.
motion: One rAF loop drives every card from a critically damped spring, writing only transforms, clip paths, opacity, and the plate size; React renders once per state change, never per frame.

The card is clipped to the exact rectangle of its inline link, with the favicons aligned, and translated onto it. As the spring runs the clip widens first and deepens after, while the translation eases home, so the link reads as unrolling into the card. A plate under the card carries its border and a shadow that lifts only mid flight.
The lane grows with the card's height on the same progress, so the toolbar below glides instead of jumping. The body fades in after the header, and the image settles from a slight zoom.
When a preview resolves, the link's width morphs to fit the title while the title rolls up and the favicon pops in.
Collapsing runs the same path backwards on a quicker spring. Dragging a card up folds it with the pointer; releasing past about 40% or with an upward flick folds it, otherwise it springs back.

The loop sleeps once cards settle, and cards land instantly when the composer is offscreen or the tab is hidden; the loading sweep pauses with them. Reduced motion and paused open and fold cards instantly and show a still tint instead of the sweep.

name: liquid-tab-bar
title: Liquid tab bar
description: Tabs with a lens selection that slides between them, swaps labels cleanly, and fills in icons as it passes.
whenToUse: Switching between a handful of peer sections with icons, such as an app's main areas.
Bottom or top bars on mobile-style layouts where the selection should feel physical.
Tabs that carry badge counts for new items.
whenNotToUse: Use tabs for text-only panels inside a page.
Use segmented-control for compact filters or view toggles.
Use morph-nav for site navigation with dropdown panels.
accessibility: Uses the tablist and tab roles with aria-selected, aria-controls, and a roving tabindex.
Each tab's accessible name includes its badge, using badgeLabel when given.
The inverted copy inside the lens is decorative; only one set of tabs is exposed.
motion: The lens slides and resizes to the new tab on the morph spring as one shape, with no stretch or squash; it leans slightly toward a hovered tab.
The label being left fades out at once and the new label fades in only as the lens arrives, so two labels never show together; icons, labels, and badges keep their places.

Grab the lens on the selected tab and drag or throw it; it lands where its momentum reaches, a quick flick always moves at least one tab, and it resists past either end. The selected tab's label opens on a spring and badge digits roll.
Reduced motion jumps the lens and labels to their places without travel or lean.

name: live-visitors
title: Live visitors
description: A realtime visitors card where the live count rolls digit by digit, new arrivals ping in on a dotted world map, the top pages reorder with bars, and signups and upgrades tick in with country flags.
whenToUse: Realtime visitors on a marketing site or app, next to signups and upgrades as they happen.
Launch days and campaigns where a team watches traffic and conversions live.
Admin and growth dashboards that need one glanceable tile for right now.
whenNotToUse: Historical trends over days or weeks; use a chart with axes.
Precise geography or per-country breakdowns; use a table or a proper map.
A single number with no context; use a stat card.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section; the count is read once as plain text ("128 people on the site now"), and the rolling digits are hidden from screen readers.
The pause button is a toggle with aria-pressed and a label that names the action; its tooltip says the same.
Status is never color alone: the dot always sits next to Live, Paused, Connecting or Reconnecting.
Each event row reads as one sentence with the country spelled out and the time in words ("Signed up, Berlin, Germany, 12 seconds ago"). Flags are decorative.
The map is decorative and hidden; the same information is in the lists.
Count changes are not announced, so screen readers are not flooded. A polite live region reports pause and resume, and says when the stream is simulated.
motion: Digits roll on their own strips (280ms ease-out) with tabular numerals, so the number never changes width; a new leading digit (99 to 100) grows in.
New visitors fade in on the map with one ring that expands and fades (900ms); events get a stronger ring and a small city label for 2s. Expired dots fade out over 400ms.
Page rows and event rows move as one step: rows slide by one row height (280ms), the new row fades in (160ms) and the last one fades out below the clip. Bars ease to their new width.
The live dot pulses every 1.6s only while live and on screen. The state label crossfades (out 100ms, in 160ms) in a reserved width.
Reduced motion keeps every update but drops the rolls, rings, slides and pulse.

name: llm-cost-calculator
title: LLM cost calculator
description: A pricing calculator for LLM workloads. Set tokens per request, requests per day and prompt caching, and eight current models re-rank by monthly cost. Bars glide and prices roll as you drag.
whenToUse: A pricing or settings page needs an honest monthly estimate for an LLM workload across several models.
People pick a model for a feature and should see how cost moves with prompt size, output length, traffic and caching.
An internal tool compares provider prices before a migration or a budget review.
whenNotToUse: Use model-picker to choose a model in a chat or composer without a cost comparison.
Use context-window to show the live token usage of one conversation against a model's context window.
Use usage-meter or usage-pricing for actual metered spend against a plan; this estimates, it does not report.
accessibility: The panel is a section named by its heading. The model list is a radio group named "Models ranked by monthly cost, lowest first" with a single tab stop on the selected model.
Rows are in DOM order by rank, so a screen reader reads them in the order shown. Each row's name says the model, the provider, its rank and its monthly cost.
Sliders are Arc sliders with real values spoken as token and request counts, not stop indexes.
One polite status region announces the selected model's monthly cost and rank once the numbers settle (not on every drag frame) and says the prices are samples calculated in the browser.
Selection is shown by a tinted row, an accent bar and aria-checked, never by color alone in the accessible tree. The error state pairs an icon with the words Prices did not load.
The large total and the rolling numbers are hidden from assistive tech where the status region and row labels already carry the value.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus uses Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Rows are placed by transform only and move to their new rank on a critically damped spring (about 240ms, no bounce), so a re-rank is one clean glide with no reflow.
Bars follow the same spring to their new share of the most expensive model.
Every price counts to its new value over 240ms on an ease-out with tabular numerals, written straight to the node so eight rows roll during a drag without re-rendering.

The model name under the total and the price line crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in) when the selection changes. State changes between loading, list, error and empty crossfade the list area at a fixed height.
Reduced motion jumps rows, bars and numbers to their end values and keeps every state and announcement. The loading pulse stops.

name: meeting-summary
title: Meeting summary
description: An AI meeting notes card: the header shows the Google Meet or Zoom mark, the attendees and the duration. Summary, Decisions and Action items stream in after a short summarizing pass. Hover any line to see the transcript quote it came from, then check off action items or send them to Linear or Notion.
whenToUse: Showing AI notes after a call in a CRM, a recruiting tool, a meeting recorder or a team workspace.
Turning a transcript into decisions and owned tasks that people can push to their tracker.
Any summary where readers should be able to check a point against what was actually said.
whenNotToUse: Live captions or a running transcript during the call; use text-stream or a transcript view.
A general task list with no meeting behind it; use checkbox rows in your own list.
Long documents with many sections; render them as a document page instead of a card.
accessibility: The card is an article named after the meeting, with h2 for the title and h3 for each section.
Timestamps are buttons with aria-expanded; the open quote is a role="tooltip" referenced by aria-describedby.
Each checkbox is a native button with role="checkbox" and aria-checked, and each checkbox and send button is labeled with the action item text, so a list of them still reads clearly.
The 16px checkbox has a 32px hit area, and the keyboard focus ring hugs the square itself.
A polite live region announces summarizing, the finished summary, checked items and sends, and says "Simulated, nothing was sent" when no onSend is wired.
Status never relies on color: a failed send shows an alert icon with a retry label, a sent item shows the target mark, its reference and a check.
The platform name is read before the date, and owners shown by first name on narrow cards keep their full name for screen readers.
motion: Summarizing lasts about one second with a shimmer on the label, then notes stream 3 to 8 words every 34ms; each chunk only fades in.

The body springs to its new height between loading, notes, error and empty (0.24s, no bounce). Owner, date and send controls reserve their space while text streams, so nothing shifts when they fade in.

Checking an item grows the accent fill in (160ms) and draws the check on (200ms ease-out), while a 1px strikethrough sweeps left to right across every wrapped line and the text eases to muted. Unchecking reverses it faster. A press scales the square to 0.9, never the row.
Send buttons crossfade mark to spinner to a sent chip while their slot springs to the new width.
Quotes fade in over 160ms with a 3px offset after a short hover intent, then switch instantly between lines.

Reduced motion skips the stream, size springs, check drawing and strikethrough sweep and keeps every end state and announcement. The pass waits until the card is on screen. The sample sends one item to Linear and ticks off another once, unless someone has already used the card.

name: mixture-of-experts
title: Mixture of experts
description: An illustration of mixture of experts routing: each token is scored by a router, travels to its top experts, and their outputs merge into the token's result.
whenToUse: Explaining why a mixture of experts model is cheap per token: only the chosen experts run, which the active parameter readout makes concrete.
Showing how a gate scores experts, picks the top k and blends their outputs, with real or sample scores.
Teaching load balancing and expert capacity, where an uneven router overloads some experts and drops tokens.
whenNotToUse: Use model-router to pick which model handles a request in a product; this card explains routing inside one model.
Use attention-map to show which tokens a token attends to, rather than which experts process it.
Use token-inspector to show tokenization, token ids and probabilities of generated text.
Use speculative-decoding to explain draft and verify generation speedups.
accessibility: The card is a labelled group. The stage lines, router bars and packets are decorative and hidden from assistive technology; every fact they show is also on a focusable element or in text.
Each token is a button whose name lists its experts and weights, such as "paid: Verbs 68%, Symbols 32%", and says when an expert skipped it at capacity. Pinning sets aria-pressed.
Each expert tile is a button named with its load, whether it is at capacity, and its role in the route on screen.
The rolling numbers are hidden from assistive technology and paired with plain text, such as "37B of 671B parameters active per token" and the load balance in percent.
First and second choices are told apart by order and label as well as color, and a skipped expert shows a warning icon, a dashed border and the word full, never color alone.
Pausing, resuming, pinning, the top k change and replay are announced through a polite status region. Autoplay itself is not announced.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One clock drives the story: the input chip slides in, a packet with a short soft trail travels to the router, the score bars grow, packets travel to the chosen experts, the tiles light up and their counters roll, and the packets curve into the merge point and out to the output chip.

Packets are drawn straight to the DOM on requestAnimationFrame; React only re-renders when a phase changes. Travel uses an in-out curve and an arc length table so dots and trails move evenly on curves.

Score bars, tile tints and connector colors are CSS transitions on transform and color. Load counters, the active parameter readout and the balance roll on tabular numerals with the smooth, critically damped spring.
Hover, keyboard focus, a pin, scrolling out of view and the pause button all stop the clock exactly where it is, and it resumes from there.
Footer text swaps with a short crossfade: the old line fades out in about 100ms while the new one fades in from 2px below.
Reduced motion drops all travel and the loop: each token's scores, experts and output land in place on a slower cadence, and the card stops on its summary.

name: model-card
title: Model card
description: A model details card where switching models rolls every price, limit and score in place, a token slider estimates monthly cost live, and benchmark bars show each model's rank on hover. Compare crossfades to a side-by-side table against any rival with the better values marked, and the card never changes size.
