whenToUse: The detail pane of a model picker, showing what the highlighted model can do and what it costs before someone selects it.
Model pages in docs or a marketplace, with limits, prices and a quick benchmark read against close rivals.
Settings where a team picks a default model and wants a side by side check against an alternative.
whenNotToUse: Use model-picker to choose between many models; pair it with this card for the details.
Use context-window to show how full a live conversation's context is.
Use a pricing table for plan pricing; this card shows per token API prices.
Do not use it for official benchmark leaderboards with many models; the bar list shows three models.
accessibility: The card is an article labelled by the model name. Specs and prices are description lists, so each value is read with its label.

The compare view is a table with column headers for the two models and a row header per spec. The better value carries a check icon and the text "better" for screen readers, so the comparison never relies on color.
A polite status region says what changed when you switch views, rivals or benchmarks (for example "Comparing Claude Opus 5.5 with Gemini 4 Argon"). Copy model id announces Copied on its own.

Benchmark bars are hidden from assistive technology; each row is focusable and labelled with the full readout (score, rank and gap to the leader). Marks are decorative and hidden, since the name is always written next to them.
Modality chips say supported or not supported to screen readers; unsupported chips are dashed as well as muted, so the difference never relies on color.

While loading, the card is aria-busy, the skeleton is hidden, Compare is disabled and the status region says Loading model details. An error is announced with role alert. Inactive panels are inert and aria-hidden.
During a text swap the outgoing value is hidden from assistive technology, so names and values are never read twice.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus uses Arc's shared focus outline.
motion: The card never changes size. Details, compare, loading and error are panels stacked in one grid cell, so the card is always as tall as the tallest panel; switching fades the old panel out in 100ms and the new one in over 160ms. Inside a panel every slot is reserved: two summary lines, all seven chips, every spec and price cell, a fixed number of benchmark rows and a readout that holds its lines.

Switching models crossfades every text value in place and rolls prices, the estimated cost, page counts and scores to their new values in tabular numerals inside reserved widths. Bars and the context gauge slide on a critically damped spring (visualDuration 0.24, no bounce).
Dragging the volume slider rolls the estimated cost live; the compare table's cost row follows the same volume.
Hovering or focusing a benchmark row tints it, fades the other rows to half opacity and crossfades the readout to its score, rank and gap, all within 160ms.
The bars grow from zero once, the first time the card is mostly in view, 40ms apart.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and drops travel: views, bars, numbers and values change in place, and the skeleton holds still.

name: model-training
title: Model training
description: Training data batches feed a small neural net diagram whose connections strengthen, a loss curve descends beside it, and an evaluation check turns green at the end.
whenToUse: An AI or ML product section that explains training, fine-tuning or evaluation in one glance.
Docs pages introducing batches, epochs, loss curves or held-out evaluation.
whenNotToUse: Use line-chart or metric-card for real, live training metrics.
Use data-flow to explain how records move through a pipeline, and pipeline-status for real job status.
accessibility: The diagram is one element with role="img" and an aria-label that walks through the whole run: batches, the forward pass, backprop strengthening the connections, the loss falling over the epochs, and the held-out evaluation passing its target.

The step bar is an ordered list of real buttons named "Stage 3, Backprop" with aria-current on the playing stage, and a play and pause button with a specific name. The caption repeats the story in words.
Nothing relies on color alone: every readout is a number, the evaluation shows Waiting, Running or Passed as a named tag next to the score, and the winning prediction is a probability.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One rAF loop writes SVG transforms, opacity, dash offsets, widths, CSS variables and a few text nodes straight to the DOM, and only when a value changed; React does not render per frame.

The whole run is a pure function of time, so the loop is seamless: at the start of each run the connections relax back to their random starting weights while the readouts crossfade from the finished run to an untrained model.

Batches fly from the stack into the input layer on an eased curve while the stack advances one slot, signals ride each connection with a smooth ease and fade at both ends, and the error travels back as a short dash. Nodes fill as a signal lands and ring as the error passes.

Each backward pass strengthens the connections it crossed, so weights, the loss curve, the epoch count and the output probabilities all step together, with the loss head gliding along the curve during each update.

Hover slows the story on a critically damped spring. The loop stops off screen, in hidden tabs, and when paused. Reduced motion shows the finished run as a still frame: learned connections, the full loss curve with its validation point, and the passed evaluation. Picking a stage then shows that stage's still frame.

name: morph-loader
title: Morph loader
description: Tiny loaders that morph between shapes and fold into a check or a cross when done.
whenToUse: Inline progress inside a button, row, or field where the result should appear in the same spot.
Short operations that end in a clear success or failure, such as save, publish, or upload.
Any spinner where a tiny, crisp, brand-consistent mark matters.
whenNotToUse: Use progress when the percentage is known.
Use skeleton when content is loading into a layout.
Use action-button when the whole button should morph its label too.
accessibility: The root is role="status" with visually hidden text that changes to label, successLabel, or errorLabel.
The drawing is aria-hidden; completion is never shown by color alone because the shape becomes a check or a cross.
Set decorative inside buttons that already announce progress, so the state is not read twice.
motion: Each stroke is a center, length, direction, bend, and width, each on its own spring, so any shape can morph into any other and interruptions keep velocity.
Dots bounce in a wave, bars grow in sequence, the ring turns while its arcs breathe, and the square tumbles a quarter turn at a time while its corners open.
On success or error the loop fades, the drawing turns forward to upright, the strokes draw the mark in order, and the mark pops once.
Reduced motion shows a static shape per state and swaps instantly.

name: morph-nav
title: Morph nav
description: A navigation bar that morphs into rich menus, search, and a compact state as one surface.
whenToUse: The top navigation of a marketing or product site with a few sections that each hold several destinations.
Headers where search should grow out of the bar instead of opening a separate modal.
Sites that want one primary action, such as Sign up, pinned to the end of the bar.
whenNotToUse: Use liquid-tab-bar for an app-style switcher between a handful of peer sections.
Use tabs for switching views inside a page.
Use dropdown-menu when you only need one menu of commands, not site navigation.
accessibility: Renders a nav landmark; the current item carries aria-current="page" and panel triggers use aria-expanded and aria-controls.
Open panels are regions labelled by their trigger; the panel closes when focus leaves the nav.
Search is a combobox driving a listbox with aria-activedescendant, and the result count is announced politely. With an empty query it lists the first five entries as Suggested.
A pointer down outside the nav closes the panel or search.
motion: The surface springs to each panel's size, with a little bounce when it grows and none when it shrinks. Moving to a neighbour slides the new panel in from that side while a highlight glides between items.
Hover opens a panel after a 60ms intent delay and leaving the nav closes it after 180ms, so crossing a gap does not flicker it shut.
Search grows out of the same surface as the bar fades and blurs away; compact and narrow states retune the bar.
Reduced motion drops travel, scale, and blur and keeps short fades.

examples.title: Tighten on scroll

name: multi-region-failover
title: Multi-region failover
description: Animated multi-region failover on a 2.5D stage: users stream requests through a global load balancer to two regions; the primary degrades, fails three health checks, traffic shifts smoothly to the healthy region, then it recovers, passes three checks and traffic ramps back to an even split.
whenToUse: A reliability, infrastructure or pricing page that needs to show why running in two regions keeps a service up during an outage.
Docs for health checks, failover policies, traffic weights or slow start, where viewers should step through detection, failover, recovery and rebalance.
Incident write-ups and postmortems that explain how traffic moved during a regional outage.
whenNotToUse: Use database-replication to show a primary database failing over to a replica.
Use circuit-breaker for one service failing fast against a failing dependency.
Use autoscale for instances added and removed with load in one place.
Use a real status or monitoring component to report actual region health.
accessibility: The drawing is role="img" with an aria-label that tells the whole story: the split, the failing region, the failed checks, the shift to the healthy region and the gradual return. Pass label to write your own.

Labels, counters, the moving health check chip and hover tags inside the drawing are part of that image, and the narrated caption is hidden from assistive technology, so screen readers hear one stable description instead of a changing loop.

The scrubber is a group of real buttons named Step 1 of 6 and so on; the current step carries aria-current="step", arrow keys, Home and End move between steps, and the pause button reports its state with aria-pressed.
Status is never color alone: every chip pairs its dot with words such as Failed checks 2/3, Out of rotation, Warming up 62% or Errors 27.3%, and failing instances also change their outline.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame loop writes SVG attributes, transforms, opacity and text directly, and only when a value changed; React never re-renders per frame.

Requests are a deterministic stream: each one is routed by the balancer weight at the moment it reaches the balancer and lands on a specific instance, which flashes. Requests to a down instance stall, turn to errors and fade.

Requests travel along real arcs at an even pace with a glide ease, so they gather at the balancer and fan out, with a shadow that slides along the floor and shrinks as they rise, which gives the 2.5D depth.

Every frame is a pure function of one clock, so the weights, counters, checks, statuses and scrubber stay in sync, jumps land exactly, and the loop is seamless because the last frame is the balanced first frame.
Pausing, speed changes and the gentle hover slowdown ease on a critically damped spring. The loop stops offscreen and in a hidden tab and resumes where it left off.
With reduced motion there is no travel or loop: the stage shows a settled frame of the failover, and the scrubber switches between settled frames of each stage.

name: now-playing
title: Now playing
description: Grow a mini player into the full player in one continuous morph.
whenToUse: Media that keeps playing while people browse, such as music, podcasts, or audio lessons.
A mini player bar that expands into a full player with artwork and a scrubber.
whenNotToUse: Use bottom-sheet or dialog for a one-off overlay that is not a player.
Use voice-recorder for recording and playing back short voice notes.
Use slider for a plain seek bar without the player chrome.
accessibility: The waveform is a slider with aria-valuetext such as "1:05 of 3:32".
Expand and collapse buttons report aria-expanded. Focus moves to the collapse button on open and back to the mini bar on close.
Previous restarts the current track when more than 3 seconds have played, and skips back otherwise. A restart calls onSeek(0).
The current track and play state are announced in a polite live region; artwork is decorative unless artworkAlt is set.
motion: The mini bar morphs into the full player with shared layout while the shell height springs to fit. In the full player, pulling the artwork down more than 70px or flicking it closes the player; an upward pull rubber-bands.
Artwork slides and blurs in the direction you skip; the waveform stretches under a scrub and level bars dance while playing.
MotionConfig follows the user's reduced motion setting, replacing travel with short fades; the level bars hold still.

name: orbit-logos
title: Orbit logos
description: An integrations showcase with brand logos orbiting your product mark on tilted rings. Hover or focus one to rest the orbit, draw a connection, and see what it does.
whenToUse: An integrations or ecosystem hero on a marketing site.
An integrations settings screen where people browse, read about, and connect tools.
A launch page showing everything a product plugs into.
whenNotToUse: Use a logo marquee for a long list of customer logos.
Use a searchable grid or table for catalogs larger than about twenty integrations.
accessibility: Logos are a labelled list of toggle buttons with aria-pressed; each name includes the category and whether it is connected.
Only one logo is in the tab order (roving tabindex), so the orbit is a single stop between the chips and the card.
The card is a labelled region with real buttons and a Docs link; opening, stepping, and filtering are announced in a polite live region.
Connected status is shown as text and an icon in the card, not by the green dot alone.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. Focus shows as the lifted chip and its name tag.
motion: One rAF loop writes chip translations and the connector; React does not render per frame, and the loop stops when everything is at rest, off screen, or the tab is hidden.
The turn eases to rest on a critically damped spring whenever the pointer or focus enters, a category is picked, or a card is open, so nothing moves while you aim.
Opening a logo springs its ring the short way to the focus spot, with a touch of overshoot. When an outer logo parks, the inner ring steps aside so the connector stays clear.
The card morphs out of the chip: it starts at the chip's box as a circle and springs to its own box, then its content fades in. Previous and next slide the content in the direction of travel.
The category highlight is a shared layout pill on the morph spring; chips scale and dim on CSS springs.
Reduced motion stops the rotation, places rings and the connector at once, and skips the morph and slides.

name: orbit-menu
title: Orbit menu
description: Hold a button and its actions orbit out, ready to pick with a drag.
whenToUse: Three to six quick actions on one object, such as a note or photo.
Touch-first surfaces where press, drag, and release should fire an action in one gesture.
whenNotToUse: Use dropdown-menu or context-menu for longer or text-heavy lists.
Use dock for tools that stay selected.
Use action-button for a single action.
accessibility: The trigger has aria-haspopup="menu", aria-expanded, and aria-controls; actions are role="menuitem" buttons named by their label.
The closed menu is inert, and a roving tabindex keeps one action in the tab order.
Confirmations such as "Pinned" are read from a role="status" region when announce is on.
motion: Actions swirl out along the arc in reading order and fold back in reverse; a lens glides between targeted actions and nearby actions lean toward the pointer.

The trigger glyph morphs between ellipsis, close, and check, and a label pill springs to fit its text. It names the targeted action, shows Release to cancel when a drag leaves the arc, and shows the done text for about 1.4 seconds after firing.

Targeting goes by angle, like a pie menu: the pointer only has to head toward an action, outside a 34px dead zone around the trigger. Releasing off the arc, or a hold without a drag, folds it away without firing.
Reduced motion drops the swirl, blur, and magnet pull, leaving short fades and instant position changes.

name: page-curl
title: Page curl
description: A small magazine you read by dragging page corners, with a real fold, lit curl, and flick to turn.
whenToUse: Editorial and brand showcases where paper is part of the story.
Menus, catalogs, and yearbooks with a handful of spreads.
whenNotToUse: Use carousel or a scrolling page for long content or content people search.
Use a document viewer for dense text that needs zoom and selection.
accessibility: The book is a focusable group with aria-roledescription="book" and the label as its name.
A polite status reads the visible pages, such as "Page 2 and 3 of 8".
Only the resting pages are in the accessibility tree; the turning copies are aria-hidden.
Previous and next are real buttons with labels and disable at the covers. The visible count and the hint are decorative duplicates of the status.
motion: The fold line is the perpendicular bisector between the corner and the pointer, so the page follows the finger from where it was grabbed.
The corner is held within a page width of the spine, like paper bound on one side.
The flap is a mirror of the sheet across the fold with a lit curl at the crease; the page below gets a soft shadow at the fold.
Release projects the pointer's momentum: past the middle or a flick turns the page on a spring that keeps the release velocity; otherwise it lays back down.

The first time the book is mostly in view, the cover corner lifts about a quarter of the page on a soft spring, holds, and lays back down. Until the first turn, entering the book with a mouse repeats it at half the size, at most every 2.5 seconds.
Hovering a corner lifts it. Hovering a page shows a chevron at its outer edge for the direction a tap turns. Taps, arrow keys, and the buttons turn along a lifted arc.
The hint fades out for good after the first drag, tap, key, or button press.
The closed book slides to center on its cover and back cover.
Reduced motion swaps spreads without the curl and skips the tease.

name: payment-flow
title: Payment flow
description: A card tap goes to a processor, then the network, then the bank and back with authorization, then settlement; each hop lights up with a status label and the amount travels as a chip.
whenToUse: A payments or checkout landing section that explains authorization and settlement.
Docs pages introducing processors, card networks, issuers, fees, and payout timing.
whenNotToUse: Use checkout-flow or checkout-live for a real checkout form.
Use webhook-fanout to explain what happens after a payment event is emitted.
accessibility: The diagram is one element with role="img" and an aria-label that tells the whole story: the amount, every hop, the approval, the fee, and the payout.
Nodes are not controls, so nothing enters the tab order; hover tags only repeat optional detail.
State never relies on color alone: every node's status line reads Checking risk, Routed to bank, Approved, Cleared, Fee $1.53, or Settled, and the approval chip carries a check and a word.
Pass caption for a visible explanation under the diagram.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One rAF loop writes transforms, opacity, dash values, a few attributes, and text nodes straight to the DOM, and only when a value changed; React does not render per frame.
The payment is a pure function of time, so the loop repeats seamlessly: tap, authorize, approve, settle, pay out, rest. The balance keeps growing from loop to loop instead of jumping back.

The amount eases from node to node and slips under each chip while it is processed, so every hop reads as enter, work, leave. The path lights in the accent behind it and turns to success as the approval travels back.
At the processor waypoint the settlement chip crossfades from the gross to the net amount, which is the fee shown as cause and effect; the balance then counts up with tabular numerals.
Speed changes, pausing, and hover (which slows the story a little) ease on a critically damped spring. The loop stops off screen, in hidden tabs, and when paused.
Reduced motion shows a still frame just after the fee: approved at checkout, the network cleared, the bank settled, and the net amount on its way to the balance.

name: photo-grid
title: Photo grid
description: Pinch through zoom levels and open any photo straight from its cell.
whenToUse: A browsable photo library or album where people zoom between column counts.
Galleries that need favorites and a full-screen viewer with a filmstrip.
Touch and trackpad users who expect pinch to change density.
whenNotToUse: Use lightbox-gallery for a masonry layout that keeps each photo's aspect ratio.
Use carousel for a short inline slideshow.
Use image-compare for before and after pairs.
accessibility: The grid is a labelled list of buttons named by each photo's alt text, with ", favorite" appended when favorited.
Zoom buttons use aria-pressed; the viewer is a labelled dialog and its filmstrip is a slider with the photo title in aria-valuetext.
Viewer changes are announced in a polite status region.
motion: Pinch zoom scales live and reflows around the photo under the fingers; the viewer grows from the tapped cell and can be dragged down to dismiss.
Counters and favorite icons roll or pop in with a short blur.
Reduced motion removes layout travel and keeps fades.

name: pii-redaction
title: PII redaction
description: A guardrail card where personal data is redacted before the prompt reaches the model. Scan marks each name, email, phone number and card with its type and swaps it for a placeholder like [EMAIL_1]. The safe prompt travels to Claude, and the reply comes back with the original values put back for the person.
whenToUse: Explaining or proving a privacy guardrail in an AI product: support assistants, health or finance copilots, enterprise chat.
A settings or onboarding screen where admins see what the PII filter does before they turn it on.
A playground where people paste text and see exactly what would reach the model.
whenNotToUse: Use ai-chat or ai-composer for the conversation itself; redact behind the scenes and show this card only where the guardrail needs explaining.
Do not rely on the built-in detector for compliance; pass a real DLP service through detect.
Use tool-call to show an arbitrary tool step in a transcript.
accessibility: A polite status region announces each phase ("Scanning for personal data", "4 items redacted", "Reply restored") and, when the reply is simulated, adds "Simulated, nothing was sent".

Status never relies on color: every phase pairs an icon with a short label, each type cell says Name, Email, Phone or Card with its token or None found, and marks in the original message carry labels such as "Email, redacted as EMAIL_1".
Scan, Stop, Send, Run again and Retry are one button whose label changes, so keyboard focus stays put through the whole flow. Reset returns focus to the message field.
Only the visible text layer is exposed to assistive tech; the hidden layers that keep the height steady are aria-hidden.
The flow strip is decorative and hidden from screen readers, since the status region already narrates each hop.
The Show original label is a real label for the switch, and the switch is disabled with a muted label until there is a safe prompt to compare.
motion: Scan highlights each entity in turn, 120ms apart, with a 160ms tint in its type color while the matching type cell crossfades from Checking to its token.
The swap to placeholders is a single crossfade between two stacked text layers (old out in 100ms, new in over 160ms), so no words slide or rewrap mid animation and the height never changes.
Each hop of the flow is one dot traveling the connector in 460ms on an ease in out curve; the active node's label shimmers while it works.
The reply streams three to six words every 34ms, each chunk only fading in, then crossfades once to the restored text.
Labels, statuses and the Reset button crossfade in place; nothing bounces and nothing changes size between states.
Reduced motion drops the travel, the stagger, the streaming and the autoplay loop, and keeps every state, label and announcement.

name: pixel-mascot
title: Pixel mascot
description: A pixel-art robot that shows what an AI assistant is doing. It idles, thinks, types, celebrates and errors in frame-stepped sprite animations, and stays crisp at every integer size from 24px to 192px.
whenToUse: A friendly generating indicator next to an assistant reply or in a chat composer.
An empty state or onboarding panel where a small character makes an AI feature feel approachable.
Image or canvas generation, where a mascot in the corner shows thinking, drawing and done.
Products with a playful or retro visual voice that still want precise, calm motion.
whenNotToUse: Detailed agent progress with steps and timings; use agent-status or agent-timeline.
Dense tables or toolbars where a 24px character is noise; use status-dot or a spinner.
Serious or regulated contexts (finance, health, legal) where a character feels flippant; use text-shimmer.
Showing model reasoning content; use reasoning-block.
accessibility: The sprite is one SVG with role="img" and a label such as "Arc is thinking" that follows the status.
A visually hidden polite live region announces status changes when the status is controlled; set announce to false when the surrounding UI already reports progress, to avoid double announcements.
Status is never color alone: each state has its own shape (thought bubble, keyboard, happy eyes, crossed eyes) and the label carries the words.
The error state uses the danger token for the crossed eyes on a tinted screen, so it reads in light and dark and with any accent.
motion: Stepped on purpose: the sprite advances on a fixed 40ms clock and moves in whole pixels. Timings are authored as ease curves in steps, for example the done jump rises fast, holds at the top for 120ms and settles without a rebound.

Status changes never cut: lids close and open, eyes slide one pixel per step, arms pass through neighbouring poses, the thought bubble and keyboard step in and out from wherever they are. A change mid animation reverses from the current frame.

Loops are seamless by construction: idle bobs on a 2s cycle with blinks and a glance on an 8s cycle, thinking cycles three dots every 1.12s, writing types an eight stroke bar every 1.6s while the eyes scan and return.
Only SVG attributes change (transform, x, y, visibility, opacity) from a requestAnimationFrame loop outside React, so there is no layout work or re-render per frame.

Pauses off screen with an IntersectionObserver and when paused is set. With reduced motion the mascot holds a clear resting pose for each status: open eyes, bubble with three dots, keyboard, happy eyes or crossed eyes.

name: prize-wheel
title: Prize wheel
description: A referral or promo prize wheel you flick to spin, with real angular momentum, a flexible pointer that ticks against each peg, weighted segments set by the host, a slow suspenseful settle, and the won segment lifting into a reward card with a copyable code.
whenToUse: A referral or launch page that rewards a signup with a discount code.
An in-product moment that grants one of several perks, such as a milestone reward.
whenNotToUse: Use a plain coupon card or copy button when everyone gets the same reward.
Avoid it in serious flows such as billing or checkout, where chance feels out of place.
accessibility: The Spin hub is a real button with a specific name. Enter or Space pressed and held winds the wheel up; releasing spins it. A screen reader activation without a press spins at a medium strength.
The wheel is one element with role="img" whose label lists every prize with its chance, so the odds are never visual only.
A polite live region announces Spinning, the prize won with its code spelled out, and copy success or failure.
While a spin runs the hub is aria-disabled instead of disabled, so focus stays on it. The hidden reward card is inert until a prize lands.
The winner is never shown by color alone: the card names it, the odds row lights up, and the announcement repeats it.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One rAF loop writes the wheel rotation, the pointer rotation, and the charge ring straight to the DOM, only when a value changed; React renders only when a spin starts and when it lands.
The wheel rotates as a composited HTML layer, so the SVG face never repaints per frame. A static metal sheen sits above it so the light stays still while the wheel turns under it.

A drag follows the pointer angle around the hub; the release velocity from the last 100ms becomes the spin. The winner is drawn by weight, then the travel is chosen as the landing spot nearest the distance that velocity would naturally carry, so the wheel leaves your hand at the speed you threw it.
The spin follows 1 - (1 - t)^3: velocity decays smoothly with no seam and the last turn crawls past the final pegs.

The pointer is a stiff, lightly damped spring that collides with the pegs as a tapered capsule: it only moves when a peg actually touches it, bends about 30 degrees until the peg clears its tip, then snaps back with a short wobble. The collision runs in substeps that follow the wheel, so no peg skips through it at full speed; fast spins rattle it and the settle ticks peg by peg.
A spin thrown from the hub or Spin again builds its speed over a few frames instead of jumping to full speed, and winding up eases in and out. A flick keeps the exact speed of your hand.
The reward card flies from the segment under the pointer to its place on a spring with a little life, one continuous movement.
The loop stops when idle, off screen, and in hidden tabs. Reduced motion removes the drift, the pointer wobble, and the flight: a spin lands at once on the prize and the card appears in place.

name: product-gallery
title: Product gallery
description: A product gallery with a hover magnifier, gliding thumbnails, and color and size variants that crossfade photos.
whenToUse: Product detail pages with several photos per color and a size picker.
Stores where shoppers need to zoom into fabric, texture, or small print.
Variants that sell out per color and should be struck through, not hidden.
whenNotToUse: Use lightbox-gallery for a photo grid that opens into a viewer, with no variants.
Use carousel for marketing slides or cards.
Use photo-grid for a masonry of images without a main photo.
accessibility: The main photo is a button labelled with the photo's alt text, its position, and Open fullscreen.
Thumbnails are a tablist; swatches and sizes are radiogroups with roving tabindex, and sold-out sizes use aria-disabled.
The viewer is a modal dialog that focuses Close on open, traps Tab, locks body scroll, and announces the photo count politely.
Every image needs a meaningful alt; thumbnails and the lens are decorative copies.
motion: The photo track springs to the photo on show and follows a finger one to one, with rubber-band edges; one flick moves one photo.
The lens rides a spring behind the pointer; rail, swatch, and size highlights glide to the active option.
The viewer grows out of the photo's own rectangle with counter-scaled corners and returns to it on close; zoom scales on a spring and pans after the pointer.
Changing color crossfades every photo from a blur. Reduced motion jumps the track, lens, and zoom, and replaces the viewer flight with a fade.

name: prompt-cache
title: Prompt cache
description: An animated explainer for prompt caching: the shared prefix of each request is cached once, later requests read it back, and the cost and time saved add up.
whenToUse: A docs page or blog post that explains why a stable prefix makes repeat requests cheaper and faster.
A pricing or usage page that shows how cache reads, writes and the time to live affect cost.
Developer onboarding for an AI product where prompt order and cache breakpoints matter.
whenNotToUse: Use context-window to show how much of a model's window a conversation fills and when it compacts.
Use token-inspector to show how text splits into tokens and what each costs.
Use model-picker or model-router when the subject is choosing a model rather than reusing a prompt.
Use a real chart of cache hit rate over time for production analytics; this is a teaching illustration with a simulated clock.
accessibility: The card is a section named for the title and marked as a simulation with sample prices.

Each request is a list item with a sentence that gives its time, message, outcome, tokens read from the cache, tokens processed, input cost and time to first token; the bars and rolling numbers are hidden from assistive technology.
Requests sent with the step button, the edit toggle, pausing and reset are announced in a polite live region. Autoplay stays silent so it never talks over the page.

Outcomes are never color alone: every status pairs an icon with a label (Cache write, Cache hit, Partial hit), cached and processed fills differ in fill and outline, and the cache status is written out as Empty, Writing, Reading, Expires in 4:52 or Expired.
The change toggle is a button with aria-pressed. Icon buttons have names and tooltips.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One requestAnimationFrame clock drives the story and runs only while playing or stepping, on screen and in a visible tab. The ring and countdown are written straight to the DOM; React renders only on events.

Processing is one linear sweep at a steady speed across the segments that need it. A cache hit fades the prefix to its cached fill while a single band of each segment's color passes once across the prefix, and the cache panel sweeps in step.

A write carries the new part of the prompt from the row into the cache on a 460ms ease out, changing from processed to cached on the way; the panel's segments land in place and its token count rolls up. The ring refills on a critically damped follow and drains as simulated time passes.
A changed segment raises a short warning line in the gap where matching stops; the cache drops everything after it before the rewrite lands.

Numbers roll from the row above, so cost and first token visibly come down, with tabular numerals in columns sized to their content. Status labels swap with one crossfade. Pausing freezes every CSS animation and the clock together.
Reduced motion opens on a finished round, drops the sweeps, the flight and the break animation, and changes values at once; play and step still work.

name: provider-keys
title: Provider keys
description: A settings card for bring-your-own-key AI products. Each provider row shows its real mark, the masked key, a status and when the key was last used. You can reveal a key for five seconds, copy, rotate or remove it with undo. Adding or rotating a key opens an inline form that checks the format as you type, then tests the connection before saving.
whenToUse: A settings page where users add their own Anthropic, OpenAI, Google AI, Mistral or xAI keys.
Showing which providers are connected, which keys were rejected, and when each key was last used.
Letting users rotate a leaked key or remove one with a short undo window.
whenNotToUse: Choosing a model for a request; use model-picker.
Managing your own product's API keys for customers with scopes and expiry; use secret-rotation or a table.
Showing spend or rate limits; use usage-meter.
accessibility: A section labelled by its title, with the rows in a list. Every icon button has a provider-specific label, such as "Copy the Anthropic key".
Status is never color alone: an icon plus Connected, Invalid, Not set or Testing. The status button's label includes the rejection reason.
Reveal is a toggle with aria-pressed; rotate and Add key report aria-expanded for the inline form.
A polite live region announces reveals, copies, test results, removals and undo. Without testKey it adds "Simulated, nothing was sent."
The form's input has a label and points at the helper line with aria-describedby; format and rejection errors set aria-invalid.
Focus is managed: the form focuses its input, Cancel returns focus to its trigger, Remove moves focus to Undo, and Undo returns it to Remove.
motion: Status, key, meta and helper text swap with one crossfade (out 100ms, in 160ms with a 2px rise) in a shared grid cell, so nothing resizes.
The inline form opens and closes on a measured height spring (visualDuration .24, no bounce) with a short fade.
The reveal countdown is a hairline ring that empties linearly over revealDuration. Icon swaps (eye, copy check) scale and fade in 160ms.
Reduced motion keeps every state and announcement, drops the countdown ring, the rise and the press scale, and slows the spinner.

name: provider-status
title: Provider status
description: A status card for the AI providers your product depends on. Each row shows the provider's real mark, its health as an icon and label, p50 latency and a 30-day uptime bar with a tooltip for each day. An incident row expands into its timeline of updates, and the card checks again on a visible countdown.
whenToUse: Showing the live health, latency and recent uptime of the model providers your product routes to.
Explaining degraded AI features to users or admins with the provider's incident updates in place.
A routing or fallback settings page where people need to see which providers are healthy right now.
whenNotToUse: A full public status page with components, subscriptions and history: build a page, not a card.
A single provider's state inside a chat header: use agent-status or a small badge.
Detailed latency charts over time: use a chart component.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section. Rows are a list; an incident row has a full-row button with aria-expanded and aria-controls, named with the provider, its health and the incident title.
Health is never color alone: every status shows an icon and a label, and day ticks carry their health in the tooltip and in the bar's label.
Each uptime bar is one tab stop with a label that sums up the 30 days. Arrow keys move through the days and a polite live region reads each one, so 180 ticks never flood the tab order.
A polite live region announces checks, refresh errors and simulated actions ("Simulated, no requests were sent").
Focus rings come from the shared :focus-visible styles; the row button's ring sits just inside the row.
motion: Health labels, latency, uptime and the summary change with a single crossfade (out in 100ms, in over 160ms with a 2px rise) inside a reserved grid cell, so nothing reflows.
The incident panel springs to its measured height with no bounce (visual duration 240ms); new updates fade in while the panel grows.
Ticks change color over 240ms. The countdown ring is a linear CSS drain that pauses with the countdown off screen; Checking swaps it for a short spinner and a shimmer label.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and drops the rise, the height spring, the spinner and the skeleton pulse.
exports: AnthropicMark, OpenaiMark, GeminiColorMark, MistralColorMark, XaiMark, AwsMark

name: reasoning-block
title: Reasoning block
description: The collapsible thinking block of an AI reply. While the model thinks, a shimmering label counts the seconds and the latest reasoning streams underneath. When it finishes, it folds to "Thought for 7s" and opens to show the full reasoning as calm steps with headings.
whenToUse: Showing a reasoning model's thinking above its answer in a chat or agent transcript.
Letting people audit why an assistant reached a recommendation without crowding the reply.
Restoring past messages where the reasoning should stay folded with its original thinking time.
whenNotToUse: Tool or function calls with inputs and outputs: use ToolCall.
A multi step agent plan with checkable tasks: use Agent plan.
A one line busy indicator with no reasoning to show: use TextShimmer on its own.
accessibility: The header is a real button with aria-expanded and aria-controls; its name is the visible label, such as "Thought for 7s".
A polite live region announces status changes only (thinking, thought for 7 seconds, stopped, interrupted), never each streamed chunk or each second.
The two line live preview is aria-hidden because the same text is in the full reasoning region, which carries aria-busy while streaming.
Status is never color alone: errors pair an alert icon with "Thinking interrupted", and the footer pairs a check, square or alert with Done, Stopped or the reason.
The no props preview says "Simulated, nothing was sent to a model" to assistive technology.
motion: Streaming is chunked: each appended chunk fades in once over 140ms. No blur, slide or per word springs.
Stop and Retry overflow a fixed 20px row, so the header is 44px in every state and never shifts when an action appears.
The live preview stays anchored to its newest line; when a line wraps, the text glides up with a bounce free spring (0.24s) instead of jumping.
Label swaps (Thinking to Thought for 7s) are a single crossfade: out in 100ms, in over 160ms with a 2px rise. The seconds counter rolls in tabular numerals inside a reserved width.

Opening, closing and the preview collapsing all animate measured height with one critically damped spring (0.26s) and one opacity fade. Only what streams in while open (a new step, paragraph or chunk) fades on its own, so nothing animates twice.
The shimmer and the self-playing loop pause off screen and in background tabs. Reduced motion keeps every end state, drops the shimmer, the glide and the chunk fades, and cuts heights instantly.

name: reasoning-tree
title: Reasoning tree
description: An illustration of tree search over thoughts: candidates are scored, weak branches fade, the best expand, and the winning path from question to answer draws in.
whenToUse: Explainers, docs and landing pages that teach tree of thoughts, beam search or test time search over reasoning steps.
Showing why a wider search can beat a greedy one, with a control the reader can change and replay.
A visual summary of how an agent weighed options before it chose a plan.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run or research-run to show a real agent's steps and output as they stream.
Use agent-loop to explain the plan, act and observe cycle of a tool using agent.
Use speculative-decoding or attention-map for token level mechanics rather than whole thoughts.
Use model-router when the decision is which model handles a request.
accessibility: The thoughts form a tree with treeitems that carry their level and position, and a roving tab stop, so the whole tree is a single Tab stop.

Every thought's accessible name is its full text with its score and its fate: not scored yet, scored, kept, pruned, on the best path, or answer. A pruned thought fades and loses its edge, and the answer has a check icon, so state never relies on color alone.
Focus and hover show the full thought in a tag next to the node; the same text is in the accessible name.
A polite status region speaks each step when you step or pause, and the answer when the search ends, but stays quiet while the search plays on its own.
The header status pairs a pause or check icon with a short label, and the working label carries a calm shimmer.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring around the node.
motion: A proposed thought fades in as its edge draws out of the parent, 20ms apart per sibling.
Scores fill as a bar with digits that roll on the same 640ms curve, using tabular numerals in a fixed width.
Pruning fades the thought to 40% and retracts its edge back into the parent. Kept thoughts turn their bar to the accent.

At the end the best path draws from the question to the answer in about 760ms with a lighter sheen at its head, each node on it lights up as the line reaches it, and the answer settles with one short press and a check.
On phones a new child glides the lines below it down on a critically damped spring before it fades in, so nothing jumps and nothing bounces.
Header labels swap with a single 160ms crossfade; the play and pause icons crossfade in place.
Reduced motion shows the finished search with the path highlighted. Stepping and playing still work, with every change applied at once and no shimmer.

name: referral-card
title: Referral card
description: A give-and-get referral card where people copy or share their invite link, invite friends by email as chips, and watch invites move from invited to signed up to earned, with the credit total counting up and a milestone reward unlocking.
whenToUse: A referral or invite program in account settings, billing or an onboarding checklist.
Showing a person what their invites have earned and how close they are to a bonus reward.
whenNotToUse: Team member invites with roles and permissions; use a members table.
Public leaderboards or affiliate payouts with many columns; use a table.
accessibility: Share buttons are icon buttons with aria-labels (Post on X, Share on LinkedIn, Share by email) and tooltips; a polite live region reports what happened, including Simulated, nothing was posted.
The hint under the email field is a polite status tied to the input with aria-describedby; errors set aria-invalid and show an alert icon plus text, never color alone.
Stages are an icon plus a word. The milestone is a progressbar with aria-valuetext such as 4 of 5 paid referrals.
The funnel is a definition list, the people a labelled list.
While sending, the field turns read only instead of disabled, so keyboard focus stays put.
motion: Numbers roll to their new value in 600ms with tabular numerals, so columns never shift.
Stage labels, the milestone line, share icons and the hint crossfade once: old out in 100ms, new in over 160ms with a 2px rise, stacked in one grid cell.
Milestone segments fill from the left in 240ms and turn to the success color when unlocked.
New invites open at the top of the list with a bounce-free height spring (0.24s) inside a fixed-height list, so the card never grows.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and drops the roll, rise and height travel; the sample program plays twice as fast.

name: reply-draft
title: Reply draft
description: An AI email reply drafter where Claude streams a reply under a received Gmail message. Quick replies steer a fresh draft, tone and length rewrite it with a single crossfade, and you can edit the finished draft before you insert it.
whenToUse: Drafting a reply to an email, ticket or message with an AI model, where the reader reviews and edits before sending.
Offering quick reply intents plus tone and length controls for generated text.
Showing an AI writing feature on a landing page with a realistic, self-playing example.
whenNotToUse: Free-form chat with a model: use a chat or composer component instead.
Inline autocomplete while typing: use ghost-text.
Sending the email itself: this component inserts a draft; your composer owns sending.
accessibility: The card is an article labelled with the sender; the reply area is a labelled section.
Quick replies are toggle buttons with aria-pressed; tone and length are radio groups with roving tabindex.
The finished draft is a plain-text editable textbox (contenteditable plaintext-only), so readers can fix a word before Insert. Edits are what onInsert receives.
A polite live region announces drafting, rewriting, ready, inserted and errors. Simulated actions say nothing was sent.
The body is aria-busy while drafting. Status uses an icon plus a short label, never color alone.
motion: Drafts stream in chunks of 3 to 8 words every 34ms; each chunk only fades in over 140ms.
Tone and length rewrites crossfade once: the old draft dims during the short rewrite, fades out in 100ms and the new one fades in over 160ms with a 2px rise.
The draft box springs to its measured height with no bounce; during a regenerate its height is held until the new draft finishes, so the card never jumps.
The selected tone and length pills glide with a bounce-free spring. Status labels crossfade; working labels use a calm shimmer.
Reduced motion: drafts appear whole, crossfades and the height spring are instant, chunk fades and the press scale are dropped.

name: response-feedback
title: Response feedback
description: A feedback control for AI replies where thumbs down opens an inline panel with reason chips and an optional note, thumbs up fills and asks what was good, and a submit shows a short thank-you before folding back into the row.
whenToUse: Collecting thumbs up and down on AI replies in a chat, copilot or search answer.
Gathering structured reasons (inaccurate, unsafe) for model evaluation or support triage.
Adding a message action row with copy and regenerate next to feedback.
whenNotToUse: Star or numeric ratings of a product or session: use rating.
General product feedback not tied to one reply: use feedback-morph.
Long surveys with many questions: use a form or dialog.
accessibility: Thumbs are toggle buttons with aria-pressed and labels Good response and Bad response; aria-expanded and aria-controls point at the panel while it is open.
Reason chips are toggle buttons with aria-pressed inside a labelled group. Selected chips invert to a solid fill, so the state never relies on hue.

A keyboard press on thumbs down moves focus to the first reason; a pointer press leaves focus where it is. After a keyboard submit, focus lands on the thank-you line and returns to the thumb when the panel folds.
A polite live region announces rating changes, sending, the thank-you state, errors, and says when nothing was sent because the send is simulated.
Errors show an icon and text next to the actions, and Submit becomes Try again.
motion: The panel opens and closes on a bounce-free spring (0.24s visual duration) that animates measured height, with a 160ms opacity fade.
Switching between the form and the thank-you line is a single crossfade (out 100ms, in 160ms, 2px rise) while the panel height springs to the new content.
The filled thumb fades in over 160ms on top of the outline, so nothing moves or resizes. Presses scale to .94 instantly and release on a spring.
The success tick draws once in 280ms.
Reduced motion: height changes cut instantly, the panel only fades, and press scales are dropped. All end states and announcements stay.

name: sand-text
title: Sand text
description: A headline made of sand that pours into the letters, crumbles where the cursor digs, and heals itself.
whenToUse: A hero headline or section title that should be fun to touch.
Short words that change on a selection, like a product name or theme.
whenNotToUse: Body copy or long headings; use in-view-title or text-reveal.
Text that must stay readable while people interact near it, like form labels.
accessibility: The real text is rendered in a visually hidden heading, so screen readers and search read it as text.
The canvas is aria-hidden. Digging is decorative and never removes the text from the accessibility tree.
motion: Letters fill bottom first like jars. Dug grains fly with the pointer's velocity and settle with a falling sand automaton.
Grains that come to rest inside a letter stick again, missing grains pour back in once the pointer rests, and loose sand outside the letters drifts away.
A new word turns the old letters loose, so the old text collapses while the new one pours in.
Reduced motion shows the letters formed, turns digging off, and swaps words instantly.

name: share-sheet
title: Share sheet
description: A Share button that opens into a panel with copy link, access level, channels, and people to send to.
whenToUse: A Share button on a document, design, or board header where people share often.
Sharing flows that combine copy link, access level, and sending to a few recent people.
Posting to a small set of channels, such as Slack or email, with in-place pending and done feedback.
whenNotToUse: Use copy-button when all you need is to copy a URL.
Use dialog when sharing needs a full form, such as roles per person or an email search.
Use popover for a small menu of share targets with no people picker.
accessibility: The trigger has aria-haspopup="dialog"; the open panel is role="dialog" labelled by its title.
Opening moves focus to Copy, sending moves it to Done, and closing returns it to the Share button.
Access options are a listbox of role="option" buttons with aria-selected and roving tabindex.
People are toggle buttons with aria-pressed; chips have a Remove <name> button.
A polite status region announces copies, picks, removals, channel results, and who a share was sent to.
A press outside the component closes the panel without stealing focus.
motion: One shape springs its width, height, and corner radius between the button, the panel, and the confirmation; faces cross with a short blur and scale.
A picked avatar flies from the recent row to its chip on a separate layer, so the scrolling chips row never clips it.
Send with nobody picked shakes the Send to row on a spring; the count in the send button rolls one digit up or down.
Reduced motion jumps the shape to size, swaps faces with a plain fade, skips the avatar flight and the shake, and slows the spinner.

name: sheet-stack
title: Sheet stack
description: Nested sheets that stack with depth, drag to dismiss, and become stacked dialogs on wide screens.
whenToUse: Mobile settings where each row opens a deeper page and back should feel spatial.
Nested pickers, such as choosing a workspace and then a project inside it.
Flows that should be a bottom sheet on phones and a centered dialog on desktop from one declaration.
whenNotToUse: Use dialog for a single confirmation or form with no nested steps.
Use bottom-sheet for one sheet with snap points.
Use multi-step-form when steps are sequential rather than drill-down.
accessibility: Each panel is a dialog labelled by its title and described by description; only the top one is aria-modal, lower ones are inert.
Opening moves focus into the new sheet; popping returns focus to the element that opened it.
The back button names the sheet it returns to; the close button reads "Close all" when more than one sheet is open.
Page scroll is locked while any sheet is open, unless contained.
motion: A new sheet rises from the bottom edge (or eases in as a dialog) while the one below scales back 5%, dims, and peeks above it.
The top sheet follows a vertical drag with rubber banding upward; the sheets below ease back up as it goes and a fling past 35% or 450px/s pops it.
Height changes spring as content changes, and all springs keep velocity when interrupted.
Reduced motion removes the depth scale, lift, and drag physics; sheets fade in and out.

name: skeleton-morph
title: Skeleton morph
description: Loading skeletons that grow into the real content, block by block, instead of swapping.
whenToUse: Profile cards, feeds, and lists that load in under a few seconds.
Dashboards where the layout is known before the data arrives.
Places where a hard swap from gray boxes to content would feel jarring.
whenNotToUse: Use skeleton for long lists of hundreds of rows; layout animation there is costly.
Use a progress indicator when loading takes more than a few seconds.
Avoid it when the loaded layout is unknown in advance.
accessibility: The root is aria-busy while loading and carries a visually hidden status with loadingLabel.
Skeleton shapes are aria-hidden; content is not rendered until it is ready, so nothing half loaded is read.
Blocks keep reading order, so focus order is the same before and after loading.
motion: Blocks resolve one after another in DOM order, 40ms apart by default.

Each placeholder stretches from its skeleton box to the content's measured box on a critically damped spring while it fades; the content sharpens out of a 4px blur underneath. Blocks change in place and never travel across the layout.
The shell eases to its new height and clips while it does, so the card border never jumps.
A calm opacity pulse runs on the skeletons while loading and stops when they resolve.
Going back to loading is immediate, so fast reloads never leave a block stuck halfway.
Reduced motion removes the pulse and the stretch and uses a short crossfade.

name: slot-text
title: Slot text
description: Text and numbers that spin into their new value on staggered slot machine reels.
whenToUse: Pricing toggles, KPI cards, dashboards changing period.
Launch moments, raffles, and reveals.
whenNotToUse: Values that update several times a second.
Long sentences; reels are for short values.
accessibility: The full value is real text in a visually hidden span; the reels are aria-hidden.
announce adds a polite live region for values that change without user action.
motion: Each reel spins with a fast start and a long, soft landing that never passes the target.
Reels stop one after another left to right; blur follows each reel's speed, so fast spins smear and landings are sharp.
A reel's width follows its new character on a critically damped spring, and new characters grow in while removed ones collapse.
Leading symbols such as a currency sign stay on their own reels, and separators stay aligned from the end, so 999 to 1,000 only spins digits.
Changing the value mid-spin restarts from the cell on screen, keeping its offset, so nothing jumps.
Reduced motion swaps values instantly.

name: smart-form-fill
title: Smart form fill
description: A paste-to-fill form card where AI reads an email signature or messy notes and fills a contact field by field. Each value flashes in with a confidence dot, its source lights up in the pasted text, low-confidence guesses ask for review, and Undo puts the old values back.
whenToUse: People paste an email signature, a forwarded message or notes and expect the record to fill itself.
You need visible confidence and an easy review path before AI-filled data is saved.
Onboarding or CRM flows where typing six fields by hand is the main friction.
whenNotToUse: Plain data entry with no unstructured source; use form-field and input.
Long multi-page applications; use multi-step-form and add a paste step to one page.
Bulk imports of many records; use a table import flow instead of one card.
accessibility: A polite live region announces each step: reading, how many fields were filled, which need review, checks, undo and save. With the default extractor it adds that the run was simulated.
Each filled input carries an aria-description with its confidence and, for low-confidence fields, the reason. Fields that need review are aria-invalid until checked or edited.
Status is never color alone: confidence shows a dot plus a percentage or a word (Review, Checked, Edited); the footer pairs an icon with text.
The check button inside a review field has a label naming the field. Save focuses the first field that still needs review.
The pasted text view is a focusable, labelled region so keyboard users can scroll it.
motion: Fields fill in form order 140ms apart. Each value fades in over 200ms and the input breathes an accent tint for 900ms; no movement, no size change.
The source span for the field being filled, hovered or focused takes a stronger tint (160ms), so cause and effect read across the card.
Labels, badges, the logo and status swap with one crossfade: out in 100ms, in over 160ms with a 2px rise. The reading label uses a calm shimmer.
Reduced motion fills every field at once, drops the tint animation and the autoplay loop, and keeps all end states. Autoplay pauses while the card is off screen.

name: social-proof-toast
title: Social proof toast
description: A stack of social proof notifications for landing and pricing pages, where recent trials, upgrades and verified purchases from people and companies arrive every few seconds. The stack pauses and fans out on hover, and visitors can dismiss any toast.
whenToUse: Showing recent trials, purchases or upgrades on a landing or pricing page.
A live activity feed for a launch or waitlist page (people joining, teams upgrading).
Highlighting verified purchases from known companies near a checkout CTA.
whenNotToUse: System feedback after a user action (saved, copied, failed): use toast or undo-toast.
Inside a signed in product where activity is not marketing: use an activity feed list.
When you do not have real events to show; fabricated social proof erodes trust.
accessibility: The stack is a labelled region (Recent activity). New toasts are not announced, so screen reader users are not interrupted every few seconds; dismissals are confirmed in a polite status.
Each dismiss button names the toast it closes, such as Dismiss: Sofia started a Pro trial.
Toasts behind the stack limit are aria-hidden and inert. Hover and keyboard focus both pause the cycle, so nothing moves while someone reads or acts.
The verified state is an icon plus a text label, never color alone. Portraits use empty alt text because the name is in the sentence.
motion: A new toast rises 16px and fades in at the front while the others step back 10px and scale down 5% each. Every move uses a bounce free spring (visual duration 0.24s); content of covered toasts fades out in 160ms so text never overlaps.
Hover or focus fans the stack out with the same spring; dismissing fades and slightly shrinks the toast in 160ms and the rest close the gap.
Toasts have a fixed 64px height, so nothing resizes between states.
Reduced motion keeps the stack and the cycle but drops travel: toasts only fade.
The cycle pauses off screen (IntersectionObserver) and in background tabs.

name: source-cards
title: Source cards
description: A row of cited sources under an AI answer where cards stream in with real site marks while the model searches, the overflow collapses into a stack of favicons, hovering lifts a preview with the passage, and an inline [n] citation highlights its card.
whenToUse: Citations under an AI search or docs assistant answer.
Showing live search progress ("Searching 3 of 8") while an agent browses.
Linking inline [n] references in generated text to the pages they came from.
whenNotToUse: A full search results page with many results and filters; use a list layout instead.
Tool calls with arguments and outputs; use tool-call.
A single link preview inside prose; use a tooltip or hover card.
accessibility: The cards are a labelled list (aria-label "Sources") marked aria-busy while searching; skeleton slots are hidden from assistive technology.
A polite live region announces status changes once: searching for the query, the number found, no sources, or the failure. Counts do not announce on every card.
Each card's name reads number, title and domain, and says when it opens in a new tab. The preview is a tooltip linked with aria-describedby while open.
SourceCitation is a real button named "Source 2: Request: text() method, developer.mozilla.org"; its highlighted state is never color alone because the card also gains an outline.
Status always pairs an icon with words: spinner and Searching, globe and the count, alert and Search failed, crossed search and No sources found.
The demo says in a live region that the search is simulated and that card clicks open nothing.
motion: Cards fade in with a 4px rise in 180ms as they arrive; skeletons crossfade out in 120ms. Nothing bounces.

Collapsing the stack or a failed search dropping its reserved slots fades the leaving slots in place (120ms) while the stack or card taking their cell fades in, and the row height glides once. Skeleton bars sit on the same 18px lines as the text that replaces them.
Counts roll 5px with tabular numerals in a reserved width; status icons and labels crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in).
The answer's height springs (bounce 0) as it streams so the cards glide down instead of stepping one line at a time; a width change cuts straight to the new height.
Previews open after a 320ms hover intent, then switch instantly between cards; they fade and rise 4px with a 0.98 scale in 160ms.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and highlight but drops the rise, scale and skeleton pulse. The demo pauses off screen.

name: speculative-decoding
title: Speculative decoding
description: An illustration of speculative decoding: a fast draft model guesses a few tokens, the target model checks them in one pass, and accepted guesses join the answer.
whenToUse: Explaining why a product answers faster: docs, model pages, inference dashboards and blog posts about latency.
Showing a recorded speculative run from your own server, with acceptance and tokens per pass for a chosen draft length.
Teaching the trade off between draft length, acceptance rate and speedup with a slider people can try.
whenNotToUse: Use text-stream to show an answer streaming to a user; this card explains the mechanism behind the speed.
Use token-inspector to look at token probabilities and alternatives for one answer.
Use model-router to explain how requests are sent to different models; speculative decoding runs two models on every request.
Use attention-map or mixture-of-experts for what happens inside a single forward pass.
accessibility: The card is a named group. The lanes are hidden from assistive technology and summarized in hidden text once each round has its verdicts: what the draft proposed, how many the target accepted and which token it wrote instead.
Each output line carries the text written so far as its accessible name, so a screen reader reads words instead of tokens.
Stats are a description list with spoken values ("2.6 times", "67 percent"); the rolling digits are decorative.
Verdicts never rely on color: accepted columns show a check, the rejected guess is struck through with an x beside the target's token, and discarded guesses fade.
A polite live region announces play, pause, restart, the comparison, a new draft length with its expected acceptance and speedup, and the finished result. It never announces every round.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Draft chips appear one by one, fading in from 4px to the left, with a short shimmer on the text while they wait.
The target's sweep fills each cell in order from a per frame CSS variable; verdict icons and the replacement token crossfade in as the sweep reaches them, and the strike draws from the left.

Accepted tokens and the target's token travel from their chips into their slot in the answer on a critically damped spring, about 20ms apart. The answer is laid out in full from the start, so the line never reflows.
Lane height follows wrapping chips on the smooth spring; the target only line opens and closes on the same spring. Stats roll per digit with tabular numerals.
Status text swaps with a short crossfade; no character morphs, blur or typewriter effects.
Reduced motion never autoplays; when played, tokens appear in place without travel, the sweep steps per column, and the shimmer, slide and rolls are off.

name: speech-player
title: Speech player
description: A read-aloud player for AI replies. The Read aloud button in the message's action row turns into a compact player with play, a scrubbable progress bar, speed and a voice picker, and a highlight follows the spoken word through the reply, karaoke style.
whenToUse: A chat or answer surface where people want a reply read out, with the spoken word followed in the text.
Accessibility and hands free reading for long AI answers, summaries or briefings.
Previewing TTS voices and speeds against real product copy.
whenNotToUse: Use dictation-button to turn speech into text in a composer.
Use a plain audio player for podcasts or long recordings without a transcript to highlight.
accessibility: The player is a labelled group. The play button's name follows its state: Play, Pause, Play again, Retry, or Preparing audio (aria-disabled while a request is in flight).
The progress bar is a slider with a value text such as "0:04 of 0:22", updated once a second rather than every frame.
A polite status region announces what changed: reading with Ava at 1× (simulated, no audio plays), paused at 0:12, switching to Leo, finished, the failure message, speed changes and feedback.
Status never relies on color: the error pairs an alert icon with "Couldn't generate audio" and the reason; dimmed upcoming words keep body contrast and are only a progress cue.
Read aloud is described by the reply text. The voice menu uses menuitemradio items with aria-checked and opens with focus on the selected voice.
The hidden layer of the dock is inert, so Tab never lands on a control that is not visible. Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus uses Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: Read aloud and Stop reading crossfade the action row and the player in the same 32px slot (out in 100ms, in 160ms with a 2px rise), so the card never changes size.

The word highlight is one rect that glides between words on a line in 150ms at 1× (about 100ms at 1.5× and 75ms at 2×, so it always lands before the next word) and cuts to the next line instead of sweeping across it. Spoken words fade from dimmed to full color.
The progress bar fill and thumb are written straight to transforms on each animation frame; the track thickens and the thumb scales in on hover, focus and drag.
Play, pause, replay, retry and the spinner swap in place with a bounce free scale and fade. Speed and voice labels crossfade over hidden copies of every option, so their buttons never resize.
The preparing label carries a calm shimmer. Reduced motion keeps every state and announcement, drops the glide, the shimmer and the sample loop, and moves the highlight instantly.

name: starter-prompts
title: Starter prompts
description: A greeting and a grid of starter cards for the empty state of an AI app. The cards are grouped into Write, Code, Analyze and Plan tabs, and a shuffle swaps them with a short staggered crossfade. Picking a card fills the composer, and cards that use a connected app show its mark (Gmail, GitHub, Notion, Linear, Google Calendar).
whenToUse: The empty state of a chat, copilot or agent, before the first message.
Teaching what an assistant can do with connected tools, such as Gmail, GitHub or Notion.
Onboarding a new workspace with a few tailored, ready to send prompts.
whenNotToUse: Inside a running conversation; use follow-up suggestion chips in the chat thread instead.
A command launcher with search; use command-palette or ai-command.
A single inline suggestion in a text field; use ghost-text.
accessibility: The component is a labelled section; the greeting is its heading.
Each card is a button whose name includes the title, the connected app and the category.
A polite live region announces picks, shuffles, sending, done and errors, and says when a send is simulated.
Status is never color alone: done shows a check and label, errors an alert icon and the message.
The send button is labelled Send message, and Stop sending while a message is in flight.
motion: Shuffle and tab changes crossfade each card's content inside a fixed frame: out in 100ms, in over 160ms with a 2px rise, staggered 35ms per card (about 100ms in total).
Picking a card focuses the composer and fades the new text in over 160ms.
The footer status and the send or stop icon crossfade; nothing moves or resizes.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and cuts the fades and the skeleton breathing.

examples.title: Your own starters and tabs
examples.code:
<StarterPrompts
  categories={[{ id: "support", label: "Support" }, { id: "sales", label: "Sales" }]}
  prompts={[
    { id: "refund", category: "support", app: "gmail", title: "Answer refund requests", description: "Draft replies for the 6 open threads", prompt: "Draft replies to the 6 open refund threads in Gmail..." },
    { id: "pipeline", category: "sales", title: "Review the pipeline", description: "Deals that slipped this month", prompt: "List the deals that slipped in October and why..." },
  ]}
  model={{ name: "GPT-6.1 Sol", mark: <OpenAIMark width={14} height={14} /> }}
/>

name: sticker-peel
title: Sticker peel
description: Peel stickers off a surface with a real curl, move them around, and stick them back down.
whenToUse: A personal or team page where people arrange badges, achievements, or brand stickers.
A launch or marketing moment that invites people to play with the product's marks.
A reward screen where earned stickers are placed on a surface.
whenNotToUse: Use reorderable-list or a sortable grid when the order of items carries meaning.
Use note-stack for content people need to read and rearrange.
Avoid it on dense work screens; it is a delight surface, not an input.
accessibility: The surface is a labelled group; each sticker is a button with aria-roledescription="sticker", its label, and aria-pressed while carried.
A visually hidden description explains the keyboard path, and a polite status region announces peeled off, picked up, stuck down, and put back.
Sticker artwork is aria-hidden; the label carries the meaning.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring. The lift and shadow of a carried sticker show which one is active.
motion: The peel is a real fold: the pulled part is mirrored across the fold line with clip-path and foreshortened a touch, showing a plain paper backing with one soft shade at the bend and a light shadow that always falls downward.

Circles peel from the point of the rim nearest the pointer; rounded shapes and pills peel from a corner along its diagonal. The fold may lean at most 35 degrees, so it is always a short, clean corner.
Hovering with a mouse lifts the nearest corner a few pixels past the outline. Moving to another corner lays the first one flat before lifting the next.
All springs are critically damped: the paper trails the finger slightly and settles without overshoot, bounce, or swing.
It comes off once the fold passes the middle, sooner on a quick tug, or once the hand has clearly carried it away. It then rises 3% with a soft shadow and follows the hand at its own angle.
Dropping lands it exactly where it is on screen and the shadow fades in 200ms. Grabbing it again while it settles catches it in place.
Reduced motion skips the peel and hover lift; pressing picks the sticker up directly and it follows the pointer 1:1.

name: stretch-refresh
title: Stretch refresh
description: Pull a feed down and a line stretches to tell you when to let go.
whenToUse: Timelines, inboxes, and activity feeds where new entries arrive at the top.
Panels that should support pull to refresh by touch, mouse drag, and trackpad scroll.
whenNotToUse: Use a plain list for static content that never refreshes.
Use pagination for paging through older items.
Use timeline for a static history of events.
accessibility: A refresh button gives keyboard and switch users the same path as the pull gesture, with aria-disabled while busy.
The feed is a labelled, focusable region and the list sets aria-busy while refreshing.
"Refreshing" and the result are announced in a polite status region.
motion: The sheet rubber-bands with growing resistance while rows spread apart; scrolling up again at the top also pulls.
A line in the gap reaches full length exactly at the threshold, runs while refreshing, then gives way to the result as new rows settle in from the top.
Reduced motion keeps the same states and only fades.

examples.title: Fill the height of a sidebar
examples.code:
<aside style={{ display: "flex", flexDirection: "column", height: "100dvh" }}>
  <StretchRefresh
    title="Activity"
    items={events}
    getKey={e => e.id}
    renderItem={e => <EventRow event={e} />}
    onRefresh={reload}
    className="grow"
  />
</aside>

name: team-switcher
title: Team switcher
description: A workspace switcher like Linear, Vercel or Slack. The trigger shows the current workspace's logo and plan. The menu has search, your role in each workspace and a Cmd+1 to 9 shortcut for each, and lets you create or join a workspace inline. A highlight glides between rows, and switching crossfades the trigger through a short loading state.
whenToUse: Switching between organizations, teams or workspaces in a multi-tenant SaaS app.
An account or project picker that needs search, roles and keyboard shortcuts.
Letting people create a new workspace or accept an invite without leaving the current page.
whenNotToUse: Picking from a short static list of options in a form: use a select or segmented control.
Global navigation across pages and commands: use the command palette block.
Switching between two or three views of the same data: use tabs.
accessibility: The trigger is a button with aria-haspopup="dialog", aria-expanded and aria-busy while switching; its label reads the workspace and its plan.
The search field is a combobox that owns a listbox and points at the highlighted row with aria-activedescendant, so focus never leaves the field while navigating.
The current workspace is aria-selected and marked with a check icon, not color alone. Errors pair an icon with text.
A polite live region announces switching, the result, and when an action was simulated ("Simulated, nothing was sent").
Closing with Escape or by choosing returns focus to the trigger. Tabbing out or clicking outside closes the menu.
motion: The menu fades and scales in from 98% over 180ms and leaves in 120ms.
One highlight glides between rows with a bounce-free spring (visualDuration 0.24) and appears in place instead of sliding in from the top.
Switching crossfades the trigger's logo, name and plan line (100ms out, 160ms in, 2px y) through a shimmer label and a spinner. Nothing resizes.
The create and join views crossfade inside a fixed-height panel with a 6px horizontal shift that follows the navigation direction.
Reduced motion keeps the crossfades and feedback as plain fades and drops the glide, shifts and scale.

name: ticket-router
title: Ticket router
description: A support ticket router where messages from Gmail, Intercom, Slack and Zendesk come in one at a time. An AI classifier labels each one with intent, sentiment and confidence, and the ticket moves into a team lane with an assignee. Low confidence tickets wait in a review lane, and one click there routes them to the suggested team.
whenToUse: Showing how an AI classifier triages inbound support messages into team queues.
A live triage widget in a helpdesk or ops dashboard, with a human review lane for low confidence.
Landing page or onboarding demos of AI routing for support products.
whenNotToUse: A full ticket inbox with search and bulk actions; use a table or list layout.
A single tool step in a chat transcript; use tool-call.
Generic multi step agent progress; use agent-status or agent-plan.
accessibility: The card is a section labelled by its title. Each lane is a list labelled with its name and ticket count.
