A polite live region announces each routing ("routed to Billing, assigned to Andre Williams"), failures, pauses and review confirmations, and says when the run is simulated and nothing was sent.
Intent, sentiment and review status always pair an icon with a text label; confidence reads as a percentage, never color alone.
Review tickets are real buttons with a label naming the subject, confidence and target lane.
motion: About two seconds per ticket: arrive 220ms, classify, labels fade in with a 50ms stagger, then a pulse draws along the connector to the target lane in 240ms and the row lands.
Rows enter and leave by animating their measured height with a bounce free spring (visualDuration .24). Counters roll in reserved tabular width.
Ticket swaps are a single crossfade: out in 100ms, in over 160ms with a small rise. No blur, no per letter motion.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and the landing highlight, and drops travel, rises and the connector draw. The flow pauses off screen.

name: ticket-tear
title: Ticket tear
description: Pull a ticket stub and it tears along the perforation hole by hole, then drops away.
whenToUse: Event tickets, boarding passes, and coupons that are used once.
A playful confirmation step where tearing means committing.
whenNotToUse: Use hold-to-confirm or a dialog for destructive actions that need clear wording.
Use a plain card for tickets that are only displayed, not redeemed.
accessibility: The stub is role="button" with the label as its name.
The flap copy of the stub used for the bend is aria-hidden, so the stub is read once.
A polite status announces "Stub torn off".
motion: Pulling down or away tears the perforation from the top, tracking the pointer directly; the tear only grows, like real paper.
The edge passes through the center of each hole and wanders between them, coarse and fine, with loose paper fibers just past it on both sides.
The loose flap follows the pull on a spring, so it has weight, and springs most of the way back when released mid-tear.
Enter, Space or the torn prop rip the rest on their own, accelerating like a perforation that has started to give; a flick finishes it even faster.
Freed, the stub pops up a hair, falls with gravity, drifts with the release speed, spins on a spring, and fades in about half a second.
Touch devices get a tiny vibration as the tear crosses each hole, where supported.
Reduced motion removes the bend, the fibers and the fall; the stub fades out.

name: time-dial
title: Time dial
description: Spin a dial to pick an hour and see which team cities are at work.
whenToUse: Planning a moment across two to five cities, such as calls, releases, or handovers.
Distributed teams that need to see at a glance who is inside working hours.
whenNotToUse: Use time-picker for a single local time.
Use date-picker or calendar when the day matters more than the hour.
Use slider for a plain numeric range.
accessibility: The dial is a focusable role="slider" with aria-valuenow in home-city minutes and a spoken aria-valuetext.
The city list uses buttons with aria-pressed for the home city.
Changes are announced through a polite live region; the SVG face and readout are aria-hidden.
motion: Drags have soft quarter-hour detents, flicks coast on a spring into the nearest quarter hour, and bounds rubber-band.
Readout digits roll like an odometer, city marks swap between knob and dot as the home city changes, and the sun and moon turn over at the day/night boundary.
Reduced motion removes flick coasting and replaces rises and blurs with plain fades.

name: tldr-toggle
title: TL;DR toggle
description: An article card with a Full, Summary and Key points switch and a length slider. Switching streams an AI summary in place of the article as the card's height springs to fit, and each key point links back to the paragraph it came from, which gets scrolled to and highlighted.
whenToUse: Offering a quick summary or key points above or in place of a long article, doc or report.
Letting readers verify AI claims against the source, through key points that link back to paragraphs.
Reading surfaces where people choose how much detail they want with a length control.
whenNotToUse: Open-ended questions about content: use an answer or chat component such as ai-answer.
Short content under a couple of paragraphs, where a summary saves no time.
Summaries of many documents at once: use a list or a digest layout instead of one card per item.
accessibility: The card is an article with the title as a heading. The mode switch is a labelled group of pressed buttons, the length is a slider whose spoken value is the target ("~60 words", "4 points"), disabled in Full mode.

A polite live region announces each run once ("Summarizing with Claude Haiku 5.5", "Summary ready, 58 words", "4 key points ready", "Stopped"), never the streamed chunks. With the simulation it adds "Simulated, nothing was sent".
The card is aria-busy while a result streams. Failures render as an alert with the message and a Try again button.

Jump links are named after their point ("Jump to paragraph 3: Partial bootstrapping loads..."), and the jump moves focus to the highlighted paragraph so screen reader and keyboard users land where the eye does.
Status is never color alone: done, stopped and failed each pair an icon with a word, and key points tick from a dashed circle to a check.
motion: The body's height follows its content on one critically damped spring (visualDuration .26, no bounce), whether a view swaps or text streams in. A container resize cuts straight to the new height.
Views swap with a single crossfade: old out in 100ms, new in over 160ms. The footer's state label and actions crossfade the same way.
Streamed chunks of 3 to 8 words arrive every 30 to 40ms and only fade in over 140ms. A cached result appears whole, with no fade.
Thinking lasts about 0.7s with a calm shimmer on its label; the footer's Writing label shimmers while text arrives, so only one shimmer runs at a time.
A jump waits for the height to settle, scrolls smoothly to the paragraph and fades a highlight in over 160ms and out over 600ms.
Reduced motion drops the height spring, the chunk fades, smooth scrolling and the icon transitions; every end state and the highlight remain.

name: tone-tuner
title: Tone tuner
description: A brand voice card where two sliders (formality and detail) and Friendly, Confident and Empathetic chips rewrite a customer reply. Each changed sentence crossfades in place, new words can be highlighted against the original, and Copy takes the current version.
whenToUse: A composer or help desk reply that offers AI tone controls before sending.
Brand voice tooling where marketers compare versions of the same copy.
Any rewrite where people want to steer with a few dials rather than write a prompt.
whenNotToUse: Free form AI editing with a prompt box: use a chat or composer instead.
Long documents: the card is sized for a message of a few paragraphs.
Exact line by line code or contract diffs: use a dedicated diff view.
accessibility: Voice chips are toggle buttons with aria-pressed inside a group named Voice.
Each slider is named (Formality, Detail) and speaks its level name, not a number.
A polite live region announces each landed rewrite with its settings, says when the sample is simulated (nothing was sent), and reports failures.
Highlighted words use a mark element and the header counts the changed words, so changes are not shown by color alone.
Status pairs an icon with a short label: Original draft, Rewriting, Rewritten or Couldn't rewrite with a Retry button.
motion: Each changed sentence fades out in 100ms, swaps while invisible and fades in over 160ms; all changed sentences swap on the same frame, so the paragraph reflows once, out of sight. Unchanged sentences never animate.

The text area reserves the height of the longest voice at the current formality and detail, so switching voice never resizes the card; a slider move eases it to the new height on a bounce free spring.
The status flips to Rewriting on the same frame as the input, with a calm shimmer, then crossfades to Rewritten.
The self playing tour pauses off screen and stops at the first interaction. Reduced motion swaps text instantly and skips the tour.

name: tool-call
title: Tool call
description: A tool call row for agent transcripts: the tool's mark and the call in plain words, a live state while it runs, and the input and output a click away, with approval and retry when needed.
whenToUse: Showing what tools an AI agent used inside a chat or agent transcript, with the arguments and results one click away.
Human in the loop actions where a call must be allowed or denied inline before it runs, such as posting a message or writing to a database.
Making failures recoverable in place: a timed out query with its reason and a Retry button.
Debug and audit views where developers need to copy exact tool inputs and outputs.
whenNotToUse: Use agent-run for a full multi step run with a plan, a timeline and live logs rather than inline rows in a message.
Use agent-approvals for a queue of pending approvals across many agents and runs.
Use research-run when the work is mostly web research with sources and a streamed report.
Use mcp-servers to manage which tools an agent can reach, not to show individual calls.
accessibility: The group header and every call row are real buttons with aria-expanded and aria-controls; a row's name reads the tool, the verb phrase and the status, such as "GitHub: Searched issues in arc-ui/web Done, 4 results, 1.2s".
Status is never color alone: each status has its own icon shape (spinner, check, alert, shield, ban), failed and waiting calls show a reason line, and the row name spells the status out.
Each call announces its status changes through a polite live region, including that the preview only simulates an action when no handler is passed.
Allow, Deny and Retry are labelled with the call they act on, such as "Allow: Post a summary to #release".
The input list is a description list; tables keep table semantics with column headers. Folded rows and lines are hidden from assistive technology until shown.
Copy buttons confirm success or failure in place and through a live region, without changing width.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared ring, inset inside rows so it is never clipped.
motion: Opening a row, opening the group and showing more lines animate height on the critically damped smooth spring, with a short opacity fade; chevrons turn on the shared CSS spring.
Opening the group staggers its rows in 20ms apart with a 6px settle. Rows appended by a live run grow in from zero height instead, so nothing below them jumps.
A row's height follows its content on the same spring when a reason line or wrapped actions appear, so a status change never resizes in one frame.
Status icons trade places with a snappy scale and fade; the success check draws itself once. The running title uses the text shimmer and settles to solid when the call finishes.
The mark stack widens on the morph spring as a new tool joins, so the header label glides instead of jumping.
Reduced motion removes the stagger, spinner rotation, shimmer travel and springs. Panels, rows and statuses change immediately and every label, announcement and focus path stays.

name: training-run
title: Training run
description: A fine-tuning job card where a live train and validation loss curve draws across a fixed step axis that doubles as the epoch progress bar. It shows the learning rate, elapsed time, ETA and the latest evals and checkpoints, has Pause and Cancel while it runs, and ends in results with a Deploy button.
whenToUse: A fine-tuning or training job page in an AI platform, where people watch loss, pause, cancel and deploy.
An eval or distillation run that reports a loss curve, checkpoints and a final score.
A product onboarding step that trains a custom model on the customer's data and ends in a deploy.
whenNotToUse: A generic multi-series chart with no job lifecycle: use line-chart.
A short agent task with steps rather than a loss curve: use agent-status.
Explaining how training works conceptually: use model-training.
accessibility: A polite live region announces status changes (Queued, Training, Paused, Completed, Failed, Deployed) and any notice, never every step.
Status is an icon plus a label, never color alone; the failure reason is text in the footer and in the event log.
The chart is a labelled group whose name carries the current step and both losses; the arrow keys inspect samples and the legend reads them out visually.
Cancel is a two step action so a stray press never stops a long run. Deploy keeps focus while loading.
Stats are a description list; event steps and numbers use tabular numerals.
motion: The curve and epoch segments ease toward each new sample every frame (exponential, 120ms), so data arriving in bursts still draws at an even pace with no jumps. A rollback or reset jumps instantly.
The y axis is fixed from the first samples and the x axis spans the whole run, so nothing rescales mid-run.
New events slide the list down with one bounce-free spring (0.24s); status, stats and footer text crossfade (100ms out, 160ms in, 2px rise).
Reduced motion: the curve jumps to each sample, the spinner and shimmer stop, and crossfades become instant.
The demo simulation freezes while the card is off screen.

name: trial-banner
title: Trial banner
description: A trial status banner where a ring counts down the days left, the copy names what the workspace loses, and the upgrade path is one click away. It comes as a slim banner, a sidebar card or a header pill. It shifts to a warning tone in the last days, has expired and upgraded states, and folds into the pill when dismissed or snoozed.
whenToUse: A SaaS app with a free trial that needs a quiet, always visible upgrade path.
Telling a workspace what it loses when the trial ends and nudging harder in the last days.
Showing an expired trial without blocking the app.
whenNotToUse: A hard paywall that blocks a feature; use a modal or an upgrade screen instead.
Generic announcements or release notes; use a plain banner or toast.
Usage limits (credits, seats); use a usage meter.
accessibility: The banner and card are labelled regions ("Pro trial"); the ring is decorative and the days are always in the text.
A polite live region announces billing, snooze and dismiss results, and says when an action was simulated.
Status never relies on color: the warning tone also changes the copy to name the end day, expired shows a lock, upgraded a check.
After dismiss or snooze, focus moves to the trial pill; reopening it moves focus to the primary action.
motion: The ring arc springs to its new length with no bounce (0.24s); its color follows the tone in 160ms.
Copy, days and icons swap with one crossfade (old out in 100ms, new in over 160ms with a 2px rise) in a shared grid cell, so nothing shifts.
Button labels morph their width without bounce; the pill label width springs to the measured text.
Reduced motion keeps every end state and drops the crossfades and springs.

name: typewriter-terminal
title: Typewriter terminal
description: A terminal that types a scripted CLI session with a seeded human cadence, colors the shell syntax, and streams output lines, progress bars and spinners, with a scrubber, play/pause and replay controls.
whenToUse: A landing page hero or install section for a developer tool, SDK, or CLI.
Docs quick starts that show what each command prints before people run it.
Changelog or launch posts that show a new command in action.
whenNotToUse: Use code-block for commands and source that people need to read and copy without waiting.
Use log-stream for real, live output from a running process.
Use code-magic-move to show how a file changes between versions.
accessibility: The root is a figure named by label. The animated screen is hidden from assistive technology, and a visually hidden ordered list gives the full transcript: every command and what it printed.

The scrubber is a real slider with role="slider", its value in seconds, and a value text that names the current step and command. Arrow keys and Page keys jump to the previous or next command, Home and End go to the start and end, and Space or K plays and pauses.

Play, pause, and replay are real buttons with specific names. Seeking, pausing, and replaying are announced in a polite live region. Autoplay is not announced, so the loop never floods a screen reader.
Status never relies on color alone: success, warning, and danger lines carry an icon, tasks show a tick, and progress shows a percentage.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One rAF loop derives the whole screen from a single session time and writes attributes, text, transforms, and opacity straight to the DOM, only when a value changed. React does not render per frame.

Typing follows a seeded human cadence: a short think before the first key, quick bursts inside words, small stalls on shifted keys and word breaks. The caret stays solid while keys land and blinks softly while it waits.

Each output line rises a few pixels and fades in. Progress bars fill with a quick start, a stall around the middle, and a steady finish, with a tabular percentage. Spinners cycle braille frames and resolve to a tick.
The screen follows the newest line on a critically damped spring, and only measures when the visible text changes. The top edge feathers lines away as they scroll off.

Scrubbing is direct: the session follows the pointer exactly, text untypes and retypes, and a release within a few pixels of a command start settles onto it. Keyboard jumps and replay glide through time on an ease in out curve, so replay visibly rewinds the session.

Play and pause ease the playback rate on a spring instead of stopping in one frame. The loop clears upward while the scrubber glides back, so it never jumps. The loop stops off screen and in hidden tabs. With reduced motion the finished session shows at once, the caret stops blinking, and the scrubber still jumps between steps.

name: upgrade-prompt
title: Upgrade prompt
description: An upgrade nudge for the moment someone hits a limit. It shows a usage meter at 50 of 50 AI credits, a rolling price with a monthly and yearly toggle, three concrete unlocks with real model marks, and Upgrade or Maybe later. Upgrading leads into a success state with the new limits, and the card never changes size between states.
whenToUse: An AI product that hits a usage limit (credits, generations, seats) and needs a tasteful, conversion focused nudge.
A paywall moment inside an app, in a dialog, popover or inline in place of the blocked result.
Offering one next plan with a monthly and yearly price.
whenNotToUse: Comparing several plans side by side: use a pricing table or plan picker.
Buying prepaid credits without a plan change: use credit-topup.
Passive usage reporting on a billing page: use a usage meter.
accessibility: The card is a labelled section ("Upgrade to Pro") with a heading, so it reads well inside a dialog or popover.
The usage bar is role="meter" with a value text such as "50 of 50 AI credits used".
Status is an icon plus a label (Limit reached, 1,950 AI credits left), never color alone.
A polite live region announces upgrading, success and errors. Without onUpgrade it says the upgrade is simulated and nothing was charged.
The rolling price is aria-hidden with a plain text copy for screen readers. Inactive states are inert and hidden, so focus never lands on a faded panel.
Upgrade stays focusable while processing (aria-busy) so keyboard focus is not lost.
motion: The usage bar fills once when it scrolls into view and settles to the new limit after the upgrade on a 0.5s bounce-free spring, moved with transform so its rounded end never stretches.
The price rolls digit by digit between monthly and yearly on a 0.28s spring, in tabular numerals so nothing shifts.
Title, description, meter label and counts crossfade: 100ms out, 160ms in with a 2px rise. Panels fade the same way with a 4px rise.
Every variant and panel shares one grid cell, so the card never changes size between offer, processing, error, success and reminder, and the buttons stay in place.
Reduced motion: the bar and price jump to their values; crossfades become plain fades.

name: vector-search
title: Vector search
description: Documents drop onto a tilted embedding plane and fold into points that cluster by topic; the index links neighbours, a query is typed, embedded and lowered onto the plane, a signal hops along the graph toward it, and a widening ring lights the nearest documents with connecting lines, similarity scores and a ranked list.
whenToUse: A feature section on semantic search, AI answers, or retrieval over a team's docs.
Docs pages introducing embeddings, nearest neighbour search, or approximate indexes.
whenNotToUse: Use search-index to explain keyword search with an inverted index.
Use a real scatter or cluster chart to show an actual embedding projection.
accessibility: The plane and its legend form one element with role="img" and an aria-label that explains the idea with the real values: how many documents cluster into which topics, the query, how many hops the search takes, and each match with its similarity score.
The step bar is a group of real buttons named for each stage, with aria-current on the playing stage, plus a named play and pause button.
Nothing relies on color alone: clusters carry name chips, matches are written out as a ranked list with titles, sources, and scores, and the counters are plain numbers.
Points are not controls, so nothing else enters the tab order; hover tags only repeat the title, topic, and source that the list and label already give.
Pointer focus draws no ring; keyboard focus shows Arc's shared focus ring.
motion: One rAF loop writes SVG transforms, opacity, dash lengths, and a few text nodes straight to the DOM, and only when a value changed; React does not render per frame.

The whole story is a pure function of time, so the loop repeats seamlessly: pages fall and fold into points, clusters and links draw in, the query is typed and lowered, the signal hops, the ring finds the matches, and the plane clears.
The signal hops along the real shortest route through the index graph, and each hop's duration scales with the link's length, so the pace stays even. Hops arc slightly above the plane.
The ring widens on an eased curve, and each match lights at the exact moment the ring reaches it; the time is solved from the curve, so halo, line, score chip, and ranked row stay in sync.
Speed changes, pausing, and hover (which slows the story a little) ease on a critically damped spring. Readout bars and result bars ease with the standard and considered durations.

The loop stops off screen, in hidden tabs, and when paused. Reduced motion shows the answer as a still frame: every point placed, the path walked, the matches linked and scored; the step bar still jumps between still frames of each stage.

name: voice-orb
title: Voice orb
description: A voice mode orb that listens, thinks, and speaks, with a live transcript and call controls.
whenToUse: A voice mode for an assistant where the user needs to see whether it is listening, thinking, or speaking.
Hands-free or call-like flows that need start, mute, a running clock, and end in one compact control.
Live captions under a speaking agent, via VoiceTranscript.
whenNotToUse: Use voice-recorder when the user records a clip to send or save.
Use chat-thread with text-stream for typed chat where no audio is involved.
Use progress or skeleton for a generic loading state; the orb implies a voice session.
accessibility: The orb is a canvas with role="img" and an aria-label that follows the state (Listening, Thinking, Speaking, Muted).
VoiceTranscript hides the animated words and announces only the completed turn through a polite live region.
The mute button uses aria-pressed and switches its label between Mute and Unmute microphone; the clock is role="timer" with a spoken minutes and seconds label.
Focus moves to mute when a session starts and back to start when it ends, so keyboard users never lose their place.
motion: Nine shape parameters (breath, wobble, swirl, tint, ring, and more) follow the state on a hand-rolled spring each frame, so state changes interrupt cleanly.
Listening swells with the input level and draws two ripple rings; speaking pulses with the output level; thinking contracts into a slow swirl.
The controls pill springs its width to fit while the start button and live controls crossfade with a small scale and blur.
Reduced motion stops the rAF loop and draws one still frame per state; transcript and controls fall back to short opacity fades.

name: voice-recorder
title: Voice recorder
description: Record with a live waveform, review and scrub, then send the take into the thread.
whenToUse: Voice notes in chats, comments, or field notes where speaking beats typing.
A thread of voice bubbles with playback and scrubbing.
whenNotToUse: Use now-playing for music or long-form audio.
Use hold-to-confirm for press-and-hold actions that do not record.
Use stopwatch to time something without audio.
accessibility: The recorder is a labelled section with a labelled message list; every control is a native button with an aria-label, such as "Stop recording at 0:04" or "Play voice message from Sam, 0:07".
Recording, review, send, and discard are announced in a polite live region that also describes the mic.
Waveforms, the live canvas, and timers are aria-hidden; the button labels carry the durations.
motion: Mic, recording bar, review, and sent bubble share one layout id, so a take morphs from the mic into the thread on a spring.
The live waveform scrolls on a canvas and playback fills the bars left to right; side buttons pop in and content crossfades with a slight blur.
Motion follows the user's reduced motion setting: layout morphs are skipped, the waveform steps instead of growing, and the thread scrolls without smoothing.

name: wallet-stack
title: Wallet stack
description: Fan a stack of cards and lift one out to see its activity.
whenToUse: A few payment cards, passes, or memberships where people open one to see its balance and activity.
Fintech or wallet screens that want a physical card metaphor with realistic materials.
whenNotToUse: Use card-stack for generic swipeable content that is not a card wallet.
Use a plain list or data-grid for many accounts.
Use expandable-card when one card just needs to grow in place.
accessibility: The stack is a labelled group with a described keyboard hint. Only the front card is in the tab order (roving tabindex); each card is a button named by issuer, product, last four digits, position, and balance, with aria-expanded while open.
The masked digits and decorative artwork are hidden from assistive technology; only the last four digits are read.
The activity region is inert until a card is open; the header switches from the card count to an All cards button that closes it.
Cycling and opening are announced in a polite live region, and focus returns to the card when it goes back into the stack.
motion: Every card's transform is one pure function of a continuous stack position, the open amount, and the fan amount, so springs, drags, and interruptions all move the same shape. Z order never changes, so cards never pop over one another.

Hovering fans the stack upward on a no-overshoot spring; the hovered card rises out of the fan and its shadow deepens. The front card tilts up to 5 degrees and a specular highlight follows the pointer, or device tilt on phones that report it.

Dragging down pushes the front card into the pocket at the bottom and brings the next one forward one to one under the pointer; dragging up pulls it back. A flick lands where its momentum projects, one card at a time, with rubber banding past the first and last card.

Choosing a card lifts it to the top on one critically damped spring while the others tuck into the pocket; its balance counts up and three transactions stagger in. Pull the open card down to put it back, or flick it.

Only transform and opacity animate: shadows fade their opacity, the light moves a pre-painted layer. MotionConfig and a reduced motion branch remove travel, tilt, and the light; state changes apply instantly.

name: in-view-title
title: In-view title
description: Bring a section title in as it scrolls into view.
whenToUse: Section headings that should animate once they scroll into view.
Feature pages where each section title needs a consistent entrance style.
Headings that should replay on each entry, via once={false}.
whenNotToUse: Use text-reveal for hero copy that animates on load.
Use scroll-highlight for a paragraph that follows scroll progress.
Use text-shimmer for status lines, not headings.
accessibility: The heading carries aria-label with the full text; the animated parts are aria-hidden.
Titles already scrolled past show immediately, and server-rendered titles appear on their own if scripts are slow.
Choose as to match the page's heading outline.
motion: Triggers when 45% of the title is visible. Opacity leads, blur clears next, and the transform settles last, so text is readable before it fully arrives.
Hiding (with once={false}) is a quick fade with no stagger.
Reduced motion shows the title instantly with no transform, blur, or mask.

demo.tail: e=>(0,l.jsx)(e.InViewTitle,{text:"Reveal text when it enters the viewport.",as:"h2",variant:"blur"})

name: text-morph
title: Text morph
description: Morph a label into its next state, letter by letter.
whenToUse: Status words that change a few letters at a time, such as Follow and Following.
Custom buttons or badges that need a morphing label without the rest of the button.
Inline counters or short state labels that should glide instead of jump.
whenNotToUse: Use word-rotate for a sentence with one cycling word.
Use button or action-swap when you want the morph plus button behaviour.
Avoid it for text that wraps, since it always renders a single line.
accessibility: The plain label is in a visually hidden span; the animated glyphs are aria-hidden.
It does not announce changes. Wrap it in your own aria-live region if a status change must be announced.
motion: Letters are matched by character and occurrence, so shared letters glide to their new positions on a spring while new letters stagger in with a blur.
The frame width springs to the new label; font loading or resizes follow immediately without animating.
Reduced motion swaps the label and width instantly.

name: text-reveal
title: Text reveal
description: Reveal a short piece of content with restrained motion.
whenToUse: Above-the-fold hero headlines that animate on page load.
Landing page intros where text must appear on first paint even if scripts are slow.
whenNotToUse: Use in-view-title for section titles further down the page.
Use scroll-highlight for a key paragraph that reveals with scroll.
Use word-rotate when one word in the headline should cycle.
accessibility: A heading carries the full text as its aria-label and the animated words are aria-hidden, so screen readers and crawlers read one clean sentence. A p keeps a visually hidden copy instead, since a paragraph cannot take a label.
Line breaks are read as spaces.
Pick the heading level with as so the page outline stays correct.
motion: Words rise out of a clip and sharpen from blur on a per-word stagger; total stagger is capped so long text never drags.
The entrance is pure CSS, so text is never left hidden when scripts load slowly.
Reduced motion drops the clip and rise and fades the words in quickly.

demo.tail: e=>(0,l.jsx)(e.TextReveal,{text:"Words blur into focus one by one.",as:"h2"})

name: text-shimmer
title: Text shimmer
description: Show ongoing work with a calm light across the words.
whenToUse: AI thinking or loading labels such as Generating summary.
Short status lines that should show ongoing work and settle when done.
whenNotToUse: Use text-stream for the response text itself.
Use skeleton for content placeholders and progress for measurable progress.
accessibility: Sets aria-busy while active; the text itself stays real, readable text.
Announce completion from your own aria-live region; the component does not.
motion: A bell-shaped highlight band in the current text color sweeps linearly over a muted base, pausing briefly between passes.
The sweep only runs while active, in view, and the page is visible; a paused band resumes where it stopped. A changed label rises in with a soft blur.
Reduced motion stops the sweep and swaps labels with a plain fade.
